response:
<advice>You do not need to break up just because he is poor. But you do need to stop financing him.</advice>
  <advice>The immediate fix is simple: stop paying for his daily expenses, stop offering dates you cannot afford for two people, and stop covering social situations to save face. If he has no money, the plan is not “you pay.” The plan is “we do something free or we don’t go.”</advice>
  <advice>Talk to him directly and plainly. Say something like: “I need to be honest. I can’t afford to keep paying for both of us. I’ve been overspending, using savings, and even lying to my parents about expenses. That has to stop. From now on, I can only pay for myself, and if we go out, it has to be something we both can actually afford.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not soften this into a negotiation about “just this once” lunch, coffee, or birthday events. The pattern is built from many small exceptions. If you leave loopholes, you will end up back in the same situation.</advice>
  <advice>You should also change your planning habits:
    <point>Set a fixed personal budget for the month.</point>
    <point>Do not spend from savings on dates or his food.</point>
    <point>Prefer free or very cheap time together.</point>
    <point>If a group custom like “birthday dinner is on the birthday person” cannot be afforded, decline the event, choose a cheaper option, or be honest with friends.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If he responds with understanding and adjusts, the relationship may be fine. If he pressures you, guilts you, expects continued support, or makes you responsible for managing his embarrassment, then the money problem is revealing a relationship problem, and breaking up would be reasonable.</advice>
  <advice>So: do not break up solely because he is poor. First, set the boundary and change your behavior. Then judge the relationship by how he handles that boundary.</advice>

response:
<advice>You’re describing a trauma response, not irrationality or weakness. Because it has lasted so long and is “near paralyzing,” the most effective path is probably trauma-focused therapy, especially with someone experienced in phobias, PTSD, or exposure therapy.</advice>
  <advice>Look for approaches like CBT with gradual exposure, EMDR, or other trauma-focused therapy. A therapist can help you retrain your body’s alarm response without pushing you too fast.</advice>
  <advice>Do not start by forcing yourself to pet dogs or stand close to them. Start with very low-intensity exposure and only move up gradually. A possible ladder could be:
    <step>Thinking about dogs while practicing slow breathing</step>
    <step>Looking at drawings or photos of calm dogs</step>
    <step>Watching short videos of friendly, predictable dogs</step>
    <step>Seeing a dog from far away in a controlled setting</step>
    <step>Standing at a distance with a calm dog present and a trusted handler</step>
    <step>Moving closer only when your anxiety drops and stays manageable</step>
    <step>Eventually interacting briefly with a very calm, well-trained dog, if and when you’re ready</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>While doing this, use regulation skills so your body learns “I can be near this and stay safe.” Helpful ones include:
    <step>Slow exhale breathing, like inhaling for 4 and exhaling for 6</step>
    <step>Grounding: naming 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear</step>
    <step>Relaxing your shoulders and unclenching your hands</step>
    <step>Reminding yourself, “This is a fear response from the past, not proof of current danger”</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>Be specific about boundaries with dog owners. You can say:

response:
Close friendship usually forms from repeated contact, gradual vulnerability, and initiative. You do not “find” close friends so much as build them.

Here is the practical way to do it:

<step>Pick 2–4 people from your existing circle whom you genuinely like and could imagine knowing better.</step>
<step>Increase one-on-one time. Group settings create familiarity, but closeness usually grows faster in smaller settings. Invite them for coffee, a walk, lunch, a call, or a simple recurring activity.</step>
<step>Be consistent. Regular contact matters more than intensity. Seeing someone every week or two builds closeness better than one unusually deep conversation every few months.</step>
<step>Take small social risks. Share slightly more of your real thoughts, preferences, worries, or experiences than you normally would, then see whether they reciprocate. Do this gradually, not all at once.</step>
<step>Ask better questions. Move beyond surface topics: what they have been thinking about lately, what is stressing them, what they are excited for, what matters to them, what they want next in life.</step>
<step>Follow up on what they tell you. Remember details and bring them up later. This is one of the clearest signals of care and attention.</step>
<step>Be the person who initiates. Many friendships stay superficial because both people wait. Suggest plans, send the text, check in, propose the next hangout before the current one ends.</step>
<step>Create routines. “Want to grab lunch every Thursday?” or “Let’s go to that class every week.” Repeated structure makes friendship easier than repeatedly negotiating plans from scratch.</step>
<step>Show reliability. Closeness depends heavily on trust. Keep plans, reply in a reasonable time, be discreet with personal information, and be emotionally steady.</step>

A useful rule: match the pace of the other person. If they open up a little, you can open up a little. If they keep things light, do not push for depth immediately. Some people become close through long, low-pressure contact rather than intense disclosure.

Also, closeness often forms around shared activity, not just conversation. Doing something together repeatedly—sports, volunteering, studying, hobbies, errands, walks—gives the friendship room to deepen naturally.

What to avoid:
<avoid>Treating closeness like a status upgrade you need quickly.</avoid>
<avoid>Oversharing very personal material too early.</avoid>
<avoid>Spreading yourself across too many acquaintances instead of investing in a few promising people.</avoid>
<avoid>Assuming lack of instant depth means lack of potential.</avoid>

If you want a simple plan, use this for the next month:
<plan>
  <item>Choose 3 people you want to know better.</item>
  <item>Invite each of them to one one-on-one hangout.</item>
  <item>During each hangout, ask 2 slightly deeper questions and share 1 personal but not overly intimate thing.</item>
  <item>Follow up within a week.</item>
  <item>If the interaction feels good, invite them again and try to establish a recurring activity.</item>
</plan>

Close friends are usually built through repeated bids for connection, not through one big breakthrough. Focus less on “How do I get close friends?” and more on “How do I steadily act like a good candidate for closeness with a few specific people?”

response:
<advice>You need to treat this as two separate problems, not one: first your safety and mental health, second your breakup/ego injury.</advice>
  <advice>If you might act on the suicidal thoughts, or feel unable to stay safe, contact emergency services now or go to the nearest ER. If you are in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988 now. If elsewhere, contact your local crisis line immediately. Do not stay alone with this if the thoughts are getting stronger.</advice>
  <advice>Do not take shrooms or acid right now. Not as an experiment, not as a shortcut, not because you feel stuck. With depression, shame, and suicidal thinking in the mix, self-medicating this way is unsafe and could make your mental state less stable.</advice>
  <advice>Cut off the healing obstacle: stop reopening this with your ex. No more closure talks, no more checking, no more trying to get your self-image repaired by the person who helped damage it. You do not need more analysis from her. You need distance.</advice>
  <advice>Your ego was not destroyed by one breakup alone. What is really hurting you now is that you built too much of your emotional stability on romantic attention. You said it yourself: when you do not have a girl to talk to, that is when you crash. That means dating is functioning like pain relief, not like connection. Until you address that, every new person will carry too much weight.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to face your own behavior plainly. Temper tantrums and controlling behavior are not small flaws. They are relationship-damaging behaviors. If you want your confidence back, do not chase it through dating. Earn it by becoming someone safer, steadier, and more self-controlled.</advice>
  <advice>Here is the immediate plan for the next 48 hours:</advice>
  <advice>1. Tell one real person today that you have been having suicidal thoughts and are not doing well. A friend, sibling, parent, or someone trustworthy.</advice>
  <advice>2. Make an appointment with a therapist or counselor as soon as possible. If cost is an issue, look for community mental health clinics, sliding-scale providers, or your primary care doctor as a starting point.</advice>
  <advice>3. Remove the drug plan. Stop looking for psychedelics.</advice>
  <advice>4. Stop contact with your ex for a while if you have not already.</advice>
  <advice>5. Sleep, eat, and get outside. These are not a full solution, but they matter more than you think when your brain is spiraling.</advice>
  <advice>Then for the next few months, work on these specific goals:</advice>
  <advice>1. Learn emotional regulation. Therapy can help with anger, shame, obsessive thinking, and abandonment sensitivity. If possible, ask about CBT or DBT-style skills.</advice>
  <advice>2. Build non-romantic structure: exercise, work/school goals, friendships, hobbies, routines. Your brain needs sources of identity that are not "someone wants me."</advice>
  <advice>3. Stay out of dating until you are no longer using it as a rescue device. A good sign you are ready is when being single feels uncomfortable sometimes but not intolerable.</advice>
  <advice>4. Replace the ex's insults with a more accurate frame: those comments were chosen to injure you. That does not make your past behavior acceptable, but it also does not make her attacks a reliable measure of your worth.</advice>
  <advice>5. Make amends through change, not rumination. The best answer to "I was immature and controlling" is "I am actively becoming different now."</advice>
  <advice>Confidence will not come from proving your ex wrong or getting another woman quickly. It will come from evidence: handling pain without collapsing, respecting boundaries, controlling your temper, and no longer needing constant romantic reassurance to feel okay.</advice>
  <advice>If you want, I can help you make a concrete no-contact plan, a same-day safety plan for the suicidal thoughts, or a step-by-step recovery plan focused on rebuilding self-respect.</advice>

  <advice>You need to treat this as two separate problems, not one: first your safety and mental health, second your breakup/ego injury.</advice>
  <advice>If you might act on the suicidal thoughts, or feel unable to stay safe, contact emergency services now or go to the nearest ER. If you are in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988 now. If elsewhere, contact your local crisis line immediately. Do not stay alone with this if the thoughts are getting stronger.</advice>
  <advice>Do not take shrooms or acid right now. Not as an experiment, not as a shortcut, not because you feel stuck. With depression, shame, and suicidal thinking in the mix, self-medicating this way is unsafe and could make your mental state less stable.</advice>
  <advice>Cut off the healing obstacle: stop reopening this with your ex. No more closure talks, no more checking, no more trying to get your self-image repaired by the person who helped damage it. You do not need more analysis from her. You need distance.</advice>
  <advice>Your ego was not destroyed by one breakup alone. What is really hurting you now is that you built too much of your emotional stability on romantic attention. You said it yourself: when you do not have a girl to talk to, that is when you crash. That means dating is functioning like pain relief, not like connection. Until you address that, every new person will carry too much weight.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to face your own behavior plainly. Temper tantrums and controlling behavior are not small flaws. They are relationship-damaging behaviors. If you want your confidence back, do not chase it through dating. Earn it by becoming someone safer, steadier, and more self-controlled.</advice>
  <advice>Here is the immediate plan for the next 48 hours:</advice>
  <advice>1. Tell one real person today that you have been having suicidal thoughts and are not doing well. A friend, sibling, parent, or someone trustworthy.</advice>
  <advice>2. Make an appointment with a therapist or counselor as soon as possible. If cost is an issue, look for community mental health clinics, sliding-scale providers, or your primary care doctor as a starting point.</advice>
  <advice>3. Remove the drug plan. Stop looking for psychedelics.</advice>
  <advice>4. Stop contact with your ex for a while if you have not already.</advice>
  <advice>5. Sleep, eat, and get outside. These are not a full solution, but they matter more than you think when your brain is spiraling.</advice>
  <advice>Then for the next few months, work on these specific goals:</advice>
  <advice>1. Learn emotional regulation. Therapy can help with anger, shame, obsessive thinking, and abandonment sensitivity. If possible, ask about CBT or DBT-style skills.</advice>
  <advice>2. Build non-romantic structure: exercise, work/school goals, friendships, hobbies, routines. Your brain needs sources of identity that are not "someone wants me."</advice>
  <advice>3. Stay out of dating until you are no longer using it as a rescue device. A good sign you are ready is when being single feels uncomfortable sometimes but not intolerable.</advice>
  <advice>4. Replace the ex's insults with a more accurate frame: those comments were chosen to injure you. That does not make your past behavior acceptable, but it also does not make her attacks a reliable measure of your worth.</advice>
  <advice>5. Make amends through change, not rumination. The best answer to "I was immature and controlling" is "I am actively becoming different now."</advice>
  <advice>Confidence will not come from proving your ex wrong or getting another woman quickly. It will come from evidence: handling pain without collapsing, respecting boundaries, controlling your temper, and no longer needing constant romantic reassurance to feel okay.</advice>
  <advice>If you want, I can help you make a concrete no-contact plan, a same-day safety plan for the suicidal thoughts, or a step-by-step recovery plan focused on rebuilding self-respect.</advice>
</response>

response:
You should treat your girlfriend’s discomfort as the main issue and address it directly but calmly.

First, talk with your girlfriend and get clear on what specifically is bothering her:
- Is it the volume of comments?
- The fact that he is going back through old photos?
- The tone of the comments?
- Whether she wants it to stop completely?

Then decide together what outcome she wants. Usually the best first step is simple and low-drama:
- She can restrict, mute, remove, or block him if she wants.
- If she would rather not do that yet, you can speak to him privately.

If you talk to him, keep it direct and non-accusatory. Something like:
“I wanted to mention something. You’ve been liking and commenting on a lot of my girlfriend’s old photos lately, and it’s making her uncomfortable. Please stop.”

That is enough. You do not need to debate his intentions. Even if he means nothing by it, the behavior is unwanted, and that’s the relevant point.

A few things to avoid:
- Don’t start with a public confrontation.
- Don’t turn it into a jealousy argument with your girlfriend.
- Don’t let him sidestep it by saying he was “just being friendly.” The effect matters more than the excuse.

If he stops, great. If he doesn’t, then escalate boundaries:
- Your girlfriend blocks or restricts him.
- You reconsider how close a friend he really is if he ignores a clear request.

The core approach is: get aligned with your girlfriend, set one clear boundary, and judge him by whether he respects it.

response:
Stop aiming for “close” as a category and focus on repeated trust-building behaviors.

A lot of friendships stall because they stay broad instead of becoming specific. To deepen them:

<step>Pick 1–3 people you actually want to know better instead of spreading energy across many acquaintances.</step>
<step>Increase contact frequency. Closeness usually comes from repeated one-on-one or small-group time, not from occasional group interactions.</step>
<step>Make concrete invitations: “Want to grab coffee this week?” “Want to go for a walk Saturday?” Specific plans build friendship faster than vague friendliness.</step>
<step>Share slightly more of yourself first, but in layers. Don’t jump to intensely personal disclosures. Offer something real but moderate, like what has been stressful, what you care about, or something you’re working through.</step>
<step>Ask better questions. Move beyond facts into perspective: “How have you been feeling about that?” “What’s been on your mind lately?” “What are you excited or worried about right now?”</step>
<step>Follow up on what they told you before. Remembering details is one of the clearest signals of interest and care.</step>
<step>Be consistent. Trust often grows less from one deep conversation than from many small moments where you show up, reply, remember, and initiate again.</step>

Also, watch for this mistake: trying to force emotional openness before enough shared time exists. Some people open up quickly; many don’t. If you push depth too early, it can make things feel unnatural.

A useful pattern is:
<example>
1. Shared time  
2. Small personal disclosure  
3. Good response  
4. More shared time  
5. Slightly deeper disclosure
</example>

If you want something practical, try this for a month:
<plan>
- Choose two people.
- Invite each of them to something one-on-one.
- In each conversation, share one slightly personal thing and ask one feeling-based question.
- Follow up within a week on something they mentioned.
</plan>

If someone keeps it casual even after that, accept that signal. Not every good connection becomes a close friendship. Depth usually comes from reciprocity, not effort alone.

response:
Start small and stop trying to say the perfect thing. Awkward usually comes from pressure, not from one bad text.

Here’s a simple rule:

1. Say something about a shared context.
2. Ask one easy question.
3. Build off her reply.

Good topics:
- class
- homework
- a teacher
- a school event
- music, shows, games, sports
- something she mentioned before

Good opener examples:
- “Hey, how did you find the homework?”
- “Did you understand what happened in class today?”
- “You said you liked [thing] — any recommendations?”
- “How was your weekend?”

response:
You should treat this as a panic/anxiety problem that is very treatable, not as something to brute-force alone.

1. Get professional help specifically for panic and phobic avoidance.
Ask a licensed mental health clinician for treatment focused on:
- CBT for panic disorder
- exposure therapy, especially flight-related exposure
- ACT or other anxiety-focused therapy if CBT is not a fit

Because flying is severely limiting your life, this is exactly the kind of problem therapy is meant to target.

2. Build a graded exposure plan instead of jumping straight onto a long flight.
A clinician can help you do this safely and systematically. Typical steps might be:
- watch videos of takeoff and turbulence
- sit with flight sounds while practicing breathing
- go to the airport without flying
- sit in the terminal
- take a very short flight with a support person
- repeat until your fear drops through experience

The key is repetition without escaping as soon as panic rises.

3. Learn panic-specific coping skills.
Useful tools include:
- slower exhale breathing, such as inhaling 4 and exhaling 6
- grounding using what you can see, hear, and feel
- naming panic symptoms as panic, not danger
- allowing symptoms to crest and fall rather than fighting them

A major goal is to stop interpreting bodily sensations as signs of catastrophe.

4. Don’t make the flight itself your only plan.
Before booking, decide:
- who knows about your anxiety
- whether you want aisle or window
- what you’ll do during boarding, takeoff, and turbulence
- whether you’ll use music, a movie, a written coping card, or guided audio
- what you’ll say to yourself when panic spikes

Keep the plan simple and rehearsed.

5. Talk to a doctor if medication might help.
For some people, short-term medication helps them begin exposure or get through early flights. This should be decided with a physician who knows your panic history, other medications, substance use, and health conditions. Don’t self-medicate with alcohol.

6. Practice not avoiding or over-relying on “safety behaviors.”
Some things help; some quietly keep the fear alive. For example, checking constantly for danger, tracking every sound, repeatedly seeking reassurance, or only flying if you have a perfect escape plan can maintain the phobia. A therapist can help you tell the difference between helpful preparation and fear-driven rituals.

7. Start with the smallest workable win.
Your first goal does not need to be “feel calm.” It can be:
- book a consultation
- drive to the airport and stay 20 minutes
- complete one therapy session
- take one short flight

Measure success by doing the step, not by having zero anxiety.

8. If your panic includes thoughts of harming yourself or you feel unable to stay safe, get urgent help now.
If that’s happening, contact emergency services or a crisis line in your area immediately.

If you want, I can help you make a step-by-step “first flight anxiety plan” for a short trip.

    <point>Losing sleep over work is a sign this is worth addressing directly, not just “putting up with.” Since it is already affecting sleep, consider speaking with your primary care doctor or a therapist if you have not already, especially if this has been going on for more than a couple of weeks.</point>
    <point>Try creating a clear shutdown routine at the end of the workday. Spend 10–15 minutes writing down: what is unfinished, what the next step is for each item, and when you will handle it. The goal is to give your brain a trusted place to “store” work so it does not keep rehearsing it at night.</point>
    <point>Set a firm boundary between work time and home time if possible: stop checking email or messages after a specific hour, turn off notifications, and keep work materials out of your bedroom or main relaxation space.</point>

    <point>If the stress is coming from workload, unclear expectations, or constant urgency, address the source during work hours.     <point>Reduce common fuel for nighttime stress: late caffeine, alcohol used to unwind, and screen-heavy work right before bed. These can make it harder for your body to come down even if the problem starts in your mind.</point>
    <point>Seek professional help sooner if you are sleeping badly most nights, feeling panicky, dreading work constantly, or noticing your mood, concentration, or health slipping. Stress-related sleep problems can become self-reinforcing, and early treatment helps.</point>
  </advice>

  <advice>You do not need to become a dictator. But you do need to become clear. Right now, you are trying to be understood through accumulated hurt, prior conversations, and obviousness. That is not working. Your next conversation needs to be explicit, concrete, and tied to actions.</advice>
  <advice>Say something close to this:
    <quote>I am unhappy because I do not feel like your partner. I feel like support staff in your life. These are the issues: you make major decisions without involving me, you leave me holding responsibilities you promised to share, and when you are home, I am still not a priority. I need a relationship where decisions, time, and responsibilities are actually shared. If that is not something you can do consistently, then this relationship cannot continue.</quote>
  </advice>
  <advice>Then make it measurable. For example:
    <point>No more major business or schedule changes without discussing them with you before decisions are made.</point>
    <point>A real division of dog care in writing: walks, training, feeding, events, and who handles what.</point>
    <point>Clear limits on your involvement in the family business. If you no longer want to help, say so plainly and step back. Do not keep participating out of guilt.</point>
    <point>Protected couple time every week that does not get absorbed by his family or work.</point>
    <point>No more agreeing to plans you believe are bad. If you say no to bringing the dog, the answer is no.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If he says, “Just tell me what to do,” do not give him a thousand tiny instructions. Give him a short list of standards. A partner should not need ongoing management to remember that promises matter and that you count.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to rebuild your own independence immediately, regardless of whether you stay. That means:
    <point>reinvesting in your own career or income,</point>
    <point>building your own local support system separate from his family,</point>
    <point>reducing your dependence on his routines and decisions,</point>
    <point>and making sure you could leave logistically if you had to.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>This matters because part of what is making you feel trapped is that your life has been absorbed into his. Whether you stay or go, that needs to change.</advice>
  <advice>About the relationship itself: do not judge it by how intense the beginning was or how aligned your goals sound in theory. Judge it by whether he can sustain changed behavior over time. If he listens, takes ownership without defensiveness, and consistently follows through for several months, there may be something to work with. If he stays confused, makes you restate basic needs endlessly, or improves briefly and then slides back, that is your answer.</advice>
  <advice>So no, it is not necessarily over because of one blowout. But it may be over if this is who he is in practice: loving, sincere, and chronically unwilling or unable to function as a partner. Love does not cancel that out.</advice>
  <advice>Your decision point is simple: after one very clear boundary-setting conversation, watch what he does. Not what he feels, not what he promises, not whether his sister thinks he is a good man. What he does.</advice>

<advice>
    <point>You usually cannot be 100% sure immediately. The better goal is not to detect someone's "true self" instantly, but to assess trustworthiness through patterns.</point>
    <point>Watch what they do when there is little benefit to them. A genuinely decent person is usually respectful, fair, and considerate even when they gain nothing from it.</point>
    <point>Pay attention to consistency. Ask yourself whether they act the same way with superiors, subordinates, strangers, service workers, family, and friends. A facade often cracks when the audience changes.</point>
    <point>Notice how they handle boundaries. If you say no, disagree, need space, or cannot help them, do they remain respectful? People pretending to be nice often become cold, guilt-tripping, manipulative, or irritated when they do not get what they want.</point>
    <point>Look at their behavior during stress, conflict, or inconvenience. Anyone can seem kind when things are easy. Character shows more clearly when they are frustrated, embarrassed, jealous, or under pressure.</point>
    <point>Compare words and actions. Do they make promises and follow through? Do they apologize and actually change? Nice-sounding language means little if their conduct repeatedly contradicts it.</point>
    <point>Be careful with people who are selectively kind. Common warning signs include excessive flattery, gossip, playing victim constantly, using private information strategically, being charming in public but cruel in private, and only helping when there is an advantage.</point>
    <point>Also watch for how they talk about others. If they constantly tear people down, reveal confidences, or create drama, assume they may eventually do the same to you.</point>
    <point>Trust gradual evidence more than strong first impressions. Do not hand over deep trust, money, secrets, or dependency quickly just because someone seems warm, familiar, or generous at first.</point>
    <point>Use small tests instead of dramatic confrontations. Share limited information, set minor boundaries, or observe them in group situations. See whether they respect you, stay reliable, and behave ethically over time.</point>
    <point>Listen to discomfort, but verify it. If something feels off, do not ignore it—but do not jump straight to accusations either. Look for repeated patterns, not one awkward moment.</point>
    <point>In workplaces especially, focus less on whether someone is "nice" and more on whether they are professional, trustworthy, respectful, and safe to deal with. Keep records if behavior affects your work.</point>
    <point>A useful rule: trust should be given in layers. Basic courtesy for everyone, moderate trust for people who are consistent, deeper trust only after time, honesty, and tested behavior.</point>
    <point>If you want one practical question to keep asking, use this: "Who are they when they do not need anything from me, and who are they when I disappoint them?" The answer is often very revealing.</point>
  </advice>

If the application asks for household income or specifically asks about a spouse, do not leave your spouse’s income off. That can be treated as an inaccurate application.

The likely consequences are:
  <point>denial of financial assistance</point>
  <point>delay while the hospital asks for corrections or proof of income</point>
  <point>loss of any discount already approved if the omission is discovered later</point>
  <point>repayment demands for assistance you were not actually eligible for</point>
  <point>possible referral for compliance or fraud review</point>

What you should do instead:
  <step>Read the application carefully and see whether it uses “household income,” “family income,” or asks whether you are married.</step>
  <step>If you are unsure whether your spouse’s income counts, call the hospital financial assistance office and ask before submitting.</step>
  <step>If you already submitted the form without that income, contact them promptly and correct it in writing.</step>
  <step>If your spouse’s income should not count because you are separated, not living together, or there are special circumstances, explain that and ask what documentation they require.</step>
  <step>If the hospital denies aid, ask for the written policy, appeal rights, and whether they offer payment plans or other hardship options.</step>

The safest course is full and accurate disclosure, with an explanation of any unusual household situation rather than leaving income out.

response:
<advice>You are allowed to set attendance rules in your own home, especially for a sit-down dinner. In fact, in this situation you should make them more explicit and enforce them before the next meal, not during it.</advice>
  <advice>Speak to your sister privately, before the next invitation goes out. Keep it simple and specific: “For dinners at my house, I need an exact headcount by the RSVP date. I’m happy to include dates or friends if I know in advance, but I can’t accommodate surprise guests at the door.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not frame this as a debate about manners or disrespect. Frame it as a hosting limit: limited chairs, limited place settings, planned meal. That is harder to argue with and less likely to escalate into family drama.</advice>
  <advice>Then put the rule in every invitation. For example: “Please RSVP by Thursday with the exact number attending. I can only seat those included in the RSVP.” That makes your expectation unmistakable.</advice>
  <advice>If your sister tests the boundary again, address it at the door calmly and briefly. Do not embarrass the extra guest. Say something like: “I’m sorry, I only planned for those who RSVP’d. We don’t have a place set for one more tonight.” If you truly cannot accommodate them comfortably, the uninvited person should not stay for dinner.</advice>
  <advice>If you decide, for family peace, to allow an extra person once in a while, make that your choice rather than an obligation. But if you do let them stay, follow up afterward: “I made it work this time, but please don’t do that again.” Otherwise the pattern will continue.</advice>
  <advice>Do not direct your frustration at the boyfriend. He may have assumed he was welcome. Your issue is with the family member who failed to give notice.</advice>
  <advice>Most important: do not handle it by letting people “stand,” making pointed comments, or improvising in a way meant to shame them. That punishes everyone at the table. The right time to enforce the boundary is before dinner or at the threshold, not by public humiliation once the meal has begun.</advice>
  <advice>So yes: set specifications, state them clearly, and enforce them consistently. “No unannounced guests at sit-down dinners” is a reasonable house rule.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You are allowed to set attendance rules in your own home, especially for a sit-down dinner. In fact, in this situation you should make them more explicit and enforce them before the next meal, not during it.</advice>
  <advice>Speak to your sister privately, before the next invitation goes out. Keep it simple and specific: “For dinners at my house, I need an exact headcount by the RSVP date. I’m happy to include dates or friends if I know in advance, but I can’t accommodate surprise guests at the door.”</advice>
  <advice>Do not frame this as a debate about manners or disrespect. Frame it as a hosting limit: limited chairs, limited place settings, planned meal. That is harder to argue with and less likely to escalate into family drama.</advice>
  <advice>Then put the rule in every invitation. For example: “Please RSVP by Thursday with the exact number attending. I can only seat those included in the RSVP.” That makes your expectation unmistakable.</advice>
  <advice>If your sister tests the boundary again, address it at the door calmly and briefly. Do not embarrass the extra guest. Say something like: “I’m sorry, I only planned for those who RSVP’d. We don’t have a place set for one more tonight.” If you truly cannot accommodate them comfortably, the uninvited person should not stay for dinner.</advice>
  <advice>If you decide, for family peace, to allow an extra person once in a while, make that your choice rather than an obligation. But if you do let them stay, follow up afterward: “I made it work this time, but please don’t do that again.” Otherwise the pattern will continue.</advice>
  <advice>Do not direct your frustration at the boyfriend. He may have assumed he was welcome. Your issue is with the family member who failed to give notice.</advice>
  <advice>Most important: do not handle it by letting people “stand,” making pointed comments, or improvising in a way meant to shame them. That punishes everyone at the table. The right time to enforce the boundary is before dinner or at the threshold, not by public humiliation once the meal has begun.</advice>
  <advice>So yes: set specifications, state them clearly, and enforce them consistently. “No unannounced guests at sit-down dinners” is a reasonable house rule.</advice>
</response>

response:
You should not do this to “move on.” If you do something painful and unwanted just to stop his anger, that is not a fix to the relationship; it is you being coerced past a clear boundary.

Tell yourself the plain truth: you already said no. That should have ended it.

What he is doing is not a misunderstanding about preferences. The problem is that he keeps pushing after you refused, gets angry, and tries to make your refusal about cheating or lack of attraction. That is sexual pressure and manipulation.

What to do next:

<step>State the boundary once, clearly and without debate: “I am not doing anal. I am not discussing it again. If you pressure me, accuse me, or punish me for saying no, I will leave/end the conversation.”</step>

<step>Do not keep arguing the merits of it. You do not need to prove it hurts enough, explain why other women do or do not do it, or persuade him that your boundary is reasonable. “No” is enough.</step>

<step>Watch his response to the boundary, not his words afterward. If he minimizes, sulks, keeps asking, guilt-trips you, gets angry, or brings up cheating again, treat that as confirmation that the issue is coercion, not communication.</step>

<step>Tell someone in real life now. A trusted friend, family member, therapist, or support line. The embarrassment is understandable, but secrecy helps coercive situations continue.</step>

<step>If you live together or spend time alone where his anger could escalate, make a safety plan: somewhere you can go, someone you can call, access to your phone, transportation, and essentials.</step>

<step>Be prepared to leave if this does not stop immediately. A partner who respects you does not keep trying to wear you down into painful sex.</step>

Also, severe pain during anal is a complete reason not to do it, permanently or otherwise. You do not owe anyone a sex act because “girls do it all the time” or because he wants reassurance. If he feels insecure, he needs to handle that without using your body to soothe himself.

If you want a simple script, use this:
“I am not consenting to anal or any sexual act I don’t want. I will not be pressured, guilted, or accused over it. If this continues, I’m done.”

If saying that feels unsafe, skip the speech and focus on getting support and creating distance. If you want, I can help you make a breakup plan or a safety plan for if he reacts badly.

Tell yourself the plain truth: you already said no. That should have ended it.

What to do next:

<step>State the boundary once, clearly and without debate: “I am not doing anal. I am not discussing it again. If you pressure me, accuse me, or punish me for saying no, I will leave/end the conversation.”</step>

<step>Do not keep arguing the merits of it. You do not need to prove it hurts enough, explain why other women do or do not do it, or persuade him that your boundary is reasonable. “No” is enough.</step>

<step>Watch his response to the boundary, not his words afterward. If he minimizes, sulks, keeps asking, guilt-trips you, gets angry, or brings up cheating again, treat that as confirmation that the issue is coercion, not communication.</step>

<step>Tell someone in real life now. A trusted friend, family member, therapist, or support line. The embarrassment is understandable, but secrecy helps coercive situations continue.</step>

<step>If you live together or spend time alone where his anger could escalate, make a safety plan: somewhere you can go, someone you can call, access to your phone, transportation, and essentials.</step>

<step>Be prepared to leave if this does not stop immediately. A partner who respects you does not keep trying to wear you down into painful sex.</step>

response:
<advice>
    <point>You probably cannot "fix" this by solving his height insecurity for him. This is mainly his issue to work through, not something you caused.</point>
    <point>Your one notable mistake was the phrasing "why do you hate me now." If you want to reopen the conversation, correct that part plainly: "I'm sorry I said hate. I was hurt and guessed wrong. What I meant was that I miss you and I want to understand."</point>
    <point>Then keep the message simple and non-argumentative. Something like: "I never wanted to make you feel worse about your height. I love you, I miss how things used to be, and I'm here whenever you want to talk."</point>
    <point>Do not debate whether he should feel jealous. If you tell him his feelings are irrational, he will probably shut down more. The better line is: "I get that you're hurting, but it hurts me to be pushed away for something I didn't do."</point>
    <point>Set a boundary too. His insecurity may explain his behavior, but it does not make it okay for him to deny you as his sister or freeze you out indefinitely. You can say: "I can give you space, but I don't want to keep being treated like I did something wrong."</point>
    <point>If your parents are reasonable, involve them carefully. Not to punish him, but to make clear that this has gone on for a year and is damaging the relationship. This is the kind of family issue where a calm parent conversation or therapy could actually help.</point>
    <point>After that, back off some. Offer the door open, then let him choose whether to walk through it. Repeatedly chasing him may just feed the tension.</point>
    <point>If he comes around, avoid making height a charged subject in either direction. No jokes, no reassurance speeches about how height doesn't matter unless he asks, and no overcompensating. Just treat him normally.</point>
    <point>The short version: apologize for the accusatory wording, make clear you miss him, state that you did not mock him and do not want to be punished for existing, involve parents if needed, and accept that the deeper change has to come from him.</point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You need to stop looking for the trick that will make this go away.</advice>
  <advice>What she seems to be grieving is not “a proposal” in the abstract. It is that her one first proposal already happened, and it happened in a way that felt rushed and unconsidered. A redo cannot become her first time. If you keep approaching this like there must be a fix she is refusing to share, you will likely make her feel even less understood.</advice>
  <advice>Your next move should be a direct, unqualified acknowledgment. Something like: “I understand now that what hurt wasn’t just that the proposal was imperfect. It’s that a once-in-a-lifetime moment felt careless, and I can’t give you that first experience back. I’m sorry for that. You do not need to tell me how to fix it.”</advice>
  <advice>That last sentence matters. Remove the burden from her. Do not ask what she would do, what you should do, or what the magic repair is. Let her be sad about it without treating her sadness like a problem she has to solve for you.</advice>
  <advice>After that, ask a narrower question: “When this comes up for you, what helps you feel understood by me?” That is different from asking how to fix the memory. She may want you to listen, to acknowledge it plainly, or to admit you mishandled something important.</advice>
  <advice>If she ever wants a new romantic milestone, let it be a new moment, not “the replacement proposal.” For example, you could plan an intentional vow renewal, anniversary letter, private ceremony, or meaningful date that honors her and shows thoughtfulness. But only do that if she wants it, and do not present it as restoring what was lost.</advice>
  <advice>If this keeps recurring and turning into the same stuck conversation, a couples therapist would be useful. Not because this is enormous in objective terms, but because it is emotionally sticky: she is carrying grief and you are trying to move too quickly into repair. A therapist can help you stay with the hurt without becoming defensive or solution-focused.</advice>
  <advice>In short: fully own that you mishandled an important moment, stop insisting there must be a fix, stop making her define the remedy, and focus on helping her feel accurately understood. That is more likely to help than any recreated proposal.</advice>

response:
You do not need to make every evening elaborate. The best plan is to mix a few easy outings with some low-effort downtime so you do not burn yourself out during your first weeks at work.

<advice>
  <point>Plan for simple after-5 activities that fit into 1 to 3 hours: casual dinners, coffee/dessert runs, a walk in a lively neighborhood, a local park, bookstore, arcade, bowling, mini golf, trivia night, pool hall, or a gym/sports activity if he is into that.</point>
  <point>Use your city’s evening options: farmers markets, food truck nights, outdoor concerts, comedy shows, museum late hours, community events, or college-town events if nearby.</point>
  <point>If he is independent, set him up with daytime solo ideas while you work: transit tips, a list of nearby places, guest pass to a gym, shopping areas, hiking trails, museums, or cafés with Wi-Fi. That way he is not waiting around all day for you.</point>
  <point>Ask him before the visit what he actually enjoys. At 19, he may prefer very different things than movies at home—food spots, gaming, nightlife-lite activities, sports, photography spots, or just exploring the area.</point>
  <point>Batch one or two slightly bigger evenings into the visit instead of trying to entertain every night. For example: one dinner out, one activity night, one relaxed night at home with takeout and a game.</point>
  <point>Keep weeknights realistic. Since you are starting a new job, avoid late nights every evening. It is better to be consistent and present for a couple of hours than exhausted and stressed.</point>
  <point>If your spouse/sibling is available, coordinate so some plans do not depend entirely on you. Shared hosting will make the visit easier on everyone.</point>
</advice>

<sample_evening_plan>
  <idea>Monday: quick dinner out + walk for ice cream</idea>
  <idea>Tuesday: board games, takeout, or cooking together at home</idea>
  <idea>Wednesday: bowling / arcade / trivia night</idea>
  <idea>Thursday: scenic walk or local event</idea>
  <idea>Friday: your bigger outing—concert, downtown visit, comedy show, or dinner somewhere fun</idea>
</sample_evening_plan>

<bottom_line>Focus on easy, repeatable evening plans, give him options for daytime independence, and do not overcommit while you are adjusting to the new job.</bottom_line>

<response>You do not need to make every evening elaborate. The best plan is to mix a few easy outings with some low-effort downtime so you do not burn yourself out during your first weeks at work.

<advice>
  <point>Plan for simple after-5 activities that fit into 1 to 3 hours: casual dinners, coffee/dessert runs, a walk in a lively neighborhood, a local park, bookstore, arcade, bowling, mini golf, trivia night, pool hall, or a gym/sports activity if he is into that.</point>

response:
<advice>
    <point>You should stop treating this as mainly a wording dispute. The central issue is not whether "affair" was the perfect term. The issue is that she asked about a category of behavior she considered disqualifying, and your answer led her to believe that history did not exist.</point>
    <point>Do not wait for her to "realize it's not a big deal." If you do that, you will confirm her fear that you still do not understand why this matters. Treat it as serious because it is serious to her.</point>
    <point>Your first repair task is to fully own the past without excuses. That means dropping all versions of:
      <subpoint>"I didn't have much of a choice."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"It wasn't really an affair."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"She used the wrong word."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"My ex had a worse affair."</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>What you need to communicate is simpler: you were still married, you had sex with someone else, she had asked about that kind of history, and your answer did not give her the information she was trying to get.</point>
    <point>Give her a little space, but do not go silent indefinitely. Send one calm message that takes responsibility and does not argue. For example:
      <subpoint>"I've thought about this and I understand why you feel misled. When you asked if I'd ever had an affair, I answered in a narrow way that left out the fact that I had cheated while still married. That information mattered to you, and I should have told you. I was wrong to minimize it or argue semantics. You don't owe me an apology. If you're willing, I'd like to answer any questions honestly and give you space to decide what you want."</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If she agrees to talk, stick to these rules:
      <subpoint>Answer directly.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not debate definitions.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not justify the cheating as meeting needs.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not compare your conduct to your ex-wife's affair.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not ask your ex to help validate you unless your girlfriend independently wants that, and even then be cautious.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>You should also be ready for the possibility that this is a dealbreaker for her even after an apology. That would not mean she is unreasonable. It would mean she set a boundary, learned information relevant to it, and reevaluated.</point>
    <point>If you want the best chance of saving the relationship, show her that you understand two separate failures:
      <subpoint>the original cheating in your marriage,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>and the later omission/minimization with her.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If you cannot sincerely say, "I chose to cheat, and I should have disclosed that when you asked," then you are not ready for the conversation yet. Work that out first, because until you actually accept responsibility, anything you say will sound like spin.</point>
  </advice>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>You should stop treating this as mainly a wording dispute. The central issue is not whether "affair" was the perfect term. The issue is that she asked about a category of behavior she considered disqualifying, and your answer led her to believe that history did not exist.</point>
    <point>Do not wait for her to "realize it's not a big deal." If you do that, you will confirm her fear that you still do not understand why this matters. Treat it as serious because it is serious to her.</point>
    <point>Your first repair task is to fully own the past without excuses. That means dropping all versions of:
      <subpoint>"I didn't have much of a choice."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"It wasn't really an affair."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"She used the wrong word."</subpoint>
      <subpoint>"My ex had a worse affair."</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>What you need to communicate is simpler: you were still married, you had sex with someone else, she had asked about that kind of history, and your answer did not give her the information she was trying to get.</point>
    <point>Give her a little space, but do not go silent indefinitely. Send one calm message that takes responsibility and does not argue. For example:
      <subpoint>"I've thought about this and I understand why you feel misled. When you asked if I'd ever had an affair, I answered in a narrow way that left out the fact that I had cheated while still married. That information mattered to you, and I should have told you. I was wrong to minimize it or argue semantics. You don't owe me an apology. If you're willing, I'd like to answer any questions honestly and give you space to decide what you want."</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If she agrees to talk, stick to these rules:
      <subpoint>Answer directly.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not debate definitions.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not justify the cheating as meeting needs.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not compare your conduct to your ex-wife's affair.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not ask your ex to help validate you unless your girlfriend independently wants that, and even then be cautious.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>You should also be ready for the possibility that this is a dealbreaker for her even after an apology. That would not mean she is unreasonable. It would mean she set a boundary, learned information relevant to it, and reevaluated.</point>
    <point>If you want the best chance of saving the relationship, show her that you understand two separate failures:
      <subpoint>the original cheating in your marriage,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>and the later omission/minimization with her.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If you cannot sincerely say, "I chose to cheat, and I should have disclosed that when you asked," then you are not ready for the conversation yet. Work that out first, because until you actually accept responsibility, anything you say will sound like spin.</point>
  </advice>
</response>

response:
Do not break up right before the trip just because the timing is convenient. That would be a high-impact decision made in the middle of an active pattern you have not seriously worked on together yet.

But do not use “we love each other” or “I’m trying” to gloss over what is actually happening. From what you wrote, the core problem is:

1. you have recurring attention/follow-through failures, including on security and safety tasks, and  
2. the two of you have a terrible repair process, so each incident reopens the whole history.

You need to treat the first part more seriously than you currently are.

Forgetting bins is one thing. Forgetting exterior locks and leaving an external office unsecured is different. Stop grouping all of these under “small mistakes.” Some are reliability issues; some are safety issues. If you want this relationship to work, act accordingly.

What to do now:

<step>Before you leave, do one calm conversation that is not a fight and is not about whether either of you should leave.</step>
<step>Say plainly that you understand the door/office/oven issues are not minor to her, and that you are not going to frame the problem as just “her feelings.”</step>
<step>Tell her you do not want to make breakup decisions in the heat of this and right before a month apart, and that you want to use therapy and the trip period constructively instead.</step>

Then put actual systems in place, especially for safety-critical tasks:

<step>External doors: use a nightly lock checklist, phone alarm, or a physical cue at bedtime.</step>
<step>Office/external space: adopt a strict “last touch” rule—if you open it, you do not leave the area until you visibly check closed + locked.</step>
<step>Appliances: create a habit of immediate visual confirmation after touching or passing them.</step>
<step>Requested tasks: use shared lists, reminders, and due times instead of relying on memory.</step>

The point is not to promise perfection. The point is to stop acting as if recurrence is inevitable and therefore something she just has to emotionally manage.

Also change how you respond in conflict. Stop saying:
- “Why do you stay with me?”
- “It feels like you hate me.”
- “The only issue I have is how you feel toward me.”

Those statements shift the conversation away from repair and into relationship panic or blame. In the moment, your job is simpler:
- acknowledge the concrete impact,
- state the fix,
- do not argue intent,
- revisit fairness later, not at peak escalation.

Something closer to:
“I see why this scared/upset you. I left it unsecured. That matters. I’m going to put X system in place so it is less likely to happen again. We can talk later about the bigger pattern once we’re both calmer.”

You should also seriously consider a proper ADHD evaluation. That does not commit you to medication. But self-diagnosing, rejecting one treatment path up front, and then saying you will definitely keep slipping up is not a strong long-term plan. Assessment could help with skills, coaching, behavioral strategies, and clearer understanding of what you are dealing with.

As for the relationship itself: do not decide now unless one of you already knows you are done. Based on what you wrote, the better course is:
- do not break up before the trip,
- start therapy,
- use the trip to create structure and reflect,
- then reassess after some actual work has been done.

If, after therapy and real behavioral changes, she still responds with stored-up contempt and cannot repair, then the relationship may not be workable. But right now, you have enough evidence that the current pattern is bad, not enough evidence that it is hopeless.

concerns: (action: "I accidentally bumped our oven, didn't realise, and didn't correct it" and "failed to shut the door and lock it when I left") Those lapses affect her sense of safety and security in her own home and workspace, especially if these are recurring kinds of oversights.

(action: "about three times a year I'll forget to put the bins out," "maybe 5 times a year I'll forget to lock the back door," and "sometimes I'll forget to do something specific that she asked me to do") Repeatedly forgetting agreed household and safety-related tasks would wear on her trust that she can rely on you.

(action: "I'm almost certain I have ADHD... I don't want to go on medication") If you believe there is an ongoing issue contributing to these mistakes, deciding against one possible treatment while the problem continues may feel to her like you are accepting the status quo more than fully pursuing solutions.

(action: "I'm usually very calm and try to stay logical, but that upsets her" and "I defend myself if I think she's being unfair") In the middle of her being upset, that can come across as dismissive, emotionally detached, or more focused on arguing your case than on understanding her distress.

(action: "I told her that it feels like she hates me sometimes, and asked her why she stays with me") That puts her in a painful position and can turn the conflict into a question of whether she should leave, rather than staying focused on repairing the specific hurt.

(action: "I told her the only issue I have with her is how she feels towards me") From her side, that would likely feel invalidating because it reduces her complaints to a problem with her feelings instead of acknowledging the real impact your repeated mistakes have on her.

(action: "I also own most of our house... <response>
Do not break up right before the trip just because the timing is convenient. That would be a high-impact decision made in the middle of an active pattern you have not seriously worked on together yet.

But do not use “we love each other” or “I’m trying” to gloss over what is actually happening. From what you wrote, the core problem is:

1. you have recurring attention/follow-through failures, including on security and safety tasks, and  
2. the two of you have a terrible repair process, so each incident reopens the whole history.

You need to treat the first part more seriously than you currently are.

Forgetting bins is one thing. Forgetting exterior locks and leaving an external office unsecured is different. Stop grouping all of these under “small mistakes.” Some are reliability issues; some are safety issues. If you want this relationship to work, act accordingly.

What to do now:

<step>Before you leave, do one calm conversation that is not a fight and is not about whether either of you should leave.</step>
<step>Say plainly that you understand the door/office/oven issues are not minor to her, and that you are not going to frame the problem as just “her feelings.”</step>
<step>Tell her you do not want to make breakup decisions in the heat of this and right before a month apart, and that you want to use therapy and the trip period constructively instead.</step>

Then put actual systems in place, especially for safety-critical tasks:

<step>External doors: use a nightly lock checklist, phone alarm, or a physical cue at bedtime.</step>
<step>Office/external space: adopt a strict “last touch” rule—if you open it, you do not leave the area until you visibly check closed + locked.</step>
<step>Appliances: create a habit of immediate visual confirmation after touching or passing them.</step>
<step>Requested tasks: use shared lists, reminders, and due times instead of relying on memory.</step>

The point is not to promise perfection. The point is to stop acting as if recurrence is inevitable and therefore something she just has to emotionally manage.

Also change how you respond in conflict. Stop saying:
- “Why do you stay with me?”
- “It feels like you hate me.”
- “The only issue I have is how you feel toward me.”

Those statements shift the conversation away from repair and into relationship panic or blame. In the moment, your job is simpler:
- acknowledge the concrete impact,
- state the fix,
- do not argue intent,
- revisit fairness later, not at peak escalation.

Something closer to:
“I see why this scared/upset you. I left it unsecured. That matters. I’m going to put X system in place so it is less likely to happen again. We can talk later about the bigger pattern once we’re both calmer.”

You should also seriously consider a proper ADHD evaluation. That does not commit you to medication. But self-diagnosing, rejecting one treatment path up front, and then saying you will definitely keep slipping up is not a strong long-term plan. Assessment could help with skills, coaching, behavioral strategies, and clearer understanding of what you are dealing with.

As for the relationship itself: do not decide now unless one of you already knows you are done. Based on what you wrote, the better course is:
- do not break up before the trip,
- start therapy,
- use the trip to create structure and reflect,
- then reassess after some actual work has been done.

If, after therapy and real behavioral changes, she still responds with stored-up contempt and cannot repair, then the relationship may not be workable. But right now, you have enough evidence that the current pattern is bad, not enough evidence that it is hopeless.
</response>

<step>Office/external space: adopt a strict “last touch” rule—if you open it, you do not leave the area until you visibly check closed + locked.</step>
<step>Appliances: create a habit of immediate visual confirmation after touching or passing them.</step>
<step>Requested tasks: use shared lists, reminders, and due times instead of relying on memory.</step>

The point is not to promise perfection. The point is to stop acting as if recurrence is inevitable and therefore something she just has to emotionally manage.

Also change how you respond in conflict. Stop saying:
- “Why do you stay with me?”
- “It feels like you hate me.”
- “The only issue I have is how you feel toward me.”

Those statements shift the conversation away from repair and into relationship panic or blame. In the moment, your job is simpler:
- acknowledge the concrete impact,
- state the fix,
- do not argue intent,
- revisit fairness later, not at peak escalation.

Something closer to:

You should also seriously consider a proper ADHD evaluation. That does not commit you to medication. But self-diagnosing, rejecting one treatment path up front, and then saying you will definitely keep slipping up is not a strong long-term plan. Assessment could help with skills, coaching, behavioral strategies, and clearer understanding of what you are dealing with.

As for the relationship itself: do not decide now unless one of you already knows you are done. Based on what you wrote, the better course is:
- do not break up before the trip,
- start therapy,
- use the trip to create structure and reflect,
- then reassess after some actual work has been done.

If, after therapy and real behavioral changes, she still responds with stored-up contempt and cannot repair, then the relationship may not be workable. But right now, you have enough evidence that the current pattern is bad, not enough evidence that it is hopeless.

response:
Stop trying to escape your whole life at once. That usually fails because routine is stronger than motivation.

Do this instead:

<step>Pick one area only: work, health, social life, home, or mindset.</step>
<step>Change one behavior that is small enough to repeat even when you do not feel like it.</step>
<step>Attach it to something you already do every day.</step>
<step>Track it for 2 weeks, not forever.</step>

Examples:
<example>After I wake up, I go outside for 10 minutes.</example>
<example>On Tuesdays, I do one new thing after work.</example>
<example>Before bed, I write down one thing I want tomorrow to look like.</example>

A rut often gets reinforced by intensity. You try something big, it fades, then you feel pulled back. So make the change boringly doable.

Also check whether this is just boredom, or something heavier:
<sign>If you feel numb, exhausted, unmotivated most days, or nothing feels rewarding, this may be more than a rut.</sign>
<sign>If that has been going on for a while, talk to a therapist or doctor.</sign>

Use this test:
<question>What is one part of my current routine that drains me?</question>
<question>What is one part that I actually want more of?</question>

Then reduce one drain and increase one meaningful thing.

If you want a practical reset, try this for the next 7 days:
<plan>
  <item>Wake up and sleep at roughly the same time.</item>
  <item>Get outside once a day.</item>
  <item>Move your body for 10 to 20 minutes.</item>
  <item>Do one thing that is different from your default routine.</item>
  <item>Spend less time on whatever makes hours disappear without helping.</item>
</plan>

Do not ask, "How do I get out of a rut?" Ask, "What is the smallest repeatable proof that my life is not on autopilot?"

Start there.

response:
You need to treat this as a pattern that harms other people, not just as a heartbreak problem after the fact.

What you describe often shows up when someone is drawn to pursuit, uncertainty, or the emotional high of being wanted, but feels discomfort when real stability and intimacy arrive. Then your mind protects itself by going cold, focusing on flaws, or building a case that the person is wrong for you. Once they leave, the loss reactivates desire. That does sound like a form of self-sabotage, and it can also fit an insecure attachment pattern, especially avoidant or fearful-avoidant dynamics.

The important part is this: the feeling itself is not the main issue. The issue is what you do with it. Right now, your response seems to be:
1. get close,
2. feel secure,
3. lose interest / nitpick,
4. behave in ways that push them away,
5. panic when they actually leave.

If you want this to stop, you need to interrupt the cycle earlier.

Here’s what to do:

<steps>
  <step>
    <title>1. Stop using breakup as clarity</title>
    <detail>When you suddenly want them back after a breakup, do not automatically treat that feeling as proof they were “the one.” It may be grief, rejection sensitivity, or fear of loss. Before contacting an ex, ask: did I actually want closeness when they were available, or do I want relief now that they’re gone?</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>2. Track the exact moment your feelings shift</title>
    <detail>Journal after dates or interactions. Write down:
      - what happened right before you went cold,
      - what thought appeared,
      - what flaw you fixated on,
      - what feeling was underneath it.
Often the hidden feeling is not “I don’t like them,” but “I feel trapped,” “I’m scared they’ll really know me,” “now I’m responsible,” or “if I stay, I could get hurt.”</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>3. Separate real incompatibility from deactivation</title>
    <detail>Ask yourself whether the issue is:
      - a genuine value mismatch,
      - repeated disrespect,
      - lack of attraction from the start,
      or
      - a small trait your brain is magnifying once intimacy deepens.
If it’s mostly small irritations that become unbearable only after closeness, that strongly suggests the problem is the pattern, not the partner.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>4. Stop making partners absorb your internal conflict</title>
    <detail>If you notice yourself nitpicking, pause. Do not turn your anxiety into criticism. Instead of “you always do X and it bothers me,” try identifying the real issue privately first: “I’m feeling myself pull away now that this is getting more real.” Your partners should not have to be worn down until they break up with you.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>5. Slow relationships down</title>
    <detail>If you get very swept up in the honeymoon phase, that intensity may be part of the cycle. Keep early dating steadier:
      - don’t over-fuse quickly,
      - maintain your routines and friends,
      - avoid fantasy-planning too early,
      - let compatibility reveal itself over time.
Intensity can mask instability.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>6. Get therapy focused on attachment and relationship patterns</title>
    <detail>This is very workable in therapy. Look for someone who understands attachment, intimacy avoidance, self-sabotage, or repetition patterns in relationships. The goal is not just to “cope with heartbreak,” but to understand why security feels deadening or threatening to you.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>7. Be careful with exes</title>
    <detail>If you repeatedly go back once someone leaves, be honest with yourself: are you trying to build something different, or are you trying to soothe the panic of abandonment? Unless you can name what will change behaviorally, going back often just reopens the same wound for both people.</detail>
  </step>
</steps>

For the heartbreak specifically:

<heartbreak>
  <point>Do not romanticize the relationship only after it ends. Write down what you actually did when they were present, not just what you feel now that they’re absent.</point>
  <point>Limit contact with exes if contact keeps reactivating the longing.</point>
  <point>When you miss them, ask: do I miss them, or do I miss being chosen, wanted, or not abandoned?</point>
  <point>Let yourself grieve without converting grief into a rescue mission.</point>
</heartbreak>

A useful question going forward is: “When someone becomes safely available to me, what story do I start telling myself that makes me pull away?” That story is probably the key.

If this pattern has happened across multiple relationships, don’t wait for another breakup to investigate it. Work on it before dating again, or at least while dating very slowly and consciously. The problem is not just that you want people after they leave. The deeper problem is that you seem to struggle to tolerate being loved once you have it.

<response>
You need to treat this as a pattern that harms other people, not just as a heartbreak problem after the fact.

What you describe often shows up when someone is drawn to pursuit, uncertainty, or the emotional high of being wanted, but feels discomfort when real stability and intimacy arrive. Then your mind protects itself by going cold, focusing on flaws, or building a case that the person is wrong for you. Once they leave, the loss reactivates desire. That does sound like a form of self-sabotage, and it can also fit an insecure attachment pattern, especially avoidant or fearful-avoidant dynamics.

The important part is this: the feeling itself is not the main issue. The issue is what you do with it. Right now, your response seems to be:
1. get close,
2. feel secure,
3. lose interest / nitpick,
4. behave in ways that push them away,
5. panic when they actually leave.

If you want this to stop, you need to interrupt the cycle earlier.

Here’s what to do:

<steps>
  <step>
    <title>1. Stop using breakup as clarity</title>
    <detail>When you suddenly want them back after a breakup, do not automatically treat that feeling as proof they were “the one.” It may be grief, rejection sensitivity, or fear of loss. Before contacting an ex, ask: did I actually want closeness when they were available, or do I want relief now that they’re gone?</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>2. Track the exact moment your feelings shift</title>
    <detail>Journal after dates or interactions. Write down:
      - what happened right before you went cold,
      - what thought appeared,
      - what flaw you fixated on,
      - what feeling was underneath it.
Often the hidden feeling is not “I don’t like them,” but “I feel trapped,” “I’m scared they’ll really know me,” “now I’m responsible,” or “if I stay, I could get hurt.”</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>3. Separate real incompatibility from deactivation</title>
    <detail>Ask yourself whether the issue is:
      - a genuine value mismatch,
      - repeated disrespect,
      - lack of attraction from the start,
      or
      - a small trait your brain is magnifying once intimacy deepens.
If it’s mostly small irritations that become unbearable only after closeness, that strongly suggests the problem is the pattern, not the partner.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>4. Stop making partners absorb your internal conflict</title>
    <detail>If you notice yourself nitpicking, pause. Do not turn your anxiety into criticism. Instead of “you always do X and it bothers me,” try identifying the real issue privately first: “I’m feeling myself pull away now that this is getting more real.” Your partners should not have to be worn down until they break up with you.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>5. Slow relationships down</title>
    <detail>If you get very swept up in the honeymoon phase, that intensity may be part of the cycle. Keep early dating steadier:
      - don’t over-fuse quickly,
      - maintain your routines and friends,
      - avoid fantasy-planning too early,
      - let compatibility reveal itself over time.
Intensity can mask instability.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>6. Get therapy focused on attachment and relationship patterns</title>
    <detail>This is very workable in therapy. Look for someone who understands attachment, intimacy avoidance, self-sabotage, or repetition patterns in relationships. The goal is not just to “cope with heartbreak,” but to understand why security feels deadening or threatening to you.</detail>
  </step>
  <step>
    <title>7. Be careful with exes</title>
    <detail>If you repeatedly go back once someone leaves, be honest with yourself: are you trying to build something different, or are you trying to soothe the panic of abandonment? Unless you can name what will change behaviorally, going back often just reopens the same wound for both people.</detail>
  </step>
</steps>

For the heartbreak specifically:

<heartbreak>
  <point>Do not romanticize the relationship only after it ends. Write down what you actually did when they were present, not just what you feel now that they’re absent.</point>
  <point>Limit contact with exes if contact keeps reactivating the longing.</point>
  <point>When you miss them, ask: do I miss them, or do I miss being chosen, wanted, or not abandoned?</point>
  <point>Let yourself grieve without converting grief into a rescue mission.</point>
</heartbreak>

A useful question going forward is: “When someone becomes safely available to me, what story do I start telling myself that makes me pull away?” That story is probably the key.

If this pattern has happened across multiple relationships, don’t wait for another breakup to investigate it. Work on it before dating again, or at least while dating very slowly and consciously. The problem is not just that you want people after they leave. The deeper problem is that you seem to struggle to tolerate being loved once you have it.
</response>

response:
<advice>You should treat his throwing things, head-bashing, and cruel statements as relationship-defining problems, not side issues. Whether or not he is on the spectrum, those behaviors make the relationship unsafe and prevent real repair. Do not talk yourself into minimizing them because you miss him.</advice>
  <advice>"Just because of lack of sex and romance" is understating the situation. What you described is chronic rejection, poor communication, failed conflict resolution, frightening anger behavior, and a relationship in which you have been compensating for unmet needs for years.</advice>
  <advice>Your guilt is partly about how you said it. Saying you don't think he has ever been in love with you was likely more injuring than necessary. If you speak again, correct that. Do not debate his inner feelings. Talk about observable reality: "I have felt unwanted, emotionally alone, and unsafe during conflict for a long time. I asked for change and it did not happen." That is clearer and fairer.</advice>
  <advice>Do not rush to reunite just to stop the pain. Missing him the day after a separation is not evidence that ending or pausing was wrong. It is evidence that attachment is painful to interrupt, especially when you have built your lives around each other.</advice>
  <advice>If you are unsure whether this is a final breakup, make the uncertainty structured instead of chaotic. Tell him you need a defined period of space, and during that period there should be no relationship talks in unplanned emotional bursts. If contact is necessary, keep it practical and time-limited.</advice>
  <advice>If there is any path to reconsidering the marriage, it should depend on concrete conditions, not promises made in distress. At minimum: no throwing things, no self-harm displays in conflict, no cruel statements, and active work with a therapist who understands autism and emotional regulation. Separate from that, the two of you would need explicit discussions about intimacy, romance, and whether your needs are actually compatible.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to ask yourself a blunt question: if he never became more sexual, romantic, or emotionally expressive than he is now, and conflict remained hard even with effort, would this still be enough for you? If the answer is no, love alone is not a reason to stay married.</advice>
  <advice>Do not frame this as you being selfish for needing sex, romance, safety, and repair. Those are core relationship needs. The mistake was not having them; it was trying for too long to survive without them and hoping love would make the deprivation tolerable.</advice>
  <advice>Right now, focus on three things: physical and emotional safety, reducing impulsive contact, and getting outside support for yourself. You are especially vulnerable to backtracking because you say neither of you has many friends and you rely on each other for everything. Increase support before making the next decision.</advice>
  <advice>If you choose to send one message soon, make it brief and stabilizing: that you are sorry for the hurtful way some things came out, that your pain and concerns are real, that you need space to think clearly, and that this is not a conversation to continue in a volatile state.</advice>
