Whether or not he is on the spectrum, those behaviors make the relationship unsafe and prevent real repair. Do not talk yourself into minimizing them because you miss him.</advice>
  <advice>"Just because of lack of sex and romance" is understating the situation. What you described is chronic rejection, poor communication, failed conflict resolution, frightening anger behavior, and a relationship in which you have been compensating for unmet needs for years.</advice>
  <advice>Your guilt is partly about how you said it. Saying you don't think he has ever been in love with you was likely more injuring than necessary. If you speak again, correct that. Do not debate his inner feelings. Talk about observable reality: "I have felt unwanted, emotionally alone, and unsafe during conflict for a long time. I asked for change and it did not happen." That is clearer and fairer.</advice>
  <advice>Do not rush to reunite just to stop the pain. Missing him the day after a separation is not evidence that ending or pausing was wrong. It is evidence that attachment is painful to interrupt, especially when you have built your lives around each other.</advice>
  <advice>If you are unsure whether this is a final breakup, make the uncertainty structured instead of chaotic. Tell him you need a defined period of space, and during that period there should be no relationship talks in unplanned emotional bursts. If contact is necessary, keep it practical and time-limited.</advice>
  <advice>If there is any path to reconsidering the marriage, it should depend on concrete conditions, not promises made in distress. At minimum: no throwing things, no self-harm displays in conflict, no cruel statements, and active work with a therapist who understands autism and emotional regulation. Separate from that, the two of you would need explicit discussions about intimacy, romance, and whether your needs are actually compatible.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to ask yourself a blunt question: if he never became more sexual, romantic, or emotionally expressive than he is now, and conflict remained hard even with effort, would this still be enough for you? If the answer is no, love alone is not a reason to stay married.</advice>
  <advice>Do not frame this as you being selfish for needing sex, romance, safety, and repair. Those are core relationship needs. The mistake was not having them; it was trying for too long to survive without them and hoping love would make the deprivation tolerable.</advice>
  <advice>Right now, focus on three things: physical and emotional safety, reducing impulsive contact, and getting outside support for yourself. You are especially vulnerable to backtracking because you say neither of you has many friends and you rely on each other for everything. Increase support before making the next decision.</advice>

response:
<advice>You need to stop looking for a workaround to women's boundaries. If she has headphones in, is mid-workout, focused between sets, walking quickly, or otherwise occupied, do not approach. There is no respectful "way around" a do-not-disturb signal.</advice>
  <advice>The gym is usually a bad place to hit on strangers. If anything ever happens there, it should be rare, brief, and easy for her to decline without awkwardness. Class is a little better, but only when conversation naturally fits the shared context.</advice>
  <advice>Do not "slowly work your way in" because you see someone often. That is more likely to feel calculated than natural. Instead, use ordinary situational conversation only when there is an actual opening.</advice>
  <advice>Examples of acceptable openings in class:
    <example>"Hey, do you know when that assignment is due?"</example>
    <example>"What did you think of today's lecture?"</example>
    <example>"Are you in this class for the major too?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>Examples of acceptable openings in shared campus settings outside active workouts:
    <example>"Is this seat taken?"</example>
    <example>"Have you tried the coffee here?"</example>
    <example>"You were in Professor X's class too, right?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>Keep the first interaction short and low-stakes. Your goal is not to force chemistry in one shot. It is to see whether she engages back. If she gives short answers, avoids eye contact, turns away, puts headphones back on, or does not ask you anything back, end it immediately.</advice>
  <advice>A good rule: only continue if she is clearly participating. If you are doing all the work, stop. Respect for disinterest is what separates normal from creepy.</advice>
  <advice>When there is actual back-and-forth over more than one interaction, be direct instead of lingering in ambiguity. Say something simple like:
    <example>"I've liked talking with you. Want to grab coffee sometime?"</example>
    <example>"Would you want to study together before the next exam?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>If she says no, seems hesitant, says she has a boyfriend, or gives a vague non-answer, take that as no. Smile, say "No worries," and move on. Do not keep trying in that space.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to get more comfortable with rejection. Right now, avoiding rejection is part of the problem. Rejection is normal data, not a disaster. One respectful ask and one respectful acceptance of no is healthier than trying to engineer a zero-risk approach.</advice>
  <advice>If your real goal is meeting women, put yourself in environments where conversation is expected: student clubs, intramurals, campus events, volunteer groups, mutual friends, study groups, parties, and social mixers. Those settings are much better than interrupting women who are trying to work out.</advice>
  <advice>So the practical formula is:
    <step>1. Don't approach through headphones or during workouts.</step>
    <step>2. Use context-based conversation only when there is a natural opening.</step>
    <step>3. Keep it brief and see if she reciprocates.</step>
    <step>4. Ask directly if there is genuine mutual engagement.</step>
    <step>5. Accept no immediately and completely.</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you follow that, you will come off much less weird than if you try to find "a way" to get around signals that someone wants to be left alone.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You need to stop looking for a workaround to women's boundaries. If she has headphones in, is mid-workout, focused between sets, walking quickly, or otherwise occupied, do not approach. There is no respectful "way around" a do-not-disturb signal.</advice>
  <advice>The gym is usually a bad place to hit on strangers. If anything ever happens there, it should be rare, brief, and easy for her to decline without awkwardness. Class is a little better, but only when conversation naturally fits the shared context.</advice>
  <advice>Do not "slowly work your way in" because you see someone often. That is more likely to feel calculated than natural. Instead, use ordinary situational conversation only when there is an actual opening.</advice>
  <advice>Examples of acceptable openings in class:
    <example>"Hey, do you know when that assignment is due?"</example>
    <example>"What did you think of today's lecture?"</example>
    <example>"Are you in this class for the major too?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>Examples of acceptable openings in shared campus settings outside active workouts:
    <example>"Is this seat taken?"</example>
    <example>"Have you tried the coffee here?"</example>
    <example>"You were in Professor X's class too, right?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>Keep the first interaction short and low-stakes. Your goal is not to force chemistry in one shot. It is to see whether she engages back. If she gives short answers, avoids eye contact, turns away, puts headphones back on, or does not ask you anything back, end it immediately.</advice>
  <advice>A good rule: only continue if she is clearly participating. If you are doing all the work, stop. Respect for disinterest is what separates normal from creepy.</advice>
  <advice>When there is actual back-and-forth over more than one interaction, be direct instead of lingering in ambiguity. Say something simple like:
    <example>"I've liked talking with you. Want to grab coffee sometime?"</example>
    <example>"Would you want to study together before the next exam?"</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>If she says no, seems hesitant, says she has a boyfriend, or gives a vague non-answer, take that as no. Smile, say "No worries," and move on. Do not keep trying in that space.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to get more comfortable with rejection. Right now, avoiding rejection is part of the problem. Rejection is normal data, not a disaster. One respectful ask and one respectful acceptance of no is healthier than trying to engineer a zero-risk approach.</advice>
  <advice>If your real goal is meeting women, put yourself in environments where conversation is expected: student clubs, intramurals, campus events, volunteer groups, mutual friends, study groups, parties, and social mixers. Those settings are much better than interrupting women who are trying to work out.</advice>
  <advice>So the practical formula is:
    <step>1. Don't approach through headphones or during workouts.</step>
    <step>2. Use context-based conversation only when there is a natural opening.</step>
    <step>3. Keep it brief and see if she reciprocates.</step>
    <step>4. Ask directly if there is genuine mutual engagement.</step>
    <step>5. Accept no immediately and completely.</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you follow that, you will come off much less weird than if you try to find "a way" to get around signals that someone wants to be left alone.</advice>
</response>

response:
Stop spamming him. Send one calm final message instead, then stop arguing about it in person.

Use something like:
“I need the money you borrowed from me. You’ve missed several dates over the past year. Please send me [amount] by [specific date]. If you can’t pay all at once, send a written plan with exact amounts and dates by [same date]. If I don’t get payment or a plan, I’ll involve an adult/school staff/your parent.”

Then do these things:

1. Keep evidence.
Save texts, screenshots, the amount, when you gave him the money, and every promised repayment date he missed.

2. Don’t confront him alone if you feel unsafe.
You said he is stronger than you and has a gambling problem. That means you should avoid cornering him, threatening him, or getting into a heated face-to-face discussion.

3. Move it to adults.
If you are both in school, tell a parent, teacher, counselor, or another trusted adult. Show them the messages and missed promises. If you are minors, involving parents/guardians is often the most realistic way to recover the money.

4. If you speak in person, keep it short and public-safe.
Say: “I’m not discussing anything else until we settle the money. Message me by tonight with when you’ll pay.” Then walk away. Don’t keep chasing the conversation.

5. Don’t lend him more money.
A gambling addict is very likely to keep stalling, borrowing, or making promises he won’t keep.

6. Be realistic.
After a year of excuses, there is a real chance you may not get it back unless an adult steps in. Your goal now is to maximize your chances safely, not to win an argument.

7. If the amount is significant and you are not minors, consider formal options.
Depending on where you live, that could mean a written demand message/letter or small claims court. But if you are in school and especially if you are under 18, adult help should come first.

Main point: one clear deadline, no more spam, no unsafe confrontation, involve adults fast.

Do not try to figure out a way to die for an insurance payout. I can’t help with suicide methods, making a death look payable, or getting around policy exclusions.

What you should do right now is put time and distance between yourself and any means of harming yourself, and contact a real person immediately:
<steps>
  <step>If you might act on this soon, call emergency services now or go to the nearest ER.</step>
  <step>Call or text a crisis line now. If you’re in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988. If elsewhere, contact your local emergency or suicide crisis service immediately.</step>
  <step>Tell one person directly: “I am thinking about killing myself and I need you to stay with me and help me get urgent support.”</step>
  <step>Do not stay alone if you are at risk.</step>
</steps>

On the insurance question: life insurance often has suicide exclusions, contestability review, and claims investigation. A suicide attempt or death can leave your family with no payout, legal and financial complications, and lasting trauma. It is not a dependable way to solve debt.

On the debt question: debt can be negotiated, refinanced, settled, disputed, put on hardship plans, or handled through legal/financial counseling. Those are solvable problems. Your death is not a financial plan.

Say this to your parents or another trusted adult exactly: “I’m in danger because I’ve been thinking about suicide over debt. I need help today.” If speaking feels impossible, send it by text right now.

If you want, I can help you with one safe next step only: drafting that text, making a short crisis plan for the next hour, or listing debt-relief options that do not involve harming yourself.

response:
You need to stop treating every worried thought as useful information.

If things "almost always" turn out much better than you expect, then your worry is not accurately warning you most of the time. It is rehearsing bad outcomes. The goal is not to eliminate concern completely; it is to train yourself to relate to it differently.

Try this:

<step>1. Separate possibility from probability.</step>
When you catch yourself worrying, ask:
- "What exactly am I predicting?"
- "How likely is this, really?"
- "What usually happens in similar situations?"

A lot of worry survives by staying vague. Make it specific.

<step>2. Write down predictions.</step>
Keep a simple note with three columns:
- What I’m worried will happen
- How likely I think it is
- What actually happened

Do this consistently. You need evidence your brain can’t keep rewriting afterward. Over time, you’ll build a record showing how often your fear exaggerates.

<step>3. Set a worry time.</step>
If a worry shows up, don’t immediately follow it. Tell yourself:
- "I’ll think about this at 7:00 for 15 minutes."

Then return to what you were doing. If it still matters during worry time, look at it then. This trains your mind that worry does not get instant access to your attention.

<step>4. Ask whether the thought is actionable.</step>
For any worry, decide:
- Can I do something about this now?
- If yes, what is the next concrete step?
- If no, then thinking about it repeatedly is not problem-solving.

Action reduces anxiety. Rumination feeds it.

<step>5. Replace reassurance-seeking with tolerance.</step>
Don’t aim for "I know for sure this will be fine." Aim for:
- "I can handle not knowing yet."
- "I don’t need certainty to move forward."

People who worry a lot often chase certainty, but certainty is rarely available.

<step>6. Stop using self-attack as motivation.</step>
Calling it a terrible habit may make you more tense, not less. A more useful frame is:
- "My brain has learned to overprepare."
That is something you can retrain. Harshness usually increases the cycle.

<step>7. Reduce physical fuel for worry.</step>
Make sure you are checking the basics:
- sleep
- caffeine
- alcohol
- constant phone/news checking
- lack of exercise

An anxious body produces an anxious mind more easily.

<step>8. Practice brief interruption skills.</step>
When you notice the spiral starting:
- take 5 slow breaths
- name 5 things you see
- relax your jaw and shoulders
- return to the next task in front of you

This will not solve the whole pattern, but it can stop escalation.

If your worry is frequent, hard to control, affects sleep, work, relationships, or you spend a lot of time mentally rehearsing bad outcomes, talk to a therapist. CBT is especially useful for this because it directly targets distorted predictions, rumination, and avoidance.

A simple rule to start today:
For the next two weeks, every time you worry, write the prediction down and check later what actually happened.

That will give you something better than a feeling: a track record.

response:
<advice>
    Stop aiming to become the "alpha" or avoid being the "beta." That framework is the biggest thing likely to make this worse. People usually respect calm self-possession, initiative, consistency, and social ease—not attempts to climb an invisible dominance ladder.

    Focus on changing your role in concrete ways:

    <point>
      Speak earlier, not louder. If plans are being made, contribute near the start: "We should try X," "I'm free Saturday," "Let's book this now." People who help create momentum tend to feel more central.
    </point>

    <point>
      Initiate one-on-one and small-group plans yourself. Do not wait for the more dominant friend to be the social engine. Invite people directly: coffee after work, a game night, a meal, a weekend activity. If you are only present when someone else organizes, you will keep feeling like you are tagging along.
    </point>

    <point>
      Build direct relationships with individuals in the group. If your bond to the group mostly runs through your close friend, then of course you will feel secondary to him. Talk to people separately, learn their interests, follow up on prior conversations, and create independent rapport.
    </point>

    <point>
      Practice concise assertiveness. Being quieter does not mean being less respected, but being passive often does. Use simple statements instead of hesitant ones. Compare:
      <example>Weak: "I don't mind, whatever you guys want."</example>
      <example>Better: "I'd rather go to the other place."</example>
      <example>Weak: "Maybe we could do this, if that's okay?"</example>
      <example>Better: "Let's do this first."</example>
    </point>

    <point>
      Bring value to interactions without trying to dominate them. Be the person who follows through, remembers details, makes useful suggestions, helps organize, introduces ideas, or keeps the mood steady. Respect often comes from reliability and presence more than charisma.
    </point>

    <point>
      Watch for self-erasing habits. If you routinely defer, laugh off your own preferences, wait to be asked, or physically hang back, people may unconsciously place you at the edge of the group. Small behavioral changes matter: stand with the group, make eye contact, finish your sentences, and do not preemptively minimize yourself.
    </point>

    <point>
      Do not turn your friend into your rival. If he is naturally more outgoing, that does not mean you have to beat him. You need your own social identity, not a higher rank than his.
    </point>

    <point>
      If there is one specific pattern of exclusion, test it directly and calmly. For example: "I've noticed plans sometimes get made without me knowing until later—can you loop me in?" That is much better than carrying a vague grievance about respect.
    </point>

    Also be honest with yourself: if this group genuinely does not make space for you even when you initiate, contribute, and connect directly, then the answer may not be "be more dominant." It may be to invest more in other friendships where your presence is naturally wanted.

    Your goal should be: more agency, more direct connection, less status obsession.
  </advice>

<advice>
    <point>
      No, it would not be wrong to decline. Being asked to volunteer is one thing; being unable to give up a full Friday shift’s wages when you rely on that income is a legitimate reason to say no.
    </point>
    <point>
      The key issue is not whether the cause is worthy. It is. The issue is that your boss is asking employees, many of them casual, to absorb the cost of the fundraiser through unpaid labor. You do not have to do that if it would hurt your household.
    </point>
    <point>
      Decline clearly and briefly. You do not need to argue the ethics of the whole event unless you want to. Something like:
      <example>
        “I’m sorry, but I can’t afford to work an unpaid shift that night. I hope the event goes well, but I won’t be able to volunteer.”
      </example>
    </point>
    <point>
      If you want, you can offer a smaller form of support that fits your budget, but only if you genuinely can. For example:
      <example>
        “I can’t donate a full unpaid shift, but I’d be happy to help in a small way that doesn’t affect my wages.”
      </example>
      That is optional, not required.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the request did not feel truly optional, pay attention to that. Group requests in a workplace can create pressure, especially for casual staff. You are allowed to treat this as a work-boundary issue, not a test of compassion.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep your explanation focused on your own situation rather than criticizing the family or the fundraiser. That avoids unnecessary hurt while still protecting your interests.
    </point>
  </advice>

response:
Stop trying to convince him to become a different kind of person, and start setting limits on what you will participate in.

Don’t say, “You never change” or “You only talk about yourself.” Say what you need instead:
- “I can listen for a bit, but I don’t have the energy for a long rant right now.”
- “I want our conversations to go both ways.”
- “If you just need to vent, ask me first.”
- “I’m going to hop off now—take care.”

If he starts monologuing again, interrupt earlier rather than waiting until you’re fed up:
- “Hold on, I want to say something too.”
- “Can we switch topics?”
- “I don’t have space for this conversation right now.”

The key is consistency. If you keep listening for a long time and only object once you’re exhausted, he may not take the boundary seriously. Short, repeated limits work better than one big frustrated talk.

Also decide what outcome you actually want:
- If you want to keep the friendship, reduce access and redirect conversations.
- If you want distance, take it without making it a debate about his personality.

If he ignores clear boundaries repeatedly, then accept that this may be the limit of the friendship. You do not need to keep serving as an audience just because you’re a nice person. Being a good friend does not require unlimited listening.

response:
What you described is not normal parent behavior, and you are not overreacting.

Your mother has crossed major boundaries:
- using you as emotional support for adult problems for years,
- making you responsible for her feelings,
- saying she loves you more than your brothers,
- lying or manipulating you about your dad not wanting you,
- sexualizing your body and identity,
- repeatedly bringing up sexual content after you were uncomfortable,
- involving your stepdad in that sexualized discussion.

That last part is especially serious. Treat it as a safety issue, not just a “bad conversation.”

What to do next:

<step>1</step>
Tell your dad. Be specific. Do not minimize it. Include the sexual comments, the claim about your body being “destined” for pregnancy, the statement that you could not be a man until sexual contact with a man, and the part about her talking to your stepdad about a genital encounter. Those details matter.

<step>2</step>
Reduce contact with your mother immediately if you can. If you are abroad now, keep communication to text or email when possible. Written communication gives you distance and a record. You do not owe her live access to you.

<step>3</step>
Do not be alone with her if you can avoid it, especially if conversations tend to become sexual, coercive, or reality-distorting. If you must interact, keep it brief and public or with another safe adult aware of the situation.

<step>4</step>
Write down what happened. Dates, approximate dates, exact phrases if you remember them, and who was present. Save messages. This is useful both for your own clarity and in case you need support from family, school staff, or a professional.

<step>5</step>
Get support where you are now:
- a college counselor,
- a therapist,
- student services,
- an LGBTQ support office or group,
- a trusted adult through school.
You need someone offline and real who can help you think through safety and boundaries.

<step>6</step>
Separate your brothers’ wellbeing from your responsibility for managing your mother. Caring about them is good, but staying exposed to harmful behavior is not the price of loving them. response:
You do it by changing the goal from “convince myself I don’t want it” to “let myself want it without obeying the want.”

Wanting something and not buying it is not a failure to satisfy yourself. It’s a normal part of having preferences while also having limits, priorities, and a future.

Use a simple process:

<step>1. Name it clearly.</step>
Tell yourself: “I want this, but I do not need it, and I am choosing not to buy it today.”  
That keeps you out of the foggy zone where every want starts sounding like a need.

<step>2. Add delay.</step>
Use a waiting rule:
- 24 hours for small purchases
- 7 days for medium ones
- 30 days for expensive ones

A lot of desire is temporary intensity, not lasting value.

<step>3. Keep a wish list instead of a cart.</step>
Put the item on a list with:
- price
- date added
- why you want it
- what problem it actually solves

If you still want it after the waiting period, you can review it calmly. Often the urge fades once it’s captured.

<step>4. Ask what you’re really buying.</step>
Sometimes the item is standing in for:
- novelty
- comfort
- status
- fantasy-self identity
- relief from boredom

If you know the real need, you can meet it more cheaply or more honestly.

<step>5. Compare it to what the money does if untouched.</step>
Don’t compare “item vs nothing.” Compare:
- item vs less financial stress
- item vs savings
- item vs travel
- item vs debt reduction
- item vs freedom later

That makes “not buying” feel like choosing something, not losing something.

<step>6. Expect a little disappointment.</step>
You do not need to eliminate all bad feelings. Sometimes the healthy choice still feels mildly bad for a moment. The goal is not “feel nothing,” but “don’t turn temporary disappointment into regret or self-pity.”

<step>7. Use language that prevents deprivation thinking.</step>
Instead of:
- “I can’t have it”
say:
- “I’m not choosing it”
- “Not now”
- “I like it, but it’s not worth the tradeoff”
- “I’m keeping my money for things I value more”

That preserves agency.

<step>8. Create a controlled fun budget.</step>
If you never allow any discretionary spending, every resisted purchase feels tragic. Give yourself a defined amount for wants. Then the question becomes: “Is this how I want to use my fun money?” not “Am I allowed to enjoy anything?”

<step>9. Review your non-purchases.</step>
Once a month, look back at things you wanted and didn’t buy. Notice how many you barely remember now. That evidence is what teaches your brain that missing a purchase is usually harmless.

A useful final rule:
If the pleasure mostly comes from imagining owning it, not from realistically using it, don’t buy it.

You don’t need to stop wanting unnecessary things. You need to get comfortable letting some wants pass through without becoming purchases. That’s a skill, and it gets easier every time you practice it.

response:
<advice>You should stop treating this as mainly a kink problem. It is a cheating and accountability problem.</advice>
  <advice>His BDSM interests are not the issue. His shame is not the issue. The issue is that, three times, he chose sexual contact with other women instead of dealing honestly with his feelings, his desires, or the state of the relationship.</advice>
  <advice>You have already done the fair things. You listened. You did not shame him. You respected his boundaries. You offered acceptance and exploration. Those were meaningful efforts, and they did not stop the behavior.</advice>
  <advice>So do not ask yourself, “How can I reassure him better?” Ask, “What evidence is there that he is willing to become trustworthy?” From what you wrote, the evidence is weak. He has explanations, but not change.</advice>
  <advice>If you stay, only do it with a hard boundary and a concrete repair plan, not with hope alone. That would mean: he fully acknowledges this was cheating, stops contacting other women, accepts transparency if you both agree to it, and gets individual therapy focused on shame, sexual self-acceptance, and dishonesty. If he will not do that consistently, staying is just volunteering for a fourth time.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to be honest about compatibility. If he cannot be sexually open with you, and you cannot trust him, the relationship may be over even if you still love each other. Love and history do not fix repeated betrayal.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let “he’s a good person” make the decision for you. People can have good qualities and still be unsafe partners. Right now, he is not behaving like a trustworthy partner.</advice>
  <advice>If you leave, that does not mean you failed to understand him. It means you refused to keep paying the price for his unresolved shame.</advice>
  <advice>A simple version to tell yourself is: “I can have compassion for why he did it without accepting it again.”</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should stop treating this as mainly a kink problem. It is a cheating and accountability problem.</advice>
  <advice>His BDSM interests are not the issue. His shame is not the issue. The issue is that, three times, he chose sexual contact with other women instead of dealing honestly with his feelings, his desires, or the state of the relationship.</advice>
  <advice>You have already done the fair things. You listened. You did not shame him. You respected his boundaries. You offered acceptance and exploration. Those were meaningful efforts, and they did not stop the behavior.</advice>
  <advice>So do not ask yourself, “How can I reassure him better?” Ask, “What evidence is there that he is willing to become trustworthy?” From what you wrote, the evidence is weak. He has explanations, but not change.</advice>
  <advice>If you stay, only do it with a hard boundary and a concrete repair plan, not with hope alone. That would mean: he fully acknowledges this was cheating, stops contacting other women, accepts transparency if you both agree to it, and gets individual therapy focused on shame, sexual self-acceptance, and dishonesty. If he will not do that consistently, staying is just volunteering for a fourth time.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to be honest about compatibility. If he cannot be sexually open with you, and you cannot trust him, the relationship may be over even if you still love each other. Love and history do not fix repeated betrayal.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let “he’s a good person” make the decision for you. People can have good qualities and still be unsafe partners. Right now, he is not behaving like a trustworthy partner.</advice>
  <advice>If you leave, that does not mean you failed to understand him. It means you refused to keep paying the price for his unresolved shame.</advice>
  <advice>A simple version to tell yourself is: “I can have compassion for why he did it without accepting it again.”</advice>
</response>

response:
You could potentially be billed for past service, but it depends on how trash service is structured where the house is.

Do this now:
<step>Call the city/county sanitation office or the actual hauler and ask how service for that address is supposed to be billed.</step>
<step>Also check whether trash charges are included in property taxes, water/sewer bills, HOA dues, or another municipal fee. The fact that there is “no account on file” does not necessarily mean the service is free.</step>
<step>Tell them the property was inherited, give the service address, the date ownership changed, and ask whether there is any outstanding balance and who is legally responsible for it.</step>
<step>Ask for the answer in writing if possible.</step>

Important distinction:
<point>If unpaid charges were incurred before your father died, those may be obligations of his estate rather than your personal debt.</point>
<point>If charges continued after you became owner and the service should have been billed, you may be responsible from the date you took ownership or accepted service, depending on local rules.</point>

You should also review:
<item>recent property tax statements</item>
<item>water/utility bills</item>
<item>closing or probate paperwork</item>
<item>any mail addressed to your father from the city or trash company</item>

If they say money is owed, ask:
<item>what period the charges cover</item>
<item>whether they are tied to the estate or to you as current owner</item>
<item>whether there are late fees</item>
<item>whether they will waive penalties because there was no active bill or account visible</item>

If probate is still open, tell the executor or probate attorney before paying old charges yourself.

So: yes, back pay is possible, but not automatic, and not necessarily all your personal responsibility. The safest move is to notify the relevant office now and get the billing basis clarified.

response:
<advice>You do know where this is coming from. It is coming from a long pattern in which Steve has had too much access to the emotional, social, and symbolic spaces that usually belong to a current partner.</advice>
  <advice>The main issue is not that James “no longer wants to hang out with your ex.” The issue is that you have treated Steve less like a peripheral friend in a shared circle and more like a special person whose place stays protected no matter what it costs your relationship.</advice>
  <advice>Your first step should be to stop arguing the principle and acknowledge the pattern plainly to James. Say, in substance: you raised this many times, I minimized it, I kept escalating the closeness with Steve, and I can see why that hurt and disrespected you.</advice>
  <advice>Do not make this apology conditional on James being “insecure” or “jealous.” Based on your own description, his reaction is not hard to understand.</advice>
  <advice>If you want to preserve your relationship with James, you need boundaries with Steve that are clear and immediate:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>Stop daily or near-daily private contact.</point>
    <point>Stop one-on-one dinners and frequent hangouts for now.</point>
    <point>Keep contact to occasional group settings if any contact continues.</point>
    <point>Do not invite Steve to family events, couple-centered events, birthdays organized by James, or intimate inner-circle gatherings.</point>
    <point>Stop behaviors that read as paired or couple-like: matching clothes, special presentation roles, flirty or boundary-blurring jokes.</point>
    <point>Remove or archive the Steve-centered social media content that is predictably hurtful, especially the nude/jokey photo.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>You also need to separate two issues that you are currently mixing together:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>Your concerns about sex, passion, dominance, and affection with James.</point>
    <point>Your attachment and boundary problems involving Steve.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>Bring the first issue to James cleanly, without mentioning Steve. For example: I want to talk about feeling more desired, more passion, and more affection between us. What you should not do is use James’s discomfort around Steve as evidence that James is failing you romantically.</advice>
  <advice>You should also ask yourself a harder question: why are you protecting this level of closeness with Steve so strongly? Shared friend group alone does not explain weekly contact, daily messaging, intimate inclusion, matching-clothes situations, and visible special status. If the honest answer is that Steve still fills an emotional role that competes with your partner, you need to admit that to yourself.</advice>
  <advice>If you are unwilling to reduce contact with Steve and redraw the relationship sharply, then be honest: you may not be in a position to offer James the kind of partnership he wants. In that case, the fair move is not to keep insisting he tolerate it.</advice>
  <advice>If you do want to repair this, act quickly and concretely. Words alone will not help much now because James has already had many chances to believe your priorities from your behavior, and your behavior has repeatedly placed Steve very high.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You do know where this is coming from. It is coming from a long pattern in which Steve has had too much access to the emotional, social, and symbolic spaces that usually belong to a current partner.</advice>
  <advice>The main issue is not that James “no longer wants to hang out with your ex.” The issue is that you have treated Steve less like a peripheral friend in a shared circle and more like a special person whose place stays protected no matter what it costs your relationship.</advice>
  <advice>Your first step should be to stop arguing the principle and acknowledge the pattern plainly to James. Say, in substance: you raised this many times, I minimized it, I kept escalating the closeness with Steve, and I can see why that hurt and disrespected you.</advice>
  <advice>Do not make this apology conditional on James being “insecure” or “jealous.” Based on your own description, his reaction is not hard to understand.</advice>
  <advice>If you want to preserve your relationship with James, you need boundaries with Steve that are clear and immediate:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>Stop daily or near-daily private contact.</point>
    <point>Stop one-on-one dinners and frequent hangouts for now.</point>
    <point>Keep contact to occasional group settings if any contact continues.</point>
    <point>Do not invite Steve to family events, couple-centered events, birthdays organized by James, or intimate inner-circle gatherings.</point>
    <point>Stop behaviors that read as paired or couple-like: matching clothes, special presentation roles, flirty or boundary-blurring jokes.</point>
    <point>Remove or archive the Steve-centered social media content that is predictably hurtful, especially the nude/jokey photo.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>You also need to separate two issues that you are currently mixing together:</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>Your concerns about sex, passion, dominance, and affection with James.</point>
    <point>Your attachment and boundary problems involving Steve.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>Bring the first issue to James cleanly, without mentioning Steve. For example: I want to talk about feeling more desired, more passion, and more affection between us. What you should not do is use James’s discomfort around Steve as evidence that James is failing you romantically.</advice>
  <advice>You should also ask yourself a harder question: why are you protecting this level of closeness with Steve so strongly? Shared friend group alone does not explain weekly contact, daily messaging, intimate inclusion, matching-clothes situations, and visible special status. If the honest answer is that Steve still fills an emotional role that competes with your partner, you need to admit that to yourself.</advice>
  <advice>If you are unwilling to reduce contact with Steve and redraw the relationship sharply, then be honest: you may not be in a position to offer James the kind of partnership he wants. In that case, the fair move is not to keep insisting he tolerate it.</advice>
  <advice>If you do want to repair this, act quickly and concretely. Words alone will not help much now because James has already had many chances to believe your priorities from your behavior, and your behavior has repeatedly placed Steve very high.</advice>
</response>

<advice>You do not need to tell him he is “selfish in bed.” You need to tell him you do not want to sleep together again.</advice>
  <advice>Keep the first message short, clear, and non-debatable. Something like:</advice>
  <example>“I’ve thought about it, and I don’t want to keep this sexual. I’d rather go back to being friends and not hook up again.”</example>
  <advice>If you want, add one sentence that makes the reason broad without turning it into a takedown:</advice>
  <example>“The sexual chemistry/compatibility isn’t there for me.”</example>
  <advice>That is enough. It answers his invitation, sets the boundary, and does not invite an argument about individual sex acts.</advice>

  <advice>If he accepts it, stop there. Do not volunteer the whole review of his sexual performance. Your goal is to end the sexual part, not teach a masterclass he did not ask for.</advice>

  <advice>If he asks why, you can be honest without being cruel:</advice>
  <example>“I didn’t feel like it was mutually satisfying for me, even though I tried to communicate in the moment. That’s why I don’t want to do it again.”</example>

  <advice>If he genuinely asks for feedback and seems able to hear it, keep it behavioral and specific, not global or contemptuous. For example:</advice>
  <example>“What didn’t work for me was that I felt like my pleasure wasn’t being paid attention to. I need a partner who responds to feedback, spends time on what feels good for me, and treats sex as mutual rather than focusing mostly on getting himself off.”</example>

  <advice>Avoid saying things like:</advice>
  <avoid>
    <item>“You’re selfish in bed.”</item>
    <item>“You learned sex from porn.”</item>
    <item>“If you’re going to be a forever bachelor, learn to make women orgasm.”</item>
    <item>“You masturbated with my body.”</item>
  </avoid>
  <advice>Those may reflect your experience, but saying them is much more likely to end the friendship than to help.</advice>

  <advice>You should also be realistic: you can ask to go back to being friends, but you cannot guarantee the friendship survives unchanged. Given that he had wanted sex for years, he may feel rejected, embarrassed, or awkward. That does not mean you should keep sleeping with him.   <steps>

  <advice>You do not need to tell him he is “selfish in bed.” You need to tell him you do not want to sleep together again.</advice>
  <advice>Keep the first message short, clear, and non-debatable. Something like:</advice>
  <example>“I’ve thought about it, and I don’t want to keep this sexual. I’d rather go back to being friends and not hook up again.”</example>
  <advice>If you want, add one sentence that makes the reason broad without turning it into a takedown:</advice>
  <example>“The sexual chemistry/compatibility isn’t there for me.”</example>
  <advice>That is enough. It answers his invitation, sets the boundary, and does not invite an argument about individual sex acts.</advice>

  <advice>If he accepts it, stop there. Do not volunteer the whole review of his sexual performance. Your goal is to end the sexual part, not teach a masterclass he did not ask for.</advice>

  <advice>If he asks why, you can be honest without being cruel:</advice>
  <example>“I didn’t feel like it was mutually satisfying for me, even though I tried to communicate in the moment. That’s why I don’t want to do it again.”</example>

  <advice>If he genuinely asks for feedback and seems able to hear it, keep it behavioral and specific, not global or contemptuous. For example:</advice>
  <example>“What didn’t work for me was that I felt like my pleasure wasn’t being paid attention to. I need a partner who responds to feedback, spends time on what feels good for me, and treats sex as mutual rather than focusing mostly on getting himself off.”</example>

  <advice>Avoid saying things like:</advice>
  <avoid>
    <item>“You’re selfish in bed.”</item>
    <item>“You learned sex from porn.”</item>
    <item>“If you’re going to be a forever bachelor, learn to make women orgasm.”</item>
    <item>“You masturbated with my body.”</item>
  </avoid>
  <advice>Those may reflect your experience, but saying them is much more likely to end the friendship than to help.</advice>

  <advice>You should also be realistic: you can ask to go back to being friends, but you cannot guarantee the friendship survives unchanged. Given that he had wanted sex for years, he may feel rejected, embarrassed, or awkward. That does not mean you should keep sleeping with him. It just means “back to normal” may not be fully available.</advice>

  <advice>If preserving the friendship matters, your best chance is:</advice>
  <steps>
    <item>Decline the hookup clearly.</item>
    <item>Do not overexplain.</item>
    <item>Do not insult his character.</item>
    <item>If he pushes, repeat the boundary instead of litigating the sexual encounter.</item>
  </steps>

  <advice>For example, if he argues:</advice>
  <example>“I’m not looking to troubleshoot this or try again. I just don’t want a sexual relationship here.”</example>

  <advice>And privately, the lesson is simpler than “how do I fix him”: when you already think someone is selfish, immature, and bad relationship material, do not make them your convenience hookup and expect a clean reset afterward.</advice>
</response>

<advice>
    <point>Stop aiming to be “interesting.” Aim to be easy to talk to. Good conversations are usually built from attention, not performance.</point>
    <point>Use a simple structure: ask, react, follow up, then share. Example:
      <example>“How was your weekend?”</example>
      <example>“Oh, you went hiking? Nice.”</example>
      <example>“Where did you go?”</example>
      <example>“I’ve been meaning to try that trail myself.”</example>
      This keeps the conversation moving without turning it into an interview.</point>
    <point>To get past small talk, ask slightly more specific questions. Instead of:
      <example>“How are you?”</example>
      try:
      <example>“What’s been the best part of your week?”</example>
      <example>“How did you get into that?”</example>
      <example>“What do you like most about it?”</example>
      <example>“What’s been keeping you busy lately?”</example>
      Specific questions give people something real to answer.</point>
    <point>Use the “thread” method. In almost every reply, people give you multiple possible threads. If someone says,
      <example>“I was tired because I stayed up finishing a project and then had class early,”</example>
      you can ask about the project, the class, being tired, or how they manage both. Pick one thread and continue.</point>
    <point>Share a little about yourself after a follow-up. If you only ask questions, it can feel formal. If you only talk about yourself, it feels one-sided. A balanced rhythm is:
      <example>them → you ask → they answer → you relate briefly → new question</example>
    </point>
    <point>Don’t confuse introversion with inability. Introversion usually means social interaction can drain you, not that you can’t learn conversation. Treat this as a skill: practiceable, repeatable, improvable.</point>
    <point>Over text, shorter is better. Don’t try to force long, perfect messages. Use:
      <example>comment + question</example>
      For example:
      <example>“That sounds stressful. Did it end up going okay?”</example>
      or
      <example>“I didn’t know you were into that—how did you start?”</example>
    </point>
    <point>Have a few reliable topic buckets ready:
      <example>current plans</example>
      <example>recent experiences</example>
      <example>opinions/preferences</example>

<point>Stop describing this to yourself and to her as “irrational.” That word is likely making the conversation harder. The issue is not whether her fear is logically justified; the issue is that she feels unsafe and unconvinced during your trips.</point>
  <point>Talk about it when you are home and calm, not during a trip and not in the middle of a reassurance spiral. Ask directly: “What does your mind tell you is happening when I travel?” and “What moments make it spike most?” Your goal is to understand the pattern, not to debate her out of it.</point>
  <point>Explain the hallway/balcony thing plainly and proactively: “When I step out, it’s to keep a co-worker from overhearing, not to hide anything from you.” Then change the setup where possible so the explanation is not the only reassurance. If you can call from a more clearly private place, do that. If your room is shared, say so upfront before the call instead of disappearing offscreen unexpectedly.</point>
  <point>Build a predictable travel routine together. Keep it simple and sustainable, for example:
    <item>a short check-in when you arrive,</item>
    <item>a message before dinner or after the work event,</item>
    <item>one planned call at a time that usually works,</item>
    <item>a goodnight text.</item>
    Predictability usually helps more than frequent ad hoc reassurance.</point>
  <point>Do not let this become an inspection system where you are repeatedly proving you are alone in your room. That may soothe her briefly but usually strengthens the anxiety long term. Reassurance is useful; surveillance is not.</point>
  <point>Ask her what would feel reassuring without crossing into monitoring. Then say clearly what you can and cannot do. For example: “I can check in consistently and be transparent about my schedule. I can’t do surprise proof-of-location calls whenever anxiety spikes.”</point>
  <point>If she found cheating statistics, do not argue statistics back at her. Statistics are not evidence about you. Bring the conversation back to your actual marriage, your actual behavior, and what trust-building habits would help.</point>
  <point>Also ask whether this fear is only about travel or whether it connects to a larger insecurity, prior betrayal, anxiety, or distance between you lately. If it has been building for months, the trips may be the trigger rather than the root cause.</point>
  <point>If the fear keeps recurring despite good-faith efforts from both of you, get couples counseling. If her anxiety is intense and persistent, individual therapy for her may also help. The target should not be “convince her harder”; it should be understanding the insecurity, setting healthy reassurance habits, and rebuilding trust without turning your work trips into a recurring crisis.</point>
  <point>A useful sentence to start with: “I don’t want to dismiss this or argue about whether you should feel it. I want to understand what happens for you when I travel, and I want us to find a way to handle it that helps you feel more secure without turning this into constant checking.”</point>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Focus less on “becoming impossible to overpower” and more on building a repeated sense of agency. The feeling you describe often lingers long after the actual danger is reduced, because your body learned powerlessness as a survival state. That means the target is not just strength; it is retraining yourself to experience choice, influence, and self-trust over and over.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep the no-contact boundary if it is helping. Powerlessness often gets reactivated by renewed exposure, even indirect exposure. If there are loopholes—checking his social media, hearing updates through relatives, drafting messages you never send—tightening those can help your nervous system stop bracing for him.
    </point>
    <point>
      Since therapy was only somewhat helpful, get more specific rather than giving up on it broadly. Look for someone explicitly experienced in trauma, childhood abuse, or CPTSD, and ask directly about modalities like EMDR, somatic therapies, trauma-focused CBT, or parts work/IFS. “General therapy” and “trauma treatment” are often very different experiences.
    </point>
    <point>
      Build competence in non-combat domains that make you feel hard to corner in real life:
      <items>
        <item>Assertiveness training or a class on boundaries</item>
        <item>Learning de-escalation and conflict skills</item>
        <item>Practical self-protection habits: exits, rides, finances, privacy, document control</item>
        <item>Strength training with measurable progress</item>
        <item>A skill where you can visibly improve—music, coding, climbing alternatives approved by your doctor, public speaking, repair work, anything concrete</item>
      </items>
      Competence reduces helplessness because it gives your brain evidence: “I can act effectively.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Work specifically on the body-state of powerlessness. Abuse often leaves people freezing, shrinking, appeasing, or mentally disappearing. Helpful practices can include:
      <items>
        <item>Grounding that uses posture: feet planted, shoulders back, slow exhale</item>
        <item>Practicing saying “no,” “stop,” and “I’m leaving” out loud</item>
        <item>Short exercises where you take up space physically and breathe through the discomfort</item>
        <item>Noticing when you automatically submit in low-stakes situations and experimenting with one small act of choice</item>
      </items>
      The point is to teach your nervous system that you can remain present and act.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep lifting if it helps, but define progress broadly. Strength matters, but so do endurance, balance, mobility, posture, and the feeling of inhabiting your body confidently. If martial arts are off the table medically, that does not mean physical empowerment is off the table.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use “micro-agency” daily. Pick small actions where you deliberately choose, act, and notice the result:
      <items>
        <item>Make one decision quickly instead of overchecking</item>
        <item>Send one message you have been avoiding</item>
        <item>Set one limit without overexplaining</item>
        <item>Leave one situation earlier when you want to</item>
      </items>
      Feeling powerful usually returns in small repetitions, not one big breakthrough.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you notice the core belief is something like “I am still the smaller, trapped one,” challenge that belief with concrete evidence rather than positive self-talk. Write down:
      <items>
        <item>What I could not do then</item>
        <item>What I can do now</item>
        <item>What protections I have now</item>
        <item>Who I can call now</item>
        <item>What choices are available now</item>
      </items>
      Trauma often collapses time. This helps separate past reality from present reality.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you want a more direct substitute for martial arts, look into medically appropriate options such as supervised strength coaching, swimming, rowing, hiking, boxing-style conditioning without sparring if safe, adaptive sports, or even voice/assertiveness coaching. The exact activity matters less than repeatedly feeling: “I can generate force, tolerate discomfort, and improve.”
    </point>
    <point>
      If these feelings become overwhelming, especially if you get panic, rage, dissociation, or strong freeze responses, that is a sign to seek trauma-focused treatment specifically, not proof that you are failing. The issue may be unresolved trauma physiology more than mindset.
    </point>
    <point>
      A useful question is: “What would a person with agency do next this week?” Not forever—just this week. Then do that. Powerlessness weakens when your actions keep proving you are no longer stuck in his world.
    </point>
  </advice>

    </point>
    <point>
      Keep the no-contact boundary if it is helping. Powerlessness often gets reactivated by renewed exposure, even indirect exposure.     </point>
    <point>
      Since therapy was only somewhat helpful, get more specific rather than giving up on it broadly. Look for someone explicitly experienced in trauma, childhood abuse, or CPTSD, and ask directly about modalities like EMDR, somatic therapies, trauma-focused CBT, or parts work/IFS. “General therapy” and “trauma treatment” are often very different experiences.
    </point>
    <point>
      Build competence in non-combat domains that make you feel hard to corner in real life:
      <items>
        <item>Assertiveness training or a class on boundaries</item>
        <item>Learning de-escalation and conflict skills</item>
        <item>Practical self-protection habits: exits, rides, finances, privacy, document control</item>
        <item>Strength training with measurable progress</item>
        <item>A skill where you can visibly improve—music, coding, climbing alternatives approved by your doctor, public speaking, repair work, anything concrete</item>
      </items>
      Competence reduces helplessness because it gives your brain evidence: “I can act effectively.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Work specifically on the body-state of powerlessness. Abuse often leaves people freezing, shrinking, appeasing, or mentally disappearing. Helpful practices can include:
      <items>
        <item>Grounding that uses posture: feet planted, shoulders back, slow exhale</item>
        <item>Practicing saying “no,” “stop,” and “I’m leaving” out loud</item>
        <item>Short exercises where you take up space physically and breathe through the discomfort</item>
        <item>Noticing when you automatically submit in low-stakes situations and experimenting with one small act of choice</item>
      </items>
      The point is to teach your nervous system that you can remain present and act.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep lifting if it helps, but define progress broadly. Strength matters, but so do endurance, balance, mobility, posture, and the feeling of inhabiting your body confidently. If martial arts are off the table medically, that does not mean physical empowerment is off the table.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use “micro-agency” daily. Pick small actions where you deliberately choose, act, and notice the result:
      <items>
        <item>Make one decision quickly instead of overchecking</item>
        <item>Send one message you have been avoiding</item>
        <item>Set one limit without overexplaining</item>
        <item>Leave one situation earlier when you want to</item>
      </items>
      Feeling powerful usually returns in small repetitions, not one big breakthrough.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you notice the core belief is something like “I am still the smaller, trapped one,” challenge that belief with concrete evidence rather than positive self-talk. Write down:
      <items>
        <item>What I could not do then</item>
        <item>What I can do now</item>
        <item>What protections I have now</item>
        <item>Who I can call now</item>
        <item>What choices are available now</item>
      </items>
      Trauma often collapses time. This helps separate past reality from present reality.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you want a more direct substitute for martial arts, look into medically appropriate options such as supervised strength coaching, swimming, rowing, hiking, boxing-style conditioning without sparring if safe, adaptive sports, or even voice/assertiveness coaching. The exact activity matters less than repeatedly feeling: “I can generate force, tolerate discomfort, and improve.”
    </point>
    <point>
      If these feelings become overwhelming, especially if you get panic, rage, dissociation, or strong freeze responses, that is a sign to seek trauma-focused treatment specifically, not proof that you are failing. The issue may be unresolved trauma physiology more than mindset.
    </point>
    <point>
      A useful question is: “What would a person with agency do next this week?” Not forever—just this week. Then do that. Powerlessness weakens when your actions keep proving you are no longer stuck in his world.
    </point>
  </advice>

You should treat this as a rules-and-documentation problem, not a gray-area workaround.

First, get the exact residency policy for the state and the specific university. Focus on:
  <item>minimum physical presence requirement</item>
  <item>what counts as financial independence</item>
  <item>whether moving primarily for education disqualifies residency</item>
  <item>required documents</item>
  <item>petition/appeal deadlines</item>
  <item>any special categories or exceptions</item>

Then contact the school’s residency review office directly and ask what you are missing by "barely" not qualifying. Ask them to be specific: is it time in state, tax status, voter registration, driver’s license, lease history, employment, dependency on parents, or something else?

Do not guess and do not try to shade facts. If you claim residency without meeting the standard, you could face reclassification, back charges, or disciplinary trouble.

If you are close to qualifying, your best move may be to delay enrollment briefly and spend that time establishing residency cleanly if the rules allow it. That can mean things like:
  <item>living in the state for the required period</item>
  <item>working there</item>
  <item>getting a state ID or driver’s license</item>
  <item>registering to vote if eligible</item>
  <item>filing state taxes there</item>
  <item>keeping leases, utility bills, and employment records</item>

Be careful: in many states, if your primary reason for being there is education, that alone can block residency for tuition purposes. That is why you need the school’s actual standard before making plans.

Also look for alternatives if waiting is not realistic:
  <item>tuition reciprocity agreements with nearby states</item>
  <item>border-county or regional tuition discounts</item>
  <item>institutional aid for out-of-state students</item>
  <item>community college transfer pathways</item>
  <item>employer tuition benefits</item>
  <item>state programs for adult learners or returning students</item>
  <item>scholarships that specifically offset nonresident tuition</item>

If you want, I can help you build a residency checklist if you tell me the state and whether you are financially independent, working, or currently living there.

response:
Stop calling this laziness for now. What you describe often comes from avoidance, overwhelm, low mood, anxiety, ADHD-type attention problems, or a learned habit loop—not a lack of intelligence or character.

Do this in order:

<step>1. Get off the phone before anything else.</step>
Put it in another room for 25 minutes. If needed, give it to someone else, use an app blocker, or turn it fully off. Do not rely on willpower while the distraction is in your hand.

<step>2. Make the task absurdly small.</step>
Not “revise for exam.” Start with one action:
- open notes
- read one page
- answer one question
- write one heading

Your only goal is 5 minutes. You are not committing to finishing, only to starting.

<step>3. Use a visible timer.</step>
Set 5 minutes. When it ends, either stop guilt-free or continue for 10 more. Starting is the bottleneck, so make the starting cost tiny.

<step>4. Remove decision-making.</step>
Write exactly what you will do next in one sentence:
“I will sit at the desk and do questions 1–3.”
Vague goals create paralysis. Specific actions reduce it.

<step>5. Work in short rounds.</step>
Try:
- 10 minutes work
- 2 minutes break
Repeat 3 times.
During breaks, do not touch the phone if possible. Stand up, drink water, stretch.

<step>6. Use external accountability.</step>
Text someone:
“I’m studying from 7:00 to 7:25. I’ll message you when done.”
If you can, study near another person or on a call with cameras on. External structure often works better than self-pressure.

<step>7. For the exam in 24 hours, stop aiming to do everything.</step>
Use triage:
- list all topics
- mark high-yield ones
- do practice questions first
- focus on likely marks, not perfect coverage

A bad plan done now beats the perfect plan delayed.

<step>8. Watch your self-talk.</step>
When you say “I’m lazy,” you create shame, and shame often leads to more avoidance. Replace it with:
“I’m stuck. My job is to make the next step smaller.”

<step>9. Build a default anti-phone setup for daily life.</step>
- charge phone outside reach
- block social apps during study/work hours
- keep only one tab open
- start work at the same place and time each day
- use paper to-do lists with only 1–3 tasks

<step>10. Get assessed if this is lifelong and severe.</step>
Because you said it has been this way all your life and you feel your life is falling apart, you should talk to a doctor, therapist, or school counselor soon. Ask specifically about:
- ADHD/executive dysfunction
- anxiety
- depression
- sleep problems

This matters because the right help may be treatment and structure, not just “try harder.”

Right now, do only this:
- put your phone in another room
- open the exam material
- set a 5-minute timer
- do one question or one page

If you want, I can help you make a 24-hour emergency exam plan right now in a very simple step-by-step format.

<advice>You should not hide it.</advice>
  <advice>A recent five-month relationship with a 19-year-old is plainly relevant information to many women in their late 20s and 30s. You already know that because several women have treated it as a dealbreaker. Once you know something materially affects others' willingness to date you, concealing it to improve your odds stops being harmless privacy and starts becoming misleading.</advice>
  <advice>The bigger problem is not just the past relationship; it's your framing of it. You keep trying to shrink it: "only teenager," "very brief," "not relevant," "I'm not a creep." But five months is not trivial, and whether it was a pattern is not the only issue. The issue for them is that you chose it at all, recently, and only later decided the age gap was too big.</advice>
  <advice>So do two things:</advice>
  <advice>First, be candid earlier. You do not need to lead with a confession on app messages, but before things get serious—and certainly before exclusivity, sex if values-based dealbreakers matter to the other person, or "future" conversations—you should disclose it plainly if past relationships are being discussed. Something like: "Last year I dated someone who was 19 for about five months. I realized the age gap was a mistake for me and ended it. I know that may matter to you, so I'd rather be upfront." Then stop talking. Let them decide.</advice>
  <advice>Second, stop arguing the point in advance. Do not call it brief, do not emphasize that it happened only once, and do not push women to agree that it "doesn't characterize" you. Those points sound defensive, not reflective. Better to show that you understand why it affects their view of your judgment.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to examine your own reasoning more honestly. If the age gap was obviously too big after five months, why was it acceptable at the start? What did you tell yourself then? What needs or preferences made that feel okay? If you cannot answer that well, women will reasonably assume you have not really reckoned with it.</advice>
  <advice>Expect that some women will still reject you over it. That is their right, and it does not become unfair because you think the relationship was legal or atypical. Your job is not to persuade them out of their boundary. Your job is to be honest and let them opt in or out with full information.</advice>
  <advice>In short: disclose, do it earlier than accidental discovery, and drop the minimizing language. If this costs you dating opportunities, that is not a reason to hide it; it is the consequence of a choice you made.</advice>

  <advice>A recent five-month relationship with a 19-year-old is plainly relevant information to many women in their late 20s and 30s. You already know that because several women have treated it as a dealbreaker. Once you know something materially affects others' willingness to date you, concealing it to improve your odds stops being harmless privacy and starts becoming misleading.</advice>
  <advice>The bigger problem is not just the past relationship; it's your framing of it. You keep trying to shrink it: "only teenager," "very brief," "not relevant," "I'm not a creep." But five months is not trivial, and whether it was a pattern is not the only issue. The issue for them is that you chose it at all, recently, and only later decided the age gap was too big.</advice>
  <advice>So do two things:</advice>
  <advice>First, be candid earlier. You do not need to lead with a confession on app messages, but before things get serious—and certainly before exclusivity, sex if values-based dealbreakers matter to the other person, or "future" conversations—you should disclose it plainly if past relationships are being discussed. Something like: "Last year I dated someone who was 19 for about five months. I realized the age gap was a mistake for me and ended it. I know that may matter to you, so I'd rather be upfront." Then stop talking. Let them decide.</advice>
  <advice>Second, stop arguing the point in advance. Do not call it brief, do not emphasize that it happened only once, and do not push women to agree that it "doesn't characterize" you. Those points sound defensive, not reflective. Better to show that you understand why it affects their view of your judgment.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to examine your own reasoning more honestly. If the age gap was obviously too big after five months, why was it acceptable at the start? What did you tell yourself then? What needs or preferences made that feel okay? If you cannot answer that well, women will reasonably assume you have not really reckoned with it.</advice>
  <advice>Expect that some women will still reject you over it. That is their right, and it does not become unfair because you think the relationship was legal or atypical. Your job is not to persuade them out of their boundary. Your job is to be honest and let them opt in or out with full information.</advice>
  <advice>In short: disclose, do it earlier than accidental discovery, and drop the minimizing language. If this costs you dating opportunities, that is not a reason to hide it; it is the consequence of a choice you made.</advice>

response:
<advice>
    <point>The first useful shift is this: you may not need to perfectly tell excitement from anxiety in the moment. Physiologically they overlap a lot—racing heart, butterflies, agitation, vigilance. The more urgent question is often not "what is this feeling?" but "how do I respond to this activation without letting it run the show?"</point>
    <point>If CBT reframing has not been enough, the missing piece may be that this is less a thought problem and more an arousal-tolerance problem. In other words, your body treats activation itself as unsafe. That means purely arguing with the thoughts may not reach the level where the cycle is being driven.</point>
    <point>Try treating the sensation as activation, not as a message. "My system is activated" is often more accurate and less loaded than either "I'm anxious" or "I'm excited." It reduces the temptation to decode it as intuition or prediction.</point>
    <point>Be careful with the intuition idea. Intuition is usually fast pattern recognition grounded in prior experience; anxiety is threat projection plus body alarm. A practical test is: does the feeling produce specific, checkable information, or just urgency and dread? If it is vague, repetitive, and pushes avoidance, it is more likely anxiety than useful intuition.</point>
    <point>Because this spikes before positive events, work on the anticipatory window, not just the event itself. Many people suffer most in the hours or days beforehand. Build a "pre-event protocol" that is the same every time so your nervous system gets repetition instead of improvisation.</point>
    <point>That protocol could be simple:
      <subpoint>eat something steadying, reduce caffeine if it worsens activation, hydrate;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>do 5–10 minutes of down-regulation: longer exhale breathing, paced breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or a brisk walk;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>limit rehearsal and prediction—set a cap on how long you are allowed to think about the event;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>arrive with a plan for the first 10 minutes so your brain is not confronting uncertainty all at once.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>Use body-based skills that do not require you to believe anything. Examples: inhale 4, exhale 6 for a few minutes; unclench jaw/shoulders/hands; orient visually around the room and name neutral objects; feel both feet on the floor; splash cold water or hold something cool if you are spiraling. These are not cures, but they can reduce the intensity enough that you are no longer fighting from max activation.</point>
    <point>Another important shift: stop using enjoyment as the measure of success. If your goal is "I must feel calm and enjoy this," your body gets monitored constantly and the anxiety gets promoted. A better metric is: "Did I go? Did I stay for the amount of time I intended? Did I make room for discomfort without obeying it?" Enjoyment often returns later, after the threat-learning changes.</point>
    <point>For events, try graded exposure specifically aimed at anticipatory anxiety. Not just doing big events, but practicing the whole sequence in smaller doses: planning a short outing, tolerating the pre-event buildup, going anyway, staying until the anxiety curve changes, and recording what actually happened. The target is teaching your body that activation can rise and fall without catastrophe.</point>
    <point>It may also help to distinguish danger from discomfort in writing before an event:
      <subpoint>What is the actual risk here?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>What is the discomfort my body is predicting?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>What would I do if discomfort shows up?</subpoint>
    Having a coping plan often works better than trying to convince yourself there is nothing to fear.</point>
    <point>Since COVID concerns are in the mix, make the risk decision once, in advance, using your values and your actual precautions. For example: venue size, masking, ventilation, vaccination, transport choices. Once that plan is set, treat repeated re-checking as anxiety behavior rather than problem-solving.</point>
    <point>Given that this has been longstanding, worsening, and physically draining, it would be reasonable to revisit a clinician rather than just collect tips. Tell them specifically: the issue is chronic anticipatory anxiety around positive events, difficulty distinguishing activation from danger, and poor response to insight/CBT alone. That may point toward approaches beyond standard cognitive reframing—e.g. exposure-focused work, ACT, interoceptive exposure, somatic regulation skills, or a medication review if appropriate.</point>
    <point>If you want a compact practice phrase, use something like: "This is activation, not instruction. I do not need to solve it before I go." That frames the body state as temporary and prevents it from becoming evidence.</point>
    <point>Most of all, stop making yourself pass the test of feeling right before living your life. Build the skill of carrying activation with you while still doing what matters. That is often how the nervous system finally learns that the concert, trip, visit, or new job is not an emergency.</point>
  </advice>

response:
Break up with him.

He cheated on you with a coworker. The central issue here is not confusion about whether you are being too harsh; it is that he violated trust in a way that is especially difficult because it happened in your workplace and with someone you have to see.

Do not make your decision based on how much a breakup would hurt him. He created this situation. If you stay, only do it because he has taken full responsibility, ended all inappropriate contact, and you genuinely want to try rebuilding trust. From what you wrote, you do not trust him, and that is a solid reason to end it.

About the job: do not quit impulsively just to absorb the consequences of his behavior. First look at the options that protect your income and stability:
<steps>
  <step>Ask whether you can change shifts, move sections, or transfer internally.</step>
  <step>Keep communication with both of them strictly professional at work.</step>
  <step>If there is gossip, retaliation, or harassment, document it and go to HR or a manager.</step>
  <step>If being there is still too painful after exploring those options, then start looking for a new job.</step>
</steps>

A practical approach:
<actions>
  <action>End the relationship clearly and briefly.</action>
  <action>Do not argue about whether cheating “meant anything.”</action>
  <action>Set a boundary that work discussions stay work-related.</action>
  <action>Lean on friends or family outside the workplace so you are not isolated.</action>
</actions>

So: yes, breaking up is the right decision based on what you described. As for the job, try transfer or scheduling changes before quitting, unless the environment becomes unmanageable.
