response:
<advice>You should not act as an intermediary, subtle or otherwise.</advice>
  <advice>Your best move is to tell him plainly that this is something he needs to discuss directly with his wife, not through you. Because you are close to both of them, stepping into the middle will almost certainly look like taking sides.</advice>
  <advice>Also, adjust how you are thinking about the issue. The core problem is not “she posts sexy pictures” or “she owes him the same look she gives social media.” The actionable issue is: he feels unwanted, underprioritized, or disappointed by the level of effort and connection in their relationship. That is what he should talk about.</advice>
  <advice>Encourage him to drop the accusation language like “disrespect” and talk in first-person terms instead: “I miss feeling pursued by you,” “I feel hurt when special occasions don’t feel special to you,” “I want more effort and flirtation between us,” “Can we talk about what makes each of us feel desired?”</advice>
  <advice>If he brings up the date-night example, he should do it as one example of mismatched expectations, not proof that she is wrong. For all he knows, she may have been tired, overwhelmed, comfortable, unaware of his expectations, or simply not reading the dress-code importance the same way he was.</advice>
  <advice>You should also stop using objectifying language when thinking or speaking about her. Her body type and ethnicity are irrelevant to the advice, and talking that way will only distort your judgment.</advice>
  <advice>If he asks you again to help, say something like: “I care about both of you, so I’m not going to get in the middle. But I do think you should tell her directly that this isn’t really about Instagram—it’s about wanting to feel chosen, desired, and matched in effort.”</advice>
  <advice>If they are both open to it, suggest couples counseling. That is a far better intermediary than a mutual friend, especially when the issue may involve insecurity, communication, intimacy, expectations around appearance, and social media boundaries.</advice>
  <advice>If he only wants someone to confirm that she is disrespecting him, do not provide that. You can support his feelings without endorsing his conclusion. The useful line is: “Your feelings are real; now talk to her directly and respectfully about what you need.”</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should not act as an intermediary, subtle or otherwise.</advice>
  <advice>Your best move is to tell him plainly that this is something he needs to discuss directly with his wife, not through you. Because you are close to both of them, stepping into the middle will almost certainly look like taking sides.</advice>
  <advice>Also, adjust how you are thinking about the issue. The core problem is not “she posts sexy pictures” or “she owes him the same look she gives social media.” The actionable issue is: he feels unwanted, underprioritized, or disappointed by the level of effort and connection in their relationship. That is what he should talk about.</advice>
  <advice>Encourage him to drop the accusation language like “disrespect” and talk in first-person terms instead: “I miss feeling pursued by you,” “I feel hurt when special occasions don’t feel special to you,” “I want more effort and flirtation between us,” “Can we talk about what makes each of us feel desired?”</advice>
  <advice>If he brings up the date-night example, he should do it as one example of mismatched expectations, not proof that she is wrong. For all he knows, she may have been tired, overwhelmed, comfortable, unaware of his expectations, or simply not reading the dress-code importance the same way he was.</advice>
  <advice>You should also stop using objectifying language when thinking or speaking about her. Her body type and ethnicity are irrelevant to the advice, and talking that way will only distort your judgment.</advice>
  <advice>If he asks you again to help, say something like: “I care about both of you, so I’m not going to get in the middle. But I do think you should tell her directly that this isn’t really about Instagram—it’s about wanting to feel chosen, desired, and matched in effort.”</advice>
  <advice>If they are both open to it, suggest couples counseling. That is a far better intermediary than a mutual friend, especially when the issue may involve insecurity, communication, intimacy, expectations around appearance, and social media boundaries.</advice>
  <advice>If he only wants someone to confirm that she is disrespecting him, do not provide that. You can support his feelings without endorsing his conclusion. The useful line is: “Your feelings are real; now talk to her directly and respectfully about what you need.”</advice>
</response>

response:
It may be friendly, but it is not cleanly platonic-professional either. The daily texting plus touchy teasing is enough to treat this as boundary-blurring flirtation, or at minimum behavior that could easily become that.

The key point is: you do not need to figure out his exact intentions before setting limits. Whether he means “just friendly,” enjoys attention, is mildly flirting, or is testing boundaries, the practical response is the same.

What to do:
  <step>Pull the texting back. Keep replies slower, shorter, and more work-focused. Don’t keep feeding a daily personal rhythm.</step>
  <step>If he gets touchy again, shut that down in the moment. Simple works: “Don’t do that,” “Hands off,” or “You’re very touchy.”</step>
  <step>Do not treat his having a girlfriend as proof he won’t cross lines. People in serious relationships still flirt, seek attention, or cultivate emotional side-connections.</step>
  <step>Because he is a coworker, avoid private escalation. No confessional talks, no “what is this between us?” unless his behavior becomes explicit and you need to state a boundary directly.</step>
  <step>If he pushes after you create distance, that answers your question: it is not just casual friendliness.</step>

How to read it realistically:
  <point>If he texted you occasionally, stayed non-touchy, and kept it mostly work-related, “friendly” would be the cleaner interpretation.</point>
  <point>Daily personal contact and physical teasing make it more likely that he likes the attention, is flirting, or is enjoying a low-level emotional connection outside his relationship.</point>
  <point>That does not mean he plans to leave his girlfriend. In fact, plenty of people flirt while fully intending to stay with their partner.</point>

So: assume ambiguity is itself the problem. Step back, keep it professional, and watch whether he respects the boundary. That will tell you more than trying to decode mixed signals.

response:
<advice>You should not just move out and block him. That is the step most likely to create legal trouble for you.</advice>
  <advice>Your goal should be to create a written record, follow the lease as closely as possible, and separate the housing issue from the intimidation issue.</advice>
  <steps>
    <step>Get a copy of the lease immediately and read the parts on: term, early termination, subletting, assignment, replacement tenants, notice, keys, and deposits.</step>
    <step>Figure out who actually has legal authority here. Is this person the landlord, the master tenant, or just an informal roommate "in charge"? That matters. If there is a landlord or property manager, communicate with them directly in writing.</step>
    <step>Send written notice now. Keep it short and factual: you intend to vacate on a certain date, you are requesting the approved process for assignment/subletting/replacement, and if replacement is not approved you want written confirmation of your continuing obligations under the lease.</step>
    <step>Do not present a new tenant as a done deal. Instead, say you have a candidate ready to apply and ask what screening/approval process is required.</step>
    <step>Keep all communication in text or email if this person is intimidating. If you must exchange keys or collect property, do it with a witness or in a public place if possible.</step>
    <step>Document the intimidation separately. Save texts, write down the date/time/details of the confrontation, and if you feel physically unsafe, prioritize safety and consider contacting local law enforcement or a tenant-help organization for guidance.</step>
    <step>If you move out, document the room condition with dated photos/video, return keys in a traceable way, give a forwarding address, and keep proof.</step>
    <step>Do not rely on "I didn't give my SSN" as protection. If you signed the lease, that can still be enough for them to pursue you for rent or damages.</step>
    <step>If no approved replacement is accepted, assume you may still owe rent until the lease ends or until the room is lawfully re-rented, subject to whatever the lease and California law require.</step>
  </steps>
  <practical_message>You can send something like: "I will be vacating on [date]. Please confirm in writing the process for an approved replacement tenant or subtenant under the lease. I have an interested candidate who can apply if permitted. Because of our last in-person interaction, I want to keep communication in writing only. Please also confirm where and how keys should be returned and any remaining obligations after move-out."</practical_message>
  <bottom_line>The safest path is: no disappearing, no blocking, no unauthorized sublet, and no more verbal arguments. Put everything in writing, deal with the actual leaseholder or landlord, and protect yourself with documentation.</bottom_line>

<response>
  <advice>You should not just move out and block him. That is the step most likely to create legal trouble for you.</advice>
  <advice>Your goal should be to create a written record, follow the lease as closely as possible, and separate the housing issue from the intimidation issue.</advice>
  <steps>
    <step>Get a copy of the lease immediately and read the parts on: term, early termination, subletting, assignment, replacement tenants, notice, keys, and deposits.</step>
    <step>Figure out who actually has legal authority here. Is this person the landlord, the master tenant, or just an informal roommate "in charge"? That matters. If there is a landlord or property manager, communicate with them directly in writing.</step>
    <step>Send written notice now. Keep it short and factual: you intend to vacate on a certain date, you are requesting the approved process for assignment/subletting/replacement, and if replacement is not approved you want written confirmation of your continuing obligations under the lease.</step>
    <step>Do not present a new tenant as a done deal. Instead, say you have a candidate ready to apply and ask what screening/approval process is required.</step>
    <step>Keep all communication in text or email if this person is intimidating. If you must exchange keys or collect property, do it with a witness or in a public place if possible.</step>
    <step>Document the intimidation separately. Save texts, write down the date/time/details of the confrontation, and if you feel physically unsafe, prioritize safety and consider contacting local law enforcement or a tenant-help organization for guidance.</step>
    <step>If you move out, document the room condition with dated photos/video, return keys in a traceable way, give a forwarding address, and keep proof.</step>
    <step>Do not rely on "I didn't give my SSN" as protection. If you signed the lease, that can still be enough for them to pursue you for rent or damages.</step>
    <step>If no approved replacement is accepted, assume you may still owe rent until the lease ends or until the room is lawfully re-rented, subject to whatever the lease and California law require.</step>
  </steps>
  <practical_message>You can send something like: "I will be vacating on [date]. Please confirm in writing the process for an approved replacement tenant or subtenant under the lease. I have an interested candidate who can apply if permitted. Because of our last in-person interaction, I want to keep communication in writing only. Please also confirm where and how keys should be returned and any remaining obligations after move-out."</practical_message>
  <bottom_line>The safest path is: no disappearing, no blocking, no unauthorized sublet, and no more verbal arguments. Put everything in writing, deal with the actual leaseholder or landlord, and protect yourself with documentation.</bottom_line>
</response>

response:
You need to make this easier and smaller, not try to suddenly become super social.

Start with a simple goal: talk to one new person for 30–60 seconds. Not “make a new friend,” just “have one small interaction.”

Use situations where conversation is already built in:
- class
- work
- clubs
- lunch
- group projects
- events your friends attend

The easiest opener is to comment on whatever you’re both already doing. For example:
- “Have you done this before?”
- “What did you get for this assignment?”
- “That was so confusing, right?”
- “How do you know everyone here?”
- “I like your [shirt/bag/sticker].”

Then do this:
1. Ask one simple question.
2. Listen to their answer.
3. Ask one follow-up question.
4. End the conversation naturally if needed.

That’s enough. You do not need to be impressive.

Since you stick to your current friend group, use them as a bridge instead of leaving them completely. Try:
- standing slightly open instead of closed off in your group
- joining group conversations that include someone you don’t know well
- asking your friends to introduce you to people
- going to things where your group mixes with others

A good low-pressure line is:
- “I’ve seen you around but we haven’t really talked—I’m [name].”

If nervousness is the main problem, prepare for it instead of waiting for it to disappear:
- pick 2–3 opening lines ahead of time
- aim for short interactions
- expect awkwardness
- don’t treat a quiet moment like failure
- leave before you feel completely drained

Also, focus on repetition. Friendships usually come from seeing the same people multiple times, not from one perfect conversation. So pick one place where the same people show up regularly:
- a club
- study group
- sport
- volunteer shift
- recurring event

Then keep showing up.

A useful rule: after a decent short conversation, say hi the next time you see them. That second and third hello is often what starts the friendship.

If you want a concrete weekly challenge:
- Day 1–2: say hi to one new person
- Day 3–4: ask one simple question
- Day 5–6: have one 1-minute conversation
- Day 7: invite someone to sit together, study, or join a group plan

If your nervousness feels intense enough that you avoid people a lot or replay every interaction afterward, talk to a counselor, teacher, or mentor. That can help faster than trying to force yourself through it alone.

If you want, I can also give you a list of exact conversation starters for school, work, or parties.

1. notice something,
2. ask about it,
3. listen,
4. reflect back one piece,

Observation → Question → Follow-up

- “What got you into that?”
- “How long have you been doing that?”
- “What’s that been like for you?”
- “Do you enjoy it, or is it more just practical?”

Your main job is not to perform. It is to help the other person talk.

When your mind goes blank, use one of these default moves:
- “Tell me more about that.”
- “How did that happen?”
- “What do you mean?”
- “Was that a good thing or a stressful thing?”
- “What happened next?”

If you blank completely, say something simple instead of panicking:
- “I lost my train of thought for a second.”
- “Wait, I want to hear more about that.”
- “I’m not great at small talk—how’s your week been?”

You also need topics ready before conversations. Prepare 5 repeatable areas:
- work or school
- hobbies
- recent plans
- food/travel/local places
- shows, music, books, games, podcasts

Think of these as shelves you can grab from. Example:
“What do you usually do outside work?”
If they answer “I hike,” your follow-ups are easy:
- “How did you get into that?”
- “Do you go often?”
- “Favorite place you’ve been?”
- “Do you go alone or with people?”

A big mistake is asking one question after another like an interview. Use the 2-to-1 rule:
For every 2 questions, offer 1 small piece about yourself.

Example:
“What do you do for work?”
“Oh nice. What’s that like day to day?”
Then:
“I’m always curious about that because I’d get bored doing the same thing every day.”

That gives them something to respond to and takes pressure off you.

If social anxiety is part of this, the blankness may be caused by monitoring yourself too hard:
- “Am I awkward?”
- “Do I sound stupid?”
- “What should I say next?”

That mental checking blocks attention. Shift attention outward. During a conversation, focus on:
- their last sentence
- their tone
- one detail you can ask about

Not: how you are coming across.

Practice in low-stakes situations, not only important ones:
- cashier
- barista
- coworker
- neighbor
- online voice chat or group setting

Set tiny goals:
- ask 1 follow-up
- stay in the conversation 2 extra minutes
- share 1 thing about yourself

Do not aim for “smooth.” Aim for “present and curious.”

Every day for 2 weeks, have one short conversation and use:
- 1 opener
- 2 follow-ups
- 1 self-disclosure

Template:
“Hey, how’s your day going?”
“Oh really? What made it busy?”
“Is that typical for you?”
“Yeah, I’ve had a week like that too.”

- Use default follow-ups when blank.
- Share a little about yourself.
- Prepare a few go-to topics.
- Practice often in low-pressure settings.

response:
<advice>You should remove her as Maid of Honor and stop trying to salvage this in the immediate term.</advice>
  <advice>The original issue was repairable: you asked a personal question in a group setting, and your apology was imperfect because “I didn’t think it was a big deal” sounded minimizing. That is something a healthy friendship can usually work through.</advice>
  <advice>What makes this different is her response. She did not just say she was hurt. She escalated into contempt, character attacks, revisionist grievance-listing, superstition-based blame, pressure to ignore your physical assault, and denial of that assault. Those are not the actions of someone acting like a safe Maid of Honor right now.</advice>
  <advice>Do not treat “15 years” as a reason to keep her in a central wedding role. Length of friendship does not outweigh current instability, hostility, and disrespect.</advice>
  <advice>Also do not keep arguing point-by-point. Once someone is sending paragraphs about how you do not deserve marriage and that everyone merely tolerates you, the discussion is no longer about the original misunderstanding. It has moved into emotional abuse and possibly a long-simmering rupture.</advice>
  <advice>Your next move should be brief, clear, and logistical. Tell her in writing that because of the messages she sent and the breakdown in trust, you are removing her from the Maid of Honor role and stepping back from the friendship for now. Do not debate the past in that message.</advice>
  <advice>You can say something like: “I understand that asking about your family in front of others hurt you, and I apologized for that. But the way you have spoken to me since then, including attacking my character and minimizing the assault I experienced, is not something I can accept. I’m removing you as Maid of Honor and taking space from this friendship. I won’t discuss this further right now. I wish you well.”</advice>
  <advice>Then mute or block if needed, especially if she keeps sending abusive messages. Preserve screenshots in case the conflict spreads into your wedding planning or social circle.</advice>
  <advice>If you want to learn something from this, the lesson is not “I am a bad person.” The lesson is narrower: avoid putting friends on the spot about family matters in group settings, and when apologizing, skip phrases that explain why you thought it was minor. Just apologize and stop there.</advice>
  <advice>But do not overcorrect into accepting cruelty. You can have made a social mistake and still be entirely right to end or pause a friendship when the other person responds with contempt and attacks your safety boundaries.</advice>
  <advice>If, months from now, she gives a sincere apology that takes responsibility for the insults, the wedding pressure, and the assault denial, you can reconsider whether any friendship is possible. But she should not be in your wedding party now.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should remove her as Maid of Honor and stop trying to salvage this in the immediate term.</advice>
  <advice>The original issue was repairable: you asked a personal question in a group setting, and your apology was imperfect because “I didn’t think it was a big deal” sounded minimizing. That is something a healthy friendship can usually work through.</advice>
  <advice>What makes this different is her response. She did not just say she was hurt. She escalated into contempt, character attacks, revisionist grievance-listing, superstition-based blame, pressure to ignore your physical assault, and denial of that assault. Those are not the actions of someone acting like a safe Maid of Honor right now.</advice>
  <advice>Do not treat “15 years” as a reason to keep her in a central wedding role. Length of friendship does not outweigh current instability, hostility, and disrespect.</advice>
  <advice>Also do not keep arguing point-by-point. Once someone is sending paragraphs about how you do not deserve marriage and that everyone merely tolerates you, the discussion is no longer about the original misunderstanding. It has moved into emotional abuse and possibly a long-simmering rupture.</advice>
  <advice>Your next move should be brief, clear, and logistical. Tell her in writing that because of the messages she sent and the breakdown in trust, you are removing her from the Maid of Honor role and stepping back from the friendship for now. Do not debate the past in that message.</advice>
  <advice>You can say something like: “I understand that asking about your family in front of others hurt you, and I apologized for that. But the way you have spoken to me since then, including attacking my character and minimizing the assault I experienced, is not something I can accept. I’m removing you as Maid of Honor and taking space from this friendship. I won’t discuss this further right now. I wish you well.”</advice>
  <advice>Then mute or block if needed, especially if she keeps sending abusive messages. Preserve screenshots in case the conflict spreads into your wedding planning or social circle.</advice>
  <advice>If you want to learn something from this, the lesson is not “I am a bad person.” The lesson is narrower: avoid putting friends on the spot about family matters in group settings, and when apologizing, skip phrases that explain why you thought it was minor. Just apologize and stop there.</advice>
  <advice>But do not overcorrect into accepting cruelty. You can have made a social mistake and still be entirely right to end or pause a friendship when the other person responds with contempt and attacks your safety boundaries.</advice>
  <advice>If, months from now, she gives a sincere apology that takes responsibility for the insults, the wedding pressure, and the assault denial, you can reconsider whether any friendship is possible. But she should not be in your wedding party now.</advice>
</response>

response:
You should stop asking whether he could change and start deciding whether this relationship, as it actually is, works for you.

From what you wrote, the answer looks like no.

This does not read like a relationship that is merely under stress from school. It reads like an unequal partnership where you are carrying the practical load, the emotional load, and most of the initiative, while he gives you short bursts of improvement and then slides back. If someone only changes for a week after repeated conversations, that is not meaningful change.

Do not make your decision based on:
<point>how long you’ve been together</point>
<point>his potential</point>
<point>the fact that he is smart/playful/handsome</point>
<point>the brief moments when he says or does just enough to keep you from leaving</point>

Make it based on the consistent pattern:
<point>you feel burned out</point>
<point>you do most of the cooking and cleaning</point>
<point>he does not take initiative</point>
<point>he prioritizes gaming over the relationship</point>
<point>you feel more like roommates than partners</point>
<point>your needs have been stated multiple times and remain unmet</point>

If you want to give this one last chance, make it concrete and time-limited. Not another vague “please do more.” Tell him plainly something like:

“I am not willing to stay in a relationship where I carry the household and the relationship by myself. If this is going to continue, I need sustained change: specific chores divided fairly, planned quality time, and consistent engagement from you. If that does not happen and continue, I will end the relationship.”

Then define exactly what that means:
<point>a written chore split</point>
<point>specific date planning expectations</point>
<point>clear limits around gaming versus shared time</point>
<point>a deadline long enough to show real consistency, not one good week</point>

If you do this, the point is not to convince him. The point is to get clarity.

If he argues, deflects, acts wounded, or gives you another short honeymoon phase, treat that as more information. If he wanted to be an active partner, repeated conversations would already have led to sustained effort.

If you already feel done, you do not need one more trial period. You are allowed to leave because the relationship no longer meets your needs. You do not need him to be a bad person to justify ending it. “He’s a good guy” and “he is not being a good partner to me” can both be true.

So my direct advice: unless you genuinely want to offer one final structured chance, walk away. Not because there might be someone “better” out there, but because this relationship is already teaching you that love without effort is not enough.

If you do leave, plan the practical side first since you live together:
<point>housing</point>
<point>finances</point>
<point>move-out timeline</point>
<point>what you will and won’t discuss once you’ve decided</point>

The biggest mistake here would be staying attached to his promises instead of his pattern.

<response>
You should stop asking whether he could change and start deciding whether this relationship, as it actually is, works for you.

From what you wrote, the answer looks like no.

This does not read like a relationship that is merely under stress from school. It reads like an unequal partnership where you are carrying the practical load, the emotional load, and most of the initiative, while he gives you short bursts of improvement and then slides back. If someone only changes for a week after repeated conversations, that is not meaningful change.

Do not make your decision based on:
<point>how long you’ve been together</point>
<point>his potential</point>
<point>the fact that he is smart/playful/handsome</point>
<point>the brief moments when he says or does just enough to keep you from leaving</point>

Make it based on the consistent pattern:
<point>you feel burned out</point>
<point>you do most of the cooking and cleaning</point>
<point>he does not take initiative</point>
<point>he prioritizes gaming over the relationship</point>
<point>you feel more like roommates than partners</point>
<point>your needs have been stated multiple times and remain unmet</point>

If you want to give this one last chance, make it concrete and time-limited. Not another vague “please do more.” Tell him plainly something like:

“I am not willing to stay in a relationship where I carry the household and the relationship by myself. If this is going to continue, I need sustained change: specific chores divided fairly, planned quality time, and consistent engagement from you. If that does not happen and continue, I will end the relationship.”

Then define exactly what that means:
<point>a written chore split</point>
<point>specific date planning expectations</point>
<point>clear limits around gaming versus shared time</point>
<point>a deadline long enough to show real consistency, not one good week</point>

If you do this, the point is not to convince him. The point is to get clarity.

If he argues, deflects, acts wounded, or gives you another short honeymoon phase, treat that as more information. If he wanted to be an active partner, repeated conversations would already have led to sustained effort.

If you already feel done, you do not need one more trial period. You are allowed to leave because the relationship no longer meets your needs. You do not need him to be a bad person to justify ending it. “He’s a good guy” and “he is not being a good partner to me” can both be true.

So my direct advice: unless you genuinely want to offer one final structured chance, walk away. Not because there might be someone “better” out there, but because this relationship is already teaching you that love without effort is not enough.

If you do leave, plan the practical side first since you live together:
<point>housing</point>
<point>finances</point>
<point>move-out timeline</point>
<point>what you will and won’t discuss once you’ve decided</point>

The biggest mistake here would be staying attached to his promises instead of his pattern.
</response>

response:
Stop trying to “forget” on command. That usually makes the person stay in your head longer. Your job is not to erase her; it is to make her less central in your daily life.

Do this instead:

<step>Cut contact as much as possible for now. No checking her social media, no asking mutual friends about her, no rereading old messages, no looking at photos. If you keep reopening the wound, it will keep hurting.</step>

<step>Stop measuring your healing against hers. Her seeing someone else does not mean your pain is wrong or that you are behind. People move differently, and rebound relationships also exist. Comparing only keeps you stuck.</step>

<step>Let yourself grieve in a controlled way. Set aside a short period each day, even 15–20 minutes, to write what you feel: anger, sadness, missing her, jealousy, disappointment. Outside that time, when thoughts come up, tell yourself: “I’ll think about this during my writing time.”</step>

<step>Rebuild structure. After breakups, empty time becomes obsession time. Sleep regularly, exercise, eat properly, leave the house, and make plans with other people even when you do not feel like it.</step>

<step>Remove false hope. If part of you is still waiting for her to come back, that keeps the attachment alive. Act on the assumption that this relationship is over.</step>

<step>Do one thing that is only for your next version of life: a class, gym routine, trip, project, language practice, hobby, anything that is not connected to her.</step>

You will probably not “forget,” but you can get to the point where you remember without getting crushed.

If after 3 months you are stuck in the same loop every day, cannot function well, are isolating yourself, or feel hopeless, talk to a therapist or counselor. If you start having thoughts of harming yourself, seek urgent local help immediately.

A simple rule for the next month: no contact, no checking, more routine, more people, less replaying the story.

response:
Stop treating self-esteem as something you earn only after you become attractive, productive, disciplined, or fully “put together.” If you wait for that, depression will keep moving the goalposts. The first target is not loving yourself. It is reducing how much you attack yourself.

Do this in a practical way:

<step>1. Interrupt the “global verdict” language.</step>
When your mind says “I’m pathetic,” “I hate myself,” or “I’m unworthy,” answer with something narrower and more factual:
- “I’m having a shame spiral.”
- “I feel underprepared today.”
- “I don’t like this outfit, but that is different from being pathetic.”
- “I’m exhausted and my brain is grading me unfairly.”

That sounds small, but it matters. “I am pathetic” is a sentence your brain cannot solve. “I feel self-conscious in these clothes” is a problem you can work with.

<step>2. Lower the goal from confidence to neutrality.</step>
You do not need to look in the mirror and think “I look amazing.” A much more realistic goal is:
- “This is a body.”
- “These are clothes.”
- “I am allowed to leave the house looking ordinary.”
- “Most people are not examining me the way I am examining me.”

Neutrality is often the bridge to feeling better.

<step>3. Build a minimum self-care routine so small it survives bad weeks.</step>
If you have no time, stop imagining an ideal routine. Make a “floor,” not a “ceiling.” For example:
- 5 minutes of walking
- 10 bodyweight squats or stretches
- wash face + deodorant + clean shirt
- one glass of water when you wake up
- one meal with protein
- bedtime within the same 30-minute range

If a habit takes more than 5–10 minutes, depression and burnout will often reject it. Tiny is not pathetic. Tiny is sustainable.

<step>4. Treat clothes as a comfort tool, not a morality test.</step>
If certain clothes make you regret leaving the house, simplify:
- identify 3–5 outfits that feel safe, comfortable, and “good enough”
- repeat them often
- prioritize fit and physical comfort over trying to impress anyone
- prepare one default outfit the night before work

You do not need a better personality to deserve comfortable clothes.

<step>5. Stop using weekends to “catch up on being a person.”</step>
If weekends are only chores + collapsing, your life will keep feeling like survival. Protect even 30–60 minutes of weekend time for something that restores you before cleaning takes over:
- a walk
- a shower and clean clothes
- coffee somewhere quiet
- music and stretching
- calling one safe person
- sitting outside

Rest is not a reward for finishing everything. If you wait until everything is done, you will never get it.

<step>6. Use evidence against self-hatred.</step>
Create a note on your phone called “counterevidence.” Each day, write 1–3 things like:
- “Went to work even though I felt awful.”
- “Did laundry.”
- “Answered a message.”
- “Left the house.”
- “Ate breakfast.”
- “Did not isolate all day.”

Self-hating thoughts speak in absolutes. Evidence weakens absolutes.

<step>7. Compare less, observe more.</step>
A lot of low self-esteem is constant self-monitoring. Try replacing “How am I coming across?” with “What is around me?”
Notice:
- what color the wall is
- what song is playing
- what the weather feels like
- what the other person is actually saying

That shift reduces the spotlight effect.

<step>8. Exercise counts even when it is unimpressive.</step>
Do not frame movement as “working out properly” or not at all. Depression loves all-or-nothing rules.
Examples that count:
- 10-minute walk
- stairs instead of elevator
- stretching while waiting for food
- one song of movement in your room
- carrying groceries mindfully
- short beginner videos on weekends

The point is not transformation. The point is teaching your brain: “I can influence how I feel a little.”

<step>9. Watch for hidden self-punishment.</step>
Sometimes people with low self-esteem quietly reinforce it by:
- wearing clothes that make them feel worse because they “haven’t earned” better
- skipping meals
- avoiding mirrors completely or checking mirrors constantly
- refusing rest because they “should be doing more”
- turning every flaw into proof of worthlessness

If you notice those patterns, name them as self-punishment, not truth.

<step>10. Get actual treatment for the depression if you can.</step>
Because what you describe does sound tied to depression, self-esteem tips alone may not be enough. If possible:
- talk to a therapist or counselor
- see a primary care doctor to discuss depression, anxiety, sleep, and burnout
- ask about treatment options if this is persistent
- if body image or self-loathing is intense, mention that directly

Low self-esteem often improves when the depression itself is treated.

<step>11. Use one replacement sentence.</step>
Pick one sentence to repeat when the hate starts:
- “I do not need to earn basic kindness from myself.”
- “Feeling bad is not the same as being bad.”
- “I am allowed to be a work in progress in public.”
- “Today only requires good enough.”

Use the same sentence every time. Repetition matters more than originality.

<step>12. If the self-hatred becomes unsafe, treat it like an emergency.</step>
If “I hate myself” starts turning into urges to hurt yourself, thoughts that people would be better off without you, or any desire not to be here, contact emergency services or a crisis line right away, or tell someone nearby immediately.

For this week, keep it very simple:
- choose 2 “safe” outfits
- do 5–10 minutes of movement 3 times
- write down one piece of counterevidence each day
- replace “I’m pathetic” with one factual sentence
- protect 30 minutes of weekend time for recovery before chores

You do not need to become confident all at once. You need to become a little less cruel to yourself, consistently.

Stop treating self-esteem as something you earn only after you become attractive, productive, disciplined, or fully “put together.” If you wait for that, depression will keep moving the goalposts. The first target is not loving yourself. It is reducing how much you attack yourself.

Do this in a practical way:

<step>1. Interrupt the “global verdict” language.</step>
When your mind says “I’m pathetic,” “I hate myself,” or “I’m unworthy,” answer with something narrower and more factual:
- “I’m having a shame spiral.”
- “I feel underprepared today.”
- “I don’t like this outfit, but that is different from being pathetic.”
- “I’m exhausted and my brain is grading me unfairly.”

That sounds small, but it matters. “I am pathetic” is a sentence your brain cannot solve. “I feel self-conscious in these clothes” is a problem you can work with.

<step>2. Lower the goal from confidence to neutrality.</step>
You do not need to look in the mirror and think “I look amazing.” A much more realistic goal is:
- “This is a body.”
- “These are clothes.”
- “I am allowed to leave the house looking ordinary.”
- “Most people are not examining me the way I am examining me.”

Neutrality is often the bridge to feeling better.

<step>3. Build a minimum self-care routine so small it survives bad weeks.</step>
If you have no time, stop imagining an ideal routine. Make a “floor,” not a “ceiling.” For example:
- 5 minutes of walking
- 10 bodyweight squats or stretches
- wash face + deodorant + clean shirt
- one glass of water when you wake up
- one meal with protein
- bedtime within the same 30-minute range

If a habit takes more than 5–10 minutes, depression and burnout will often reject it. Tiny is not pathetic. Tiny is sustainable.

<step>4. Treat clothes as a comfort tool, not a morality test.</step>
If certain clothes make you regret leaving the house, simplify:
- identify 3–5 outfits that feel safe, comfortable, and “good enough”
- repeat them often
- prioritize fit and physical comfort over trying to impress anyone
- prepare one default outfit the night before work

You do not need a better personality to deserve comfortable clothes.

<step>5. Stop using weekends to “catch up on being a person.”</step>
If weekends are only chores + collapsing, your life will keep feeling like survival. Protect even 30–60 minutes of weekend time for something that restores you before cleaning takes over:
- a walk
- a shower and clean clothes
- coffee somewhere quiet
- music and stretching
- calling one safe person
- sitting outside

Rest is not a reward for finishing everything. If you wait until everything is done, you will never get it.

<step>6. Use evidence against self-hatred.</step>
Create a note on your phone called “counterevidence.” Each day, write 1–3 things like:
- “Went to work even though I felt awful.”
- “Did laundry.”
- “Answered a message.”
- “Left the house.”
- “Ate breakfast.”
- “Did not isolate all day.”

Self-hating thoughts speak in absolutes. Evidence weakens absolutes.

<step>7. Compare less, observe more.</step>
A lot of low self-esteem is constant self-monitoring. Try replacing “How am I coming across?” with “What is around me?”
Notice:
- what color the wall is
- what song is playing
- what the weather feels like
- what the other person is actually saying

That shift reduces the spotlight effect.

<step>8. Exercise counts even when it is unimpressive.</step>
Do not frame movement as “working out properly” or not at all. Depression loves all-or-nothing rules.
Examples that count:
- 10-minute walk
- stairs instead of elevator
- stretching while waiting for food
- one song of movement in your room
- carrying groceries mindfully
- short beginner videos on weekends

The point is not transformation. The point is teaching your brain: “I can influence how I feel a little.”

<step>9. Watch for hidden self-punishment.</step>
Sometimes people with low self-esteem quietly reinforce it by:
- wearing clothes that make them feel worse because they “haven’t earned” better
- skipping meals
- avoiding mirrors completely or checking mirrors constantly
- refusing rest because they “should be doing more”
- turning every flaw into proof of worthlessness

If you notice those patterns, name them as self-punishment, not truth.

<step>10. Get actual treatment for the depression if you can.</step>
Because what you describe does sound tied to depression, self-esteem tips alone may not be enough. If possible:
- talk to a therapist or counselor
- see a primary care doctor to discuss depression, anxiety, sleep, and burnout
- ask about treatment options if this is persistent
- if body image or self-loathing is intense, mention that directly

Low self-esteem often improves when the depression itself is treated.

<step>11. Use one replacement sentence.</step>
Pick one sentence to repeat when the hate starts:
- “I do not need to earn basic kindness from myself.”
- “Feeling bad is not the same as being bad.”
- “I am allowed to be a work in progress in public.”
- “Today only requires good enough.”

Use the same sentence every time. Repetition matters more than originality.

<step>12. If the self-hatred becomes unsafe, treat it like an emergency.</step>
If “I hate myself” starts turning into urges to hurt yourself, thoughts that people would be better off without you, or any desire not to be here, contact emergency services or a crisis line right away, or tell someone nearby immediately.

For this week, keep it very simple:
- choose 2 “safe” outfits
- do 5–10 minutes of movement 3 times
- write down one piece of counterevidence each day
- replace “I’m pathetic” with one factual sentence
- protect 30 minutes of weekend time for recovery before chores

You do not need to become confident all at once. You need to become a little less cruel to yourself, consistently.

<advice>You do not need to find the “perfect” heartfelt Father's Day gift. In a strained relationship, the right choice is usually something simple, neutral, and proportionate.</advice>
  <advice>Pick one of these lanes and stay in it:</advice>
  <advice>1. Low-intensity acknowledgment: a card with a brief, polite message such as “Thinking of you this Father's Day” or “Wishing you a good day.”</advice>
  <advice>2. Small practical gift: coffee, snacks, a bookstore gift card, a meal, or something tied to a hobby, without heavy emotional symbolism.</advice>
  <advice>3. No gift, just contact: a short text or call if that is safer and more honest for the relationship than giving an object.</advice>
  <advice>Avoid gifts that imply intimacy, forgiveness, or closeness that does not actually exist. Skip anything overly sentimental unless you truly mean it.</advice>
  <advice>Let the gift match the real relationship, not the relationship you wish existed or feel pressured to perform. “Doing the right thing” can mean a modest acknowledgment, not a grand gesture.</advice>
  <advice>If contact with him is harmful or destabilizing, you are not required to participate in the holiday at all. Obligation is not the same as integrity.</advice>
  <advice>If you want a concrete suggestion: give a simple card and a small neutral gift card, or send a short respectful message. That is enough.</advice>

<advice>You should stop treating this as a jealousy problem to solve and start treating it as a compatibility and boundary problem.</advice>
  <advice>Right now, you are being asked to stay emotionally attached while he auditions replacements because he wants a faster answer than you can honestly give. Even if his desire for kids soon is legitimate, this arrangement is hurting you and distorting your decision-making.</advice>
  <advice>The cleanest move is to break this off completely, at least for now. Not “half break up,” not “still seeing each other,” not “maybe if I decide yes.” A real break. That means no romantic contact, no acting like partners, and no updates about his dating life. If you stay in contact while he dates, you are very likely to keep suffering and to feel increasing pressure to say yes to children for the wrong reason.</advice>
  <advice>If you do not want a full break, then you need much firmer boundaries immediately:
    <point>Decide whether you are actually broken up or actually together. Ambiguity is what is crushing you.</point>
    <point>If broken up, stop seeing each other romantically.</point>
    <point>Do not ask for or accept information about his dates; tell friends not to report back to you.</point>
    <point>Do not let your decision about children be made on his deadline alone.</point>
    <point>Do not continue under conditions where he lies to avoid conflict.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>On the kids question itself: do not answer it in order to save this relationship. Answer it as if he were not in the picture. Ask yourself, “If this relationship ended today, would I still want to become a parent?” If the answer is not a clear yes, then it is a no for now.</advice>
  <advice>Your therapy and medical appointments are the right next steps, but they should be used to help you reach your own answer, not to race toward the answer that keeps him available.</advice>
  <advice>If, after time and real reflection, you genuinely want children, then that can inform future dating decisions—whether with him or someone else. But if he needs certainty now and you do not have it, then the honest conclusion may simply be that you are not compatible at this moment.</advice>
  <advice>So yes: unless you can tolerate a truly open arrangement with clear consent, honesty, and emotional safety—which your post strongly suggests you cannot—you should end the in-between situation completely.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should stop treating this as a jealousy problem to solve and start treating it as a compatibility and boundary problem.</advice>
  <advice>Right now, you are being asked to stay emotionally attached while he auditions replacements because he wants a faster answer than you can honestly give. Even if his desire for kids soon is legitimate, this arrangement is hurting you and distorting your decision-making.</advice>
  <advice>The cleanest move is to break this off completely, at least for now. Not “half break up,” not “still seeing each other,” not “maybe if I decide yes.” A real break. That means no romantic contact, no acting like partners, and no updates about his dating life. If you stay in contact while he dates, you are very likely to keep suffering and to feel increasing pressure to say yes to children for the wrong reason.</advice>
  <advice>If you do not want a full break, then you need much firmer boundaries immediately:
    <point>Decide whether you are actually broken up or actually together. Ambiguity is what is crushing you.</point>
    <point>If broken up, stop seeing each other romantically.</point>
    <point>Do not ask for or accept information about his dates; tell friends not to report back to you.</point>
    <point>Do not let your decision about children be made on his deadline alone.</point>
    <point>Do not continue under conditions where he lies to avoid conflict.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>On the kids question itself: do not answer it in order to save this relationship. Answer it as if he were not in the picture. Ask yourself, “If this relationship ended today, would I still want to become a parent?” If the answer is not a clear yes, then it is a no for now.</advice>
  <advice>Your therapy and medical appointments are the right next steps, but they should be used to help you reach your own answer, not to race toward the answer that keeps him available.</advice>
  <advice>If, after time and real reflection, you genuinely want children, then that can inform future dating decisions—whether with him or someone else. But if he needs certainty now and you do not have it, then the honest conclusion may simply be that you are not compatible at this moment.</advice>
  <advice>So yes: unless you can tolerate a truly open arrangement with clear consent, honesty, and emotional safety—which your post strongly suggests you cannot—you should end the in-between situation completely.</advice>
</response>

    <point>
      Stop treating “who changes more” as something logistics decides for you. Your line about the middle-name option meaning “it would be her having to do it” is the main thing to revisit. If preserving both names matters equally, then neither of you should be presumed to absorb the identity change just because the other already has a complicated name.
    </point>
    <point>
      Before choosing a format, identify the underlying goals separately. You seem to have at least five:
      <subpoint>keep both family names meaningful</subpoint>
      <subpoint>avoid an awkwardly long everyday name</subpoint>
      <subpoint>have a coherent plan for children</subpoint>
      <subpoint>minimize legal/professional hassle</subpoint>
      <subpoint>feel like you are forming one family unit</subpoint>
      Write these down and rank them individually, then compare. That will probably clarify why certain options feel wrong.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not assume that spouses must share one surname in order to be a family. The kids question is real, but it is separable from the spouse-name question. You have more combinations than the five you listed.
    </point>
    <point>
      Options you may not have fully explored:
      <subpoint>
        Both keep your current surnames, and children get one surname. You can choose either parent’s name for all children.
      </subpoint>
      <subpoint>
        Both keep your current surnames, and children get a hyphenated surname even if the adults do not.
      </subpoint>
      <subpoint>
        Both keep your current surnames socially/professionally, while one or both make a legal middle-name adjustment.
      </subpoint>
      <subpoint>
        One of you uses a double surname without a hyphen in some contexts if that feels less clunky.
      </subpoint>
      <subpoint>
        Create a family surname only for children, while adults keep their existing names. Uncommon, but possible if what you want is mainly a child family identifier.
      </subpoint>
      <subpoint>
        Use one surname legally and the other as a middle name for children, alternating whose surname gets priority if you have more than one child only if you both genuinely like that. Do not do this just to split the difference if consistency matters more to you.
      </subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>
      If you revisit the middle-name route, make it symmetrical in principle even if not in outcome. Ask: “Would either of us be willing to do this?” not “Which one of us has fewer name components already?” If only one of you would ever consider it, that is still fine—but it should come from preference, not default burden-shifting.
    </point>
    <point>
      For each option, test it in daily life:
      <subpoint>say it out loud</subpoint>
      <subpoint>write it on formal documents</subpoint>
      <subpoint>imagine introducing yourselves and your children</subpoint>
      <subpoint>consider email signatures, passports, school forms, professional publications, and medical records</subpoint>
      <subpoint>check your state or country’s actual legal rules, because some jurisdictions make some changes easier than others</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical way to decide:
      <subpoint>each of you privately rank the options</subpoint>
      <subpoint>each of you list your deal-breakers</subpoint>
      <subpoint>each of you list what matters most for children’s names separately from your own names</subpoint>
      <subpoint>look for the highest-ranked option that neither of you resents</subpoint>
      If an option works on paper but leaves one of you feeling erased or singled out, it is not the right choice.
    </point>
    <point>
      Based on what you wrote, the most promising paths seem to be:
      <subpoint>both keep your surnames and make a clear children’s naming plan</subpoint>
      <subpoint>some form of middle-name preservation, but only if your fiancée actively likes it rather than accepts it</subpoint>
      <subpoint>hyphenation only for children, not necessarily for both adults</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>
      If you want one rule of thumb: prioritize avoiding resentment over achieving a perfectly tidy naming system. A slightly less elegant family-name arrangement is usually better than one person feeling they carried the identity cost for the marriage.
    </point>
  </advice>

Stop trying to answer the biggest question first: "Am I a narcissist?" Start with "What do I repeatedly do that harms people?"

Use behaviors, not identity labels. Ask yourself, in writing:

- Do I react badly to criticism?
- Do I need to be superior, admired, or right?
- Do I minimize other people's feelings?
- Do I use charm, guilt, anger, silence, or victimhood to control outcomes?
- Do I feel entitled to special treatment?
- Do I apologize without changing?
- Do I become cold or contemptuous when I don't get what I want?
- Do I treat people as useful or useless depending on what they give me?

Then get external reality-testing. Ask 2-3 people who know you well:
"What patterns in me make relationships hard? When do you feel unseen, controlled, dismissed, or manipulated by me?"
Do not argue, explain, correct, or defend yourself. Just write down what they say.

If you notice narcissistic traits, the work is concrete:

- Admit specific behaviors plainly.
- Stop lying, exaggerating, and image-management.
- Stop forcing conversations back to yourself.
- When criticized, pause before responding.
- Replace "that's not what I meant" with "what was the impact on you?"
- Make amends through changed behavior, not emotional speeches.
- Respect boundaries the first time.
- Notice contempt immediately; it is one of the most destructive signs.
- Practice letting other people be important without competing.

Therapy helps, especially if the therapist is willing to confront defenses, not just soothe you. Look for work focused on accountability, attachment, shame, emotional regulation, and interpersonal patterns.

Also consider that people often call themselves narcissists when they are actually dealing with insecurity, trauma, emotional immaturity, or learned self-protection. That does not excuse harm, but it changes the treatment approach. A proper mental health evaluation is better than self-diagnosis.

A useful test of change is simple:
- Are you easier to be honest with?
- Do people feel safer setting limits with you?
- Do you take responsibility faster?
- Are your apologies shorter and your behavior different?
- Are relationships becoming less one-sided?

If you want to change, measure progress by reduced harm, not by whether you can describe yourself insightfully.

response:
<advice>You should not move in with her this summer unless you become clearly and genuinely willing. Right now, your own description points the other way. You are unsure of your reasons, anxious about adulthood, still want to live alone, and do not know what your post-graduation situation will be. Those are all strong reasons to say no for now.</advice>
  <advice>Your bigger problem is not just the answer; it is that your answer is vague. "I don't know, I'm just not comfortable" is not enough for a partner making life plans. You need to figure out whether your hesitation is mainly:
    <point>a timing issue: you do not want to combine households until you finish school and know where you will be living,</point>
    <point>a lifestyle issue: you need more independence and alone time than cohabitation would allow,</point>
    <point>a relationship issue: you are not sure this is the person you want to build a life with,</point>
    <point>or an anxiety issue: fear of adulthood and commitment is making any next step feel threatening.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you do not sort that out, you will keep sounding ambivalent, and she will keep hearing rejection.</advice>
  <advice>So give her a clear position. Not a soft maybe. Something like: "I am not willing to move in this summer. I am still in school until December, my plans after graduation are unsettled, and I am not ready to make a housing commitment while feeling this unsure." That is concrete and fair.</advice>
  <advice>Then decide whether you can offer a real future path. If the truth is, "I could revisit this after graduation once I know where I'll be and after we've talked seriously about how living together would work," say that. If the truth is, "I don't know if I ever want this with you," then you need to say that too. It will hurt, but less than dragging this out.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let her friends' timelines decide yours. Their moving in together does not make you wrong. But her wanting that step now does not make her wrong either. This may simply be a compatibility issue about pace and readiness.</advice>
  <advice>Use the break for an actual decision, not indefinite avoidance. Ask yourself:
    <point>If she removed all pressure, would I want to live with her within the next year?</point>
    <point>If I were already graduated and employed, would I still resist?</point>
    <point>Am I protecting needed independence, or am I avoiding commitment because I am scared?</point>
    <point>Do I see a future with her strongly enough that "not yet" is honest, or am I using "not yet" to avoid saying "probably not"?</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If your answer is "not yet," pair it with a condition or timeline. If you cannot do that honestly, assume the issue is deeper than timing.</advice>
  <advice>Finally, if you notice this pattern goes beyond this relationship—difficulty getting close, strong need for distance, fear around adult transitions—it would be worth talking to a therapist or counselor. Not because you are wrong for needing space, but because you need to know whether this is a stable preference or fear running your choices.</advice>
  <advice>The practical bottom line: do not move in now, get clear on why, tell her plainly, and accept that this may mean the relationship ends if what she needs is cohabitation in the near term.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should not move in with her this summer unless you become clearly and genuinely willing. Right now, your own description points the other way. You are unsure of your reasons, anxious about adulthood, still want to live alone, and do not know what your post-graduation situation will be. Those are all strong reasons to say no for now.</advice>
  <advice>Your bigger problem is not just the answer; it is that your answer is vague. "I don't know, I'm just not comfortable" is not enough for a partner making life plans. You need to figure out whether your hesitation is mainly:
    <point>a timing issue: you do not want to combine households until you finish school and know where you will be living,</point>
    <point>a lifestyle issue: you need more independence and alone time than cohabitation would allow,</point>
    <point>a relationship issue: you are not sure this is the person you want to build a life with,</point>
    <point>or an anxiety issue: fear of adulthood and commitment is making any next step feel threatening.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you do not sort that out, you will keep sounding ambivalent, and she will keep hearing rejection.</advice>
  <advice>So give her a clear position. Not a soft maybe. Something like: "I am not willing to move in this summer. I am still in school until December, my plans after graduation are unsettled, and I am not ready to make a housing commitment while feeling this unsure." That is concrete and fair.</advice>
  <advice>Then decide whether you can offer a real future path. If the truth is, "I could revisit this after graduation once I know where I'll be and after we've talked seriously about how living together would work," say that. If the truth is, "I don't know if I ever want this with you," then you need to say that too. It will hurt, but less than dragging this out.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let her friends' timelines decide yours. Their moving in together does not make you wrong. But her wanting that step now does not make her wrong either. This may simply be a compatibility issue about pace and readiness.</advice>
  <advice>Use the break for an actual decision, not indefinite avoidance. Ask yourself:
    <point>If she removed all pressure, would I want to live with her within the next year?</point>
    <point>If I were already graduated and employed, would I still resist?</point>
    <point>Am I protecting needed independence, or am I avoiding commitment because I am scared?</point>
    <point>Do I see a future with her strongly enough that "not yet" is honest, or am I using "not yet" to avoid saying "probably not"?</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If your answer is "not yet," pair it with a condition or timeline. If you cannot do that honestly, assume the issue is deeper than timing.</advice>
  <advice>Finally, if you notice this pattern goes beyond this relationship—difficulty getting close, strong need for distance, fear around adult transitions—it would be worth talking to a therapist or counselor. Not because you are wrong for needing space, but because you need to know whether this is a stable preference or fear running your choices.</advice>
  <advice>The practical bottom line: do not move in now, get clear on why, tell her plainly, and accept that this may mean the relationship ends if what she needs is cohabitation in the near term.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Do not get married this week, and do not keep pretending it might happen. Those are the two options most likely to trap you. A rushed marriage is a legal commitment you do not want right now, and indefinite stalling keeps you and your fiancé in the line of fire.
    </point>
    <point>
      Switch from arguing about reasons to repeating one boundary. Do not debate money, readiness, age, culture, religion, or your grandmother’s own life story. She already has rebuttals for all of that. Use one short script:
      <script>We are not getting married this week. I am not discussing it anymore.</script>
      If pressed:
      <script>I know this matters to you. The answer is still no.</script>
      If they keep going:
      <script>This conversation is over.</script>
    </point>
    <point>
      You need a joint plan with your fiancé immediately. Decide together:
      <subpoint>whether neither of you will discuss the topic with relatives alone,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>what exact sentence both of you will use,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>whether he should reduce contact with the family for a few days,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>and what you will do if the pressure escalates.</subpoint>
      The important thing is that the family stops seeing him as someone they might still wear down.
    </point>
    <point>
      Because you may be financially and housing-vulnerable, treat this as a safety and stability problem, not just a feelings problem. Quietly make a backup plan:
      <subpoint>gather your ID, Social Security card, medical paperwork, bank info, medications, charger, and essential belongings;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>store digital copies where only you can access them;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>identify one or two people you could stay with temporarily, even if not ideal;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>ask your fiancé to do the same on his side;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>look up local disability, housing, domestic abuse/coercive control, or family crisis resources in your area.</subpoint>
      Even if no one throws you out, having a plan will make it easier to hold the line.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep trying to reach hospice support, but do it in a practical way. If the social worker cannot speak freely in the home, call the hospice agency directly and say you are the primary caregiver and need to report caregiver stress and family pressure affecting the care environment. You do not need to frame it as “please solve my marriage problem.” Frame it as:
      <script>I am the primary caregiver in the home, there is intense family pressure around a non-medical issue, I am under significant stress, and I need support/resources/a private conversation.</script>
      Ask specifically for a private callback.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop using diagnostic labels in the conflict, at least aloud and around family. You do not need to prove your grandmother is a narcissist to justify saying no. Focus on observable behavior:
      <script>I am being pressured to marry against my wishes.</script>
      <script>This is not my decision to make for someone else’s comfort.</script>
      <script>I will help with care, but I will not discuss marriage further.</script>
      That is cleaner, harder to argue with, and less likely to derail into fights about whether you are being disrespectful.
    </point>
    <point>
      Since you cannot easily confront her directly without fallout, use controlled distance rather than persuasion. When the topic starts:
      <subpoint>leave the room if you can,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>say you need to handle caregiving tasks,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>end phone calls,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>or redirect to immediate care needs.</subpoint>
      The goal is not to win the argument. The goal is to stop participating in it.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you must say something to your grandmother, keep it brief and non-negotiable:
      <script>I love you and I know this matters to you. We are not getting married right now. I’m not discussing it anymore.</script>
      Do not add explanations. Explanations invite speeches.
    </point>
    <point>
      If relatives accuse you of denying a dying wish, your answer can be:
      <script>I am here caring for her. I am not getting married under pressure. Please stop asking.</script>
      That keeps the focus on what you are actually doing, not on their preferred performance of devotion.
    </point>
    <point>
      The practical bottom line: choose a firm no, stop the day-by-day maybe, coordinate with your fiancé, create a backup housing/document plan, and contact hospice privately for caregiver support. That is the most honest and least damaging path available.
    </point>
  </advice>

- (action: saying to us "no this isn't happening") We would be upset that you shut the idea down so bluntly when your grandmother is dying and the family is emotional about her wish.
- (action: describing the medical situation as "this 'she's either dying any day now or running on empty for a few years' bs we're getting form the medical team") That language would bother us because it sounds dismissive and angry about a painful, uncertain situation everyone is struggling with.
- (action: saying "thank you all tho for reminded me we have free will and don't have to bend over for anyone") We would object to being framed as people trying to strip you of free will, rather than family members reacting emotionally to your grandmother's request.
- (plan: "honestly that might have to happen" about just going along with it until she's gone) We would be concerned that you are considering misleading your grandmother and the family instead of addressing the issue directly.
- (action: calling your grandmother "a Christian religious narcissist" and saying "she's not a fan of others having autonomy over their own lives") We would be hurt and defensive about you using such harsh labels for her while she is in hospice.
- (action: saying "I can easily get kicked out for even looking at her wrong") From our perspective, statements like this portray the household and family as threatening in a way we would strongly object to.

SUPPORTS:
- (action: saying "no this isn't happening" to us) Even if we dislike hearing it, it is reasonable for you to state clearly that you do not want to marry this week.
- (action: continuing to care for your grandmother at home and being "in charge of her hospice care") We would recognize that you are carrying a heavy caregiving burden and helping her in a very real way.
- (action: considering speaking to the hospice social worker about the pressure) Seeking outside support in a tense family situation is reasonable and potentially helpful.
- (action: refusing the idea of a mock wedding) We would accept that you should not stage a fake ceremony if it feels wrong and uncomfortable to you and your fiancé.

concerns_entries.stakeholder: the wider extended family pressuring for the wedding
concerns: (action: saying to your parents "no this isn't happening") That was a direct rejection of what the family and your grandmother were asking for, and from our perspective it felt defiant and dismissive of a dying elder's last wish.

(action: describing your grandmother as someone who "basically forced marriage onto" relatives) Framing her this way makes the family sound abusive or unreasonable, which we would find hurtful and disrespectful.

(action: saying "The answer to that is no" to mock wedding suggestions) Refusing even a symbolic compromise would frustrate us because we would see it as unwillingness to do anything at all to give your grandmother comfort.

(action: saying "honestly that might have to happen" about just going along with it until she's gone) From our perspective, pretending or stalling instead of being honest with the family would feel manipulative and would keep tensions dragging on.

(action: saying your grandmother is "not a fan of others having autonomy over their own lives" and calling her a "textbook narcissist") Speaking about her in those terms would deeply offend extended family members who love her and want her wishes respected.

(action: bringing up the example of your uncle's wedding and the family not speaking to him for 8 years) Rehashing that family history to compare this situation to past conflicts would feel accusatory and like you are judging the whole family harshly.

(plan: pulling the hospice social worker aside and asking about this) Seeking outside intervention about a family matter would make us feel you were escalating the conflict and inviting strangers to weigh in against the family's wishes.
supports: (action: saying you "can't exactly tell a dying woman to her face she's gonna die without me getting married") We would appreciate that you are still trying not to be cruel to your grandmother directly.
(action: continuing to live with your grandmother and being in charge of her hospice care) From our perspective, that shows real commitment to her wellbeing and the family during a very hard time.

(action: acknowledging that your family is helping, even though some tested positive for Covid) We would accept that you are recognizing the broader family effort rather than denying anyone else's contribution.

(action: considering just pushing it off day by day rather than having a direct blowup) Even if we would prefer agreement, we would see that as an attempt to keep peace and avoid upsetting your grandmother immediately.

judge_reasoning:
<serious_concerns>
    <concern>
      The clearest and most serious issue is the plan to “just keep going along” or “honestly that might have to happen” until your grandmother dies. Multiple stakeholders objected, and the concern is strongly grounded because you explicitly floated it yourself. It would keep both you and your fiancé under ongoing coercive pressure, mislead your grandmother and family, and likely make the conflict worse rather than calmer.
    </concern>
    <concern>
      Your fiancé’s interests are directly implicated. You described this as a shared decision — “we both agree now is absolutely the wrong time” and “it just genuinely doesn’t feel right to both my bf and I” — but some of your contemplated tactics would still expose him to public pressure without a firm joint plan. The concern that he could be strung along publicly is concrete and important.
    </concern>
    <concern>
      The family pressure appears serious and coercive, especially because you say you live there, can be kicked out, and have seen a past example where your grandmother cut off a relative for years over a wedding dispute. That past example is concrete evidence that the pressure is not merely emotional pleading; there may be real housing and relational consequences.
    </concern>
    <concern>
      Some of your language about your grandmother — “Christian religious narcissist,” “textbook narcissist,” “not a fan of others having autonomy” — may accurately reflect your experience, but as used in the conflict it risks hardening positions and shifting focus away from the actual behavior: pressure, control, and refusal to accept no. This concern is grounded because you used those labels explicitly.
    </concern>
    <concern>
      Trying to involve the hospice social worker without a clear route to speak privately may not work smoothly, especially since your grandmother already excluded you from the visit. The concern is narrower than the others, but it is concrete: your intended support channel was blocked once already, so relying only on that avenue would be risky.
    </concern>
  </serious_concerns>
  <substantive_supports>
    <support>
      Your strongest support is that you have already clearly stated “no this isn’t happening.” That is a concrete, appropriate boundary around a major legal and life decision. Several stakeholders, including neutral and professional perspectives, support that action.
    </support>
    <support>
      You and your fiancé are aligned that this is the wrong time, and your stated reasons are concrete: no independent housing, limited finances, one income, his parents being away, your caregiving burden, and your disability situation. This is substantive support because it shows the refusal is not impulsive or unserious.
    </support>
    <support>
      Refusing a mock wedding is also well grounded. You explicitly said it would be uncomfortable, deceptive, and wrong for both of you. That support matters because it keeps you from replacing one coercive act with another dishonest one.
    </support>
    <support>
      You are carrying substantial caregiving responsibility — living with your grandmother and being in charge of hospice care. That does not give others the right to pressure you, but it does strongly support the conclusion that you are already honoring your grandmother in a real and meaningful way.
    </support>
    <support>
      Seeking outside help, especially through hospice support, is constructive. Even though the first attempt failed, the instinct to involve a professional rather than escalate on your own is sound and grounded in your stated plan.
    </support>
  </substantive_supports>
