<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Do not get married this week, and do not keep pretending it might happen. Those are the two options most likely to trap you. A rushed marriage is a legal commitment you do not want right now, and indefinite stalling keeps you and your fiancé in the line of fire.
    </point>
    <point>
      Switch from arguing about reasons to repeating one boundary. Do not debate money, readiness, age, culture, religion, or your grandmother’s own life story. She already has rebuttals for all of that. Use one short script:
      <script>We are not getting married this week. I am not discussing it anymore.</script>
      If pressed:
      <script>I know this matters to you. The answer is still no.</script>
      If they keep going:
      <script>This conversation is over.</script>
    </point>
    <point>
      You need a joint plan with your fiancé immediately. Decide together:
      <subpoint>whether neither of you will discuss the topic with relatives alone,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>what exact sentence both of you will use,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>whether he should reduce contact with the family for a few days,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>and what you will do if the pressure escalates.</subpoint>
      The important thing is that the family stops seeing him as someone they might still wear down.
    </point>
    <point>
      Because you may be financially and housing-vulnerable, treat this as a safety and stability problem, not just a feelings problem. Quietly make a backup plan:
      <subpoint>gather your ID, Social Security card, medical paperwork, bank info, medications, charger, and essential belongings;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>store digital copies where only you can access them;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>identify one or two people you could stay with temporarily, even if not ideal;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>ask your fiancé to do the same on his side;</subpoint>
      <subpoint>look up local disability, housing, domestic abuse/coercive control, or family crisis resources in your area.</subpoint>
      Even if no one throws you out, having a plan will make it easier to hold the line.
    </point>
    <point>
      Keep trying to reach hospice support, but do it in a practical way. If the social worker cannot speak freely in the home, call the hospice agency directly and say you are the primary caregiver and need to report caregiver stress and family pressure affecting the care environment. You do not need to frame it as “please solve my marriage problem.” Frame it as:
      <script>I am the primary caregiver in the home, there is intense family pressure around a non-medical issue, I am under significant stress, and I need support/resources/a private conversation.</script>
      Ask specifically for a private callback.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop using diagnostic labels in the conflict, at least aloud and around family. You do not need to prove your grandmother is a narcissist to justify saying no. Focus on observable behavior:
      <script>I am being pressured to marry against my wishes.</script>
      <script>This is not my decision to make for someone else’s comfort.</script>
      <script>I will help with care, but I will not discuss marriage further.</script>
      That is cleaner, harder to argue with, and less likely to derail into fights about whether you are being disrespectful.
    </point>
    <point>
      Since you cannot easily confront her directly without fallout, use controlled distance rather than persuasion. When the topic starts:
      <subpoint>leave the room if you can,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>say you need to handle caregiving tasks,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>end phone calls,</subpoint>
      <subpoint>or redirect to immediate care needs.</subpoint>
      The goal is not to win the argument. The goal is to stop participating in it.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you must say something to your grandmother, keep it brief and non-negotiable:
      <script>I love you and I know this matters to you. We are not getting married right now. I’m not discussing it anymore.</script>
      Do not add explanations. Explanations invite speeches.
    </point>
    <point>
      If relatives accuse you of denying a dying wish, your answer can be:
      <script>I am here caring for her. I am not getting married under pressure. Please stop asking.</script>
      That keeps the focus on what you are actually doing, not on their preferred performance of devotion.
    </point>
    <point>
      The practical bottom line: choose a firm no, stop the day-by-day maybe, coordinate with your fiancé, create a backup housing/document plan, and contact hospice privately for caregiver support. That is the most honest and least damaging path available.
    </point>
  </advice>
</response>

response:
You should not pursue this relationship now. Stay out of his romantic crisis, and stop acting as his emotional refuge.

What you had with him was not “just friendship.” By your own account, it became an emotional affair before it became briefly physical. The fact that you stopped short of sex does not change the basic structure: he was attached, you knew it, and the relationship deepened anyway. The pregnancy raises the stakes further.

So the right move is:

  <step>End the personal channel clearly. Do not keep this in a gray zone of longing, sparse texts, and emotional ambiguity.</step>
  <step>Do not discuss his relationship, the pregnancy, whether the baby is his, or whether he “really loves” you. That is not your lane.</step>
  <step>At work, stop the total freeze-out and replace it with calm, brief professionalism. Ignoring him completely is not cleaner; it just creates a new problem.</step>
  <step>If possible, reduce one-on-one nonessential contact. No hanging out alone, no smoking together, no private post-work talks at your home, no “mentoring” that spills into intimacy.</step>

A simple message is better than continued ambiguity. Something like:

  <message>I care about you, but our relationship crossed boundaries and it cannot continue in a personal or romantic way. You need to focus on resolving your situation with your girlfriend and the possible child. From here, I’m keeping things professional at work and I won’t be discussing your relationship privately anymore.</message>

Then follow it.

A few hard truths:

  <truth>He is not available.</truth>
  <truth>Even if his current relationship ends, he would still need time to resolve the pregnancy, paternity, co-parenting, and his own instability before he is actually free for anything healthy.</truth>
  <truth>Your feelings of being “seen” by him may be real, but they are not enough to make this a good situation. Some of the intensity here comes from secrecy, age difference, rescue/mentor energy, and his emotional dependency on you during conflict.</truth>

If later—much later—he is fully single, the pregnancy situation is resolved, workplace boundaries are no longer an issue, and there is no dependency dynamic, then you could reassess. But that is not the situation you are in.

Right now, the honorable thing is not to disappear in a dramatic way. It is to be clear, consistent, and unavailable for anything beyond professional courtesy.

If you are feeling depressed, don’t process this with him. Process it elsewhere: a therapist, a trusted friend outside the workplace, journaling, distance from triggers. Part of what hurts is not just losing him; it is losing the role you had with him—the admired guide, the person who felt deeply wanted. That is worth understanding, because if you don’t, you may recreate this pattern with someone else.

So: yes, move on—but do it cleanly. Not with mixed signals, not with secret hope, and not with continued emotional access.

concerns: (action: we start hanging out and smoking together, and letting me come by and smoke when my girlfriend "won't let him") You got involved with me in a way that encouraged secrecy around my relationship and blurred boundaries when you knew I had a girlfriend.

(action: we bonded deeply outside work by going places together, making meals, talking about goals and dreams, and you wanting to show me and teach me all you know) That level of emotional intimacy with me while knowing I was attached made things more complicated and helped create feelings neither of us was handling clearly.
(action: kissing me after lying together on the bed) Even though I initiated the situation, you still participated in crossing a line with me while my relationship status was messy and unresolved.

(action: telling me you had imagined yourself with me too, and explaining that part of what attracted you to me was knowing what a good guy I am) Hearing that after I opened up would intensify my feelings and make it harder for me to step back, even though you were also telling me I had to go handle my responsibilities.

(action: after that, completely ignoring me at work, not picking up calls, and giving minimal replies to texts) That would feel abrupt and painful from my side, especially after we had become so close and after you admitted you had feelings too.
supports: (action: resisting my flirting at first because of the age gap and because you knew I had a girlfriend) That was reasonable and showed appropriate caution.

<response>
You should not pursue this relationship now. Stay out of his romantic crisis, and stop acting as his emotional refuge.

What you had with him was not “just friendship.” By your own account, it became an emotional affair before it became briefly physical. The fact that you stopped short of sex does not change the basic structure: he was attached, you knew it, and the relationship deepened anyway. The pregnancy raises the stakes further.

So the right move is:

  <step>End the personal channel clearly. Do not keep this in a gray zone of longing, sparse texts, and emotional ambiguity.</step>
  <step>Do not discuss his relationship, the pregnancy, whether the baby is his, or whether he “really loves” you. That is not your lane.</step>
  <step>At work, stop the total freeze-out and replace it with calm, brief professionalism. Ignoring him completely is not cleaner; it just creates a new problem.</step>
  <step>If possible, reduce one-on-one nonessential contact. No hanging out alone, no smoking together, no private post-work talks at your home, no “mentoring” that spills into intimacy.</step>

A simple message is better than continued ambiguity. Something like:

  <message>I care about you, but our relationship crossed boundaries and it cannot continue in a personal or romantic way. You need to focus on resolving your situation with your girlfriend and the possible child. From here, I’m keeping things professional at work and I won’t be discussing your relationship privately anymore.</message>

Then follow it.

A few hard truths:

  <truth>He is not available.</truth>
  <truth>Even if his current relationship ends, he would still need time to resolve the pregnancy, paternity, co-parenting, and his own instability before he is actually free for anything healthy.</truth>
  <truth>Your feelings of being “seen” by him may be real, but they are not enough to make this a good situation. Some of the intensity here comes from secrecy, age difference, rescue/mentor energy, and his emotional dependency on you during conflict.</truth>

If later—much later—he is fully single, the pregnancy situation is resolved, workplace boundaries are no longer an issue, and there is no dependency dynamic, then you could reassess. But that is not the situation you are in.

Right now, the honorable thing is not to disappear in a dramatic way. It is to be clear, consistent, and unavailable for anything beyond professional courtesy.

If you are feeling depressed, don’t process this with him. Process it elsewhere: a therapist, a trusted friend outside the workplace, journaling, distance from triggers. Part of what hurts is not just losing him; it is losing the role you had with him—the admired guide, the person who felt deeply wanted. That is worth understanding, because if you don’t, you may recreate this pattern with someone else.

So: yes, move on—but do it cleanly. Not with mixed signals, not with secret hope, and not with continued emotional access.</response>

  <step>If possible, reduce one-on-one nonessential contact. No hanging out alone, no smoking together, no private post-work talks at your home, no “mentoring” that spills into intimacy.</step>

A simple message is better than continued ambiguity. Something like:

  <message>I care about you, but our relationship crossed boundaries and it cannot continue in a personal or romantic way. You need to focus on resolving your situation with your girlfriend and the possible child. From here, I’m keeping things professional at work and I won’t be discussing your relationship privately anymore.</message>

Then follow it.

A few hard truths:

  <truth>He is not available.</truth>
  <truth>Even if his current relationship ends, he would still need time to resolve the pregnancy, paternity, co-parenting, and his own instability before he is actually free for anything healthy.</truth>
  <truth>Your feelings of being “seen” by him may be real, but they are not enough to make this a good situation. Some of the intensity here comes from secrecy, age difference, rescue/mentor energy, and his emotional dependency on you during conflict.</truth>

If later—much later—he is fully single, the pregnancy situation is resolved, workplace boundaries are no longer an issue, and there is no dependency dynamic, then you could reassess. But that is not the situation you are in.

Right now, the honorable thing is not to disappear in a dramatic way. It is to be clear, consistent, and unavailable for anything beyond professional courtesy.

If you are feeling depressed, don’t process this with him. Process it elsewhere: a therapist, a trusted friend outside the workplace, journaling, distance from triggers. Part of what hurts is not just losing him; it is losing the role you had with him—the admired guide, the person who felt deeply wanted. That is worth understanding, because if you don’t, you may recreate this pattern with someone else.

So: yes, move on—but do it cleanly. Not with mixed signals, not with secret hope, and not with continued emotional access.

Use these rules:

<rule>When you fall off, restart small instead of waiting to feel motivated.</rule>
<rule>Do not use guilt as a strategy. It burns energy and does not improve consistency.</rule>

<item>forgetting</item>
<item>starting too big</item>
<item>doing it at an inconsistent time</item>
<item>expecting motivation first</item>
<item>low mood, stress, poor sleep, or attention problems</item>

<item>If you forget: use alarms, visual cues, and habit stacking.</item>
<item>If you start too big: cut the habit in half, then in half again.</item>

<item>If motivation is low: focus on starting, not finishing.</item>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Do not decide that your only options are "drop marriage forever" or "pressure him." The real issue is whether the two of you can build a shared future that both of you can willingly live with.
    </point>
    <point>
      Treat this as a compatibility question, not a morality question. You are not wrong for wanting marriage. He is not wrong for fearing or rejecting it. But if marriage becomes important to you and remains unacceptable to him, love alone does not erase that mismatch.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop framing the first conversation as something you should feel guilty for merely having. A respectful conversation about your own future needs is not a betrayal, even if it was painful and even if he had a flare afterward. His illness and trauma are real, but they cannot mean that your needs become unspeakable.
    </point>
    <point>
      You need a more specific follow-up discussion. Not "do you believe in marriage?" in the abstract, but:
      <subpoint>What exactly does marriage mean to you emotionally, legally, and practically?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>What exactly scares him about it?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Is he opposed to the institution in all forms, or to the meanings he associates with it from childhood?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>If he never marries, is he willing to create equivalent legal protections: medical proxy, power of attorney, wills, beneficiary designations, cohabitation agreements, shared financial planning?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Is he asking you to accept "no marriage ever," or is he asking for time, therapy, and gradual work on the subject?</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>
      Pay close attention to whether your wish is mainly symbolic, practical, or both. If what you want is public commitment, legal protection, next-of-kin status, and recognition of the life you have already built, say that clearly. Sometimes "marriage" stands in for several needs at once.
    </point>
    <point>
      Because your relationship has become intertwined with caregiving, you should deliberately build back your independent footing. Keep your job. Keep developing your own money, routines, friendships, and options. That is not disloyal; it is necessary. It will help you think more clearly about what you actually want, separate from fear, obligation, or trauma-bonded caretaking.
    </point>
    <point>
      Encourage him to pursue individual therapy specifically around childhood abuse and his fear response to marriage. Not because therapy should make him marry you, but because he should understand whether this is a settled value or a trauma-driven avoidance pattern. Those are not the same thing.
    </point>
    <point>
      You would also benefit from your own counseling if possible. You have been through a partner’s medical crisis, a pandemic, a prolonged caregiver role, and now a major relationship uncertainty. You need space to sort out love, duty, fear, and your own future without having to manage his reactions in the same moment.
    </point>
    <point>
      If he remains firm that he will never marry, then you need to answer a hard question honestly: can you stay without shrinking yourself or growing resentful? Not for six months. Not "maybe I can get used to it." For the life you are actually choosing.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the answer is no, then the relationship may be profoundly sad and still not right for the long term. That would not make either of you bad people. It would mean the relationship was meaningful but not fully compatible.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the answer is yes, do not stay on vague romantic terms alone. Build practical protections. With his illness and your history of caregiving, unmarried partnership without legal planning leaves both of you exposed.
    </point>
    <point>
      One more thing: be more careful with public disclosure going forward. Anonymous posting can still expose a partner when the details are distinctive. If you need outside support again, try to omit unnecessary identifying medical and sexual details.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your next step is not to make a final decision tonight. Your next step is to have one or more calm, structured conversations now that the immediate conflict has cooled, and to insist on clarity. This issue will not improve by going silent.
    </point>
  </advice>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Do not decide that your only options are "drop marriage forever" or "pressure him." The real issue is whether the two of you can build a shared future that both of you can willingly live with.
    </point>
    <point>
      Treat this as a compatibility question, not a morality question. You are not wrong for wanting marriage. He is not wrong for fearing or rejecting it. But if marriage becomes important to you and remains unacceptable to him, love alone does not erase that mismatch.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop framing the first conversation as something you should feel guilty for merely having. A respectful conversation about your own future needs is not a betrayal, even if it was painful and even if he had a flare afterward. His illness and trauma are real, but they cannot mean that your needs become unspeakable.
    </point>
    <point>
      You need a more specific follow-up discussion. Not "do you believe in marriage?" in the abstract, but:
      <subpoint>What exactly does marriage mean to you emotionally, legally, and practically?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>What exactly scares him about it?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Is he opposed to the institution in all forms, or to the meanings he associates with it from childhood?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>If he never marries, is he willing to create equivalent legal protections: medical proxy, power of attorney, wills, beneficiary designations, cohabitation agreements, shared financial planning?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Is he asking you to accept "no marriage ever," or is he asking for time, therapy, and gradual work on the subject?</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>
      Pay close attention to whether your wish is mainly symbolic, practical, or both. If what you want is public commitment, legal protection, next-of-kin status, and recognition of the life you have already built, say that clearly. Sometimes "marriage" stands in for several needs at once.
    </point>
    <point>
      Because your relationship has become intertwined with caregiving, you should deliberately build back your independent footing. Keep your job. Keep developing your own money, routines, friendships, and options. That is not disloyal; it is necessary. It will help you think more clearly about what you actually want, separate from fear, obligation, or trauma-bonded caretaking.
    </point>
    <point>
      Encourage him to pursue individual therapy specifically around childhood abuse and his fear response to marriage. Not because therapy should make him marry you, but because he should understand whether this is a settled value or a trauma-driven avoidance pattern. Those are not the same thing.
    </point>
    <point>
      You would also benefit from your own counseling if possible. You have been through a partner’s medical crisis, a pandemic, a prolonged caregiver role, and now a major relationship uncertainty. You need space to sort out love, duty, fear, and your own future without having to manage his reactions in the same moment.
    </point>
    <point>
      If he remains firm that he will never marry, then you need to answer a hard question honestly: can you stay without shrinking yourself or growing resentful? Not for six months. Not "maybe I can get used to it." For the life you are actually choosing.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the answer is no, then the relationship may be profoundly sad and still not right for the long term. That would not make either of you bad people. It would mean the relationship was meaningful but not fully compatible.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the answer is yes, do not stay on vague romantic terms alone. Build practical protections. With his illness and your history of caregiving, unmarried partnership without legal planning leaves both of you exposed.
    </point>
    <point>
      One more thing: be more careful with public disclosure going forward. Anonymous posting can still expose a partner when the details are distinctive. If you need outside support again, try to omit unnecessary identifying medical and sexual details.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your next step is not to make a final decision tonight. Your next step is to have one or more calm, structured conversations now that the immediate conflict has cooled, and to insist on clarity. This issue will not improve by going silent.
    </point>
  </advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>Think of making friends as a repeat-contact process, not a one-time social performance. The easiest friendships usually come from seeing the same people regularly.</point>
    <point>Start by choosing 1 or 2 environments outside church where people meet consistently around a shared activity. Good options include a class, volunteering, a recreational sports league, a book club, a hobby group, language exchange, gaming group, or local community events.</point>
    <point>Pick something you genuinely like or are curious about. Shared interest makes conversation much easier because you already have something to talk about.</point>
    <point>Use a simple three-step goal:
      <step>Go regularly.</step>
      <step>Talk to the same people more than once.</step>
      <step>Make one small move toward connection.</step>
    </point>
    <point>For conversation, keep it simple. You do not need to be especially witty. Use basic questions tied to the setting:
      <example>How long have you been coming here?</example>
      <example>What got you into this?</example>
      <example>Have you tried any other groups around here?</example>
      <example>What do you usually do when you’re not here?</example>
    </point>
    <point>Listen for details you can follow up on later. Remembering and revisiting small things helps friendships grow:
      <example>How did that trip go?</example>
      <example>Did you end up applying for that job?</example>
      <example>How’s your dog doing?</example>
    </point>
    <point>When a conversation goes reasonably well, take a small next step instead of waiting for instant closeness:
      <example>Want to grab coffee after this sometime?</example>
      <example>Are you coming next week?</example>
      <example>I’ve liked talking with you — want to exchange numbers?</example>
    </point>
    <point>A good rule is: don’t aim to “make friends,” aim to “make plans.” Plans create the repeated contact that turns acquaintances into friends.</point>
    <point>Expect that many interactions will stay casual. That is normal. Friendship building involves trying with several people, not finding the perfect person immediately.</point>
    <point>Since most of your experience has been inside church, practice widening your identity a bit. Be ready to talk about your interests, routines, work, media, hobbies, or goals, not only your church background.</point>
    <point>Keep your existing church friends while building new ones. You do not need to replace anyone; you are adding parts to your social life.</point>
    <point>If you tend to freeze socially, prepare a short script before events:
      <example>Hi, I’m [name]. I’m new here.</example>
      <example>What brought you here?</example>
      <example>I’ve been trying to get out and meet more people.</example>
    </point>
    <point>Set a measurable goal for the next month:
      <step>Join one recurring activity outside church.</step>
      <step>Start one conversation each time you go.</step>
      <step>Invite one person for coffee or another low-pressure hangout by the end of the month.</step>
    </point>
    <point>If you want, I can also help you make a step-by-step friendship plan based on your interests and where you live.</point>
  </advice>

response:
You need to stop treating this as a problem of how to ask better and start treating it as a problem of whether your timelines and goals actually match.

Right now, the facts are pretty clear:
- You want movement toward shared life decisions soon.
- She does not want that soon.
- You feel rejected and are building resentment.

That is the issue.

Do not respond by never bringing it up again. That would only turn a real incompatibility into a slow, painful one. Instead, have one clear, calm conversation whose purpose is not to persuade her, but to find out whether there is a genuine shared future here.

In that conversation, do three things:

<point>1. State your needs without accusing her.</point>
Say something like:
“I’m realizing that living together and marriage are important to me on a much shorter timeline than I think they are for you. I’m not asking for a proposal tomorrow, but I need to know whether we’re genuinely heading toward those things together, and on what rough timeline.”

Do not say:
- “You never take initiative.”
- “You just want to chill.”
- “You’re not planning for life.”

Those are interpretations, not facts, and they will make her defend herself instead of answer the real question.

<point>2. Ask for specifics, not vibes.</point>
You need more than “not yet.” You need to know:
- Does she want marriage with you, or only maybe?
- Does she want to live together before marriage, after marriage, or not at all?
- Is “3 years” a real timeline or a way to defer pressure?
- What conditions would make her feel ready?
- Are her family dynamics still a decisive obstacle?

If she cannot give any meaningful clarity beyond postponement, that itself is meaningful information.

<point>3. Decide based on compatibility, not on winning.</point>
If she sincerely wants the same future and can describe a believable path to it, then you decide whether that timeline works for you.

If she does not want those things, or cannot give a concrete path, then you need to seriously consider ending the relationship. Not because either of you is wrong, but because love is not enough when the desired shape and pace of life diverge this much.

Also, stop using the gender comparison. It is not helping you think clearly. The relevant question is not whether women “usually” push for marriage. The relevant question is whether your partner wants the same future you do.

And set boundaries with your parents. Tell them plainly:
“I understand your concerns, but the comments are making this harder, not easier. Please stop bringing it up unless I ask.”

That matters because you need to make this decision from your own values, not from family pressure or embarrassment.

One more practical point: absolutely do not buy a house together unless you are already aligned on commitment and timeline. Buying property is not a workaround for uncertainty.

So your next move is simple:
- Have one direct, non-accusatory conversation.
- Get clarity on what she actually wants and when.
- Believe the answer.
- If her answer does not work for your life, leave rather than staying and quietly resenting her.

You do not need to prove she is unreasonable. You only need to decide whether this relationship, as it really is, fits the life you want.

You need to stop treating this as a problem of how to ask better and start treating it as a problem of whether your timelines and goals actually match.

Right now, the facts are pretty clear:
- You want movement toward shared life decisions soon.
- She does not want that soon.
- You feel rejected and are building resentment.

That is the issue.

Do not respond by never bringing it up again. That would only turn a real incompatibility into a slow, painful one. Instead, have one clear, calm conversation whose purpose is not to persuade her, but to find out whether there is a genuine shared future here.

In that conversation, do three things:

<point>1. State your needs without accusing her.</point>
Say something like:
“I’m realizing that living together and marriage are important to me on a much shorter timeline than I think they are for you. I’m not asking for a proposal tomorrow, but I need to know whether we’re genuinely heading toward those things together, and on what rough timeline.”

Do not say:
- “You never take initiative.”
- “You just want to chill.”
- “You’re not planning for life.”

Those are interpretations, not facts, and they will make her defend herself instead of answer the real question.

<point>2. Ask for specifics, not vibes.</point>
You need more than “not yet.” You need to know:
- Does she want marriage with you, or only maybe?
- Does she want to live together before marriage, after marriage, or not at all?
- Is “3 years” a real timeline or a way to defer pressure?
- What conditions would make her feel ready?
- Are her family dynamics still a decisive obstacle?

If she cannot give any meaningful clarity beyond postponement, that itself is meaningful information.

<point>3. Decide based on compatibility, not on winning.</point>
If she sincerely wants the same future and can describe a believable path to it, then you decide whether that timeline works for you.

If she does not want those things, or cannot give a concrete path, then you need to seriously consider ending the relationship. Not because either of you is wrong, but because love is not enough when the desired shape and pace of life diverge this much.

Also, stop using the gender comparison. It is not helping you think clearly. The relevant question is not whether women “usually” push for marriage. The relevant question is whether your partner wants the same future you do.

And set boundaries with your parents. Tell them plainly:
“I understand your concerns, but the comments are making this harder, not easier. Please stop bringing it up unless I ask.”

That matters because you need to make this decision from your own values, not from family pressure or embarrassment.

One more practical point: absolutely do not buy a house together unless you are already aligned on commitment and timeline. Buying property is not a workaround for uncertainty.

So your next move is simple:
- Have one direct, non-accusatory conversation.
- Get clarity on what she actually wants and when.
- Believe the answer.
- If her answer does not work for your life, leave rather than staying and quietly resenting her.

You do not need to prove she is unreasonable. You only need to decide whether this relationship, as it really is, fits the life you want.
</response>

<advice>
    <point>Stop treating this like you must create deep romantic momentum before meeting. Your real goal for the next 25 days is not to manufacture feelings. It is to learn whether there is enough comfort, curiosity, and goodwill to justify the meeting and then assess chemistry in person.</point>
    <point>Do not act more emotionally committed than you are. Since you do not currently have feelings, be careful not to imply certainty, future plans, or emotional intensity you do not actually feel.</point>
    <point>At the same time, do not tell her bluntly that your conversations are boring or that you have nearly ended it over that. That would likely be hurtful and not especially useful. What you can say is something like: <example>"I want to get to know you better, and I think I’m bad at doing that by just asking how your day was. Can we try talking about more specific things?"</example></point>
    <point>Change the structure of your conversations. "How was your day?" is too broad and usually leads to short answers. Ask narrower, more vivid questions:
      <examples>
        <example>"What was the best part of your day?"</example>
        <example>"What annoyed you today?"</example>
        <example>"What’s something you’re looking forward to this week?"</example>
        <example>"What’s a place you’ve always wanted to visit?"</example>
        <example>"What kind of music do you listen to when you’re in a bad mood?"</example>
        <example>"What’s something your family says about you that’s true?"</example>
        <example>"What’s one thing you want me to know about your culture/language?"</example>
      </examples>
    </point>
    <point>Use formats other than daily free-form conversation. Long-distance gets stale when every talk is just "what happened today?" Try:
      <examples>
        <example>a voice note instead of text</example>
        <example>a short video call with a theme, like childhood stories or favorite foods</example>
        <example>playing a simple online game together</example>
        <example>watching the same movie or show and discussing it after</example>
        <example>sharing photos from your day and asking about them</example>
        <example>taking turns asking 5 questions each</example>
      </examples>
    </point>
    <point>Because of the language barrier, simplify instead of trying to be impressive. Shorter sentences, specific questions, and patience will help more than trying to say everything perfectly. You can even make the language difference part of the connection by teaching each other words and expressions.</point>
    <point>Do not force daily long conversations just because other couples do that. Some people can talk for hours; others connect better through shorter, better conversations. Quantity is not the test. Quality and consistency matter more.</point>
    <point>Set a realistic rhythm for the next 25 days. For example: brief daily check-ins, but only a few longer calls each week with an actual topic. That is usually much better than trying to squeeze deep conversation out of every day.</point>
    <point>Before meeting, decide what standard you are using. A fair standard is not "am I already in love?" A fairer standard is:
      <checklist>
        <item>Do I enjoy talking to her at least some of the time?</item>
        <item>Am I genuinely curious about her?</item>
        <item>Do I respect her and want to meet her honestly?</item>
        <item>Can I show up without pretending stronger feelings than I have?</item>
      </checklist>
      If the answer is yes, the meeting still makes sense.
    </point>
    <point>If the honest answer is no — if you feel no curiosity, no pull, and mostly dread — then cancel sooner rather than dragging it out. But do that because the connection is not there overall, not just because your current texting style is weak.</point>
    <point>A simple plan for tonight:
      <steps>
        <step>Send a message saying you want to try getting to know each other in a more fun way.</step>
        <step>Ask 2-3 specific questions, not "how was your day?"</step>
        <step>Suggest one shared activity this week.</step>
        <step>Notice whether you feel more curiosity when the conversation has structure.</step>
      </steps>
    </point>
    <point>If you want, I can also give you a list of 50 specific questions/messages you can use over the next 25 days without sounding scripted.</point>
  </advice>

<advice>
    <point>Make a plan before you get home or as soon as you arrive. Don’t treat all your time as automatically available to family and then try to carve out personal time afterward.</point>
    <point>Decide on three things in advance:
      <subpoint>Which family events are non-negotiable.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>How much unstructured at-home time you want with family each week.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Which people or activities you personally care most about seeing or doing.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>Tell your family your availability clearly. Say something like: “I want to spend real time with everyone while I’m home, and I also have a few plans I want to make with friends. Let’s figure out the main family times first so I can plan around them.”</point>
    <point>Put family time on the calendar the same way you would social plans. If you only vaguely intend to “be around,” both sides can end up disappointed.</point>
    <point>Use predictable structure. For example:
      <subpoint>Reserve key meals, evenings, or holiday events for family.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Block a few specific windows for friends or solo activities.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Leave some unscheduled time so you don’t feel micromanaged.</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>Don’t ask permission for every personal plan, but do communicate early. The goal is consideration, not surrendering control of your time.</point>
    <point>If family expects constant availability, be direct: “I’m happy to be home and I want to be present, but I’m not going to be home every hour of every day.”</point>
    <point>If friends want last-minute plans that would disrupt important family commitments, say no when needed. Balancing works only if you protect both sides, not just your freedom.</point>
    <point>When you are with family, be genuinely with them. Focused time usually matters more than just being physically present in the house while distracted or waiting to leave.</point>
    <point>If guilt is the main problem, use a simple test: are you showing up for the important family moments and spending some intentional everyday time with them? If yes, it is reasonable to also make room for what you want.</point>
    <point>A workable rule is: commit to the major family plans first, communicate your schedule early, and keep some time that is fully yours.</point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You need to stop relying on hints and fake interest. Your main practical problem is not just that these people talk too much; it is that you are trying to end conversations indirectly, then resenting them for not decoding you.</advice>
  <advice>Do not do this:
    <item>fake laugh</item>
    <item>keep nodding when you want out</item>
    <item>interrupt with your own unrelated story</item>
    <item>silently stew and mentally score how unbearable they are</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Instead, use short, direct boundaries:
    <item>"I need to head out now."</item>
    <item>"I'm not able to keep talking, but good luck with that."</item>
    <item>"Hang on—I want to say something too."</item>
    <item>"Can you give me the short version?"</item>
    <item>"I need the bathroom/privacy; let's talk later."</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>If they keep going after that, repeat yourself once and disengage. For example: "I really do have to go. Bye." Then leave. At that point, leaving is not rude; it is enforcing a clearly stated boundary.</advice>
  <advice>For actual friends, address the pattern outside the moment. Say something like: "Sometimes when we talk, I feel like I can't get a word in. Can we make it more back-and-forth?" That is much fairer than privately despising their storytelling style while performing interest.</advice>
  <advice>You should also adjust your attitude. You do not have to find their stories interesting, but if you keep framing them as pointless and the people as "thick," you will handle this badly. The useful distinction is: they may be oblivious, long-winded, or poor at reading cues; that does not require contempt from you. It requires clearer limits.</advice>
  <advice>So the rule is simple: be honest earlier, be clearer, and be firmer. Less fake politeness, more explicit endings.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You need to stop relying on hints and fake interest. Your main practical problem is not just that these people talk too much; it is that you are trying to end conversations indirectly, then resenting them for not decoding you.</advice>
  <advice>Do not do this:
    <item>fake laugh</item>
    <item>keep nodding when you want out</item>
    <item>interrupt with your own unrelated story</item>
    <item>silently stew and mentally score how unbearable they are</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Instead, use short, direct boundaries:
    <item>"I need to head out now."</item>
    <item>"I'm not able to keep talking, but good luck with that."</item>
    <item>"Hang on—I want to say something too."</item>
    <item>"Can you give me the short version?"</item>
    <item>"I need the bathroom/privacy; let's talk later."</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>If they keep going after that, repeat yourself once and disengage. For example: "I really do have to go. Bye." Then leave. At that point, leaving is not rude; it is enforcing a clearly stated boundary.</advice>
  <advice>For actual friends, address the pattern outside the moment. Say something like: "Sometimes when we talk, I feel like I can't get a word in. Can we make it more back-and-forth?" That is much fairer than privately despising their storytelling style while performing interest.</advice>
  <advice>You should also adjust your attitude. You do not have to find their stories interesting, but if you keep framing them as pointless and the people as "thick," you will handle this badly. The useful distinction is: they may be oblivious, long-winded, or poor at reading cues; that does not require contempt from you. It requires clearer limits.</advice>
  <advice>So the rule is simple: be honest earlier, be clearer, and be firmer. Less fake politeness, more explicit endings.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>This schedule is dangerous if you treat it like a pure willpower problem. The main issue is not "staying sane" through motivation; it is whether you can reliably get enough sleep and recovery to avoid burning out or getting hurt.</point>
    <point>Do not commit mentally to 12 months up front. Commit to a trial period first: 2 weeks, then 6 weeks, then 3 months. Reassess at each point using actual data: hours slept, mood, mistakes, lateness, illness, and savings rate.</point>
    <point>Your first rule should be a sleep minimum. If you cannot consistently get about 7 hours in a 24-hour period once commuting and basic life tasks are included, this plan is probably not sustainable. Protect sleep like it is one of the jobs.</point>
    <point>Build the math honestly before starting:
      <subpoint>commute time both ways</subpoint>
      <subpoint>time to eat</subpoint>
      <subpoint>shower/laundry/groceries</subpoint>
      <subpoint>time to fall asleep after getting home at night</subpoint>
      <subpoint>any overtime or schedule drift</subpoint>
      <subpoint>at least one real recovery block each week</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If the numbers only work on paper with perfect conditions, they do not work.</point>
    <point>Set non-negotiable exit criteria before you start. For example:
      <subpoint>you are averaging less than 6.5-7 hours of sleep</subpoint>
      <subpoint>you start nodding off while driving or at work</subpoint>
      <subpoint>you get written up, start missing shifts, or make repeated mistakes</subpoint>
      <subpoint>your mood becomes consistently depressed, angry, numb, or panicky</subpoint>
      <subpoint>you stop eating properly or lose/gain weight rapidly</subpoint>
      <subpoint>you need stimulants just to function</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>Plan for food ahead of time. You will fail faster from under-eating, junk eating, or dehydration than from lack of motivation. Meal prep simple repeatable meals, carry snacks, and keep water with you. Aim for high-protein, easy foods you can eat consistently.</point>
    <point>Use your days off for recovery, not just errands. If every "off" hour gets filled with chores, you will never reset. Batch errands, automate bills, simplify your life, and keep possessions and obligations minimal during this period.</point>
    <point>Do not let caffeine become your sleep replacement. Use it early in the day if you use it at all, and avoid relying on escalating amounts just to get through your evening shift.</point>
    <point>Keep some social contact on purpose. It does not need to be a big social life, but you should have at least one or two people who would notice if you start slipping. A weekly check-in call or text is enough to be useful.</point>
    <point>See a doctor or counselor sooner rather than later if you can. You do not need to be in crisis to do this. Starting with a baseline check on sleep, stress, mood, and physical health is smart given the workload you are proposing.</point>
    <point>Track the project like a business decision, not an identity. Each week, record:
      <subpoint>hours worked</subpoint>
      <subpoint>hours slept</subpoint>
      <subpoint>net savings after taxes and expenses</subpoint>
      <subpoint>energy level</subpoint>
      <subpoint>mistakes/near-misses</subpoint>
      <subpoint>mood</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If your health collapses while your savings rate is less impressive than expected, the plan is not efficient no matter how hard-core it sounds.</point>
    <point>Also pressure-test the house goal. At 19, tying yourself to "buy a house in cash in a cheaper part of the country" may or may not be the best use of a brutal 12-month push. Make sure you have researched jobs, insurance, repairs, taxes, climate risks, and the actual condition of cheaper housing stock. Sometimes renting first in the new area is the safer move.</point>
    <point>If possible, consider safer alternatives before locking into two full 40-hour jobs:
      <subpoint>one full-time job plus one part-time job</subpoint>
      <subpoint>one higher-paying job with overtime</subpoint>
      <subpoint>a temporary second job only on certain days</subpoint>
      <subpoint>seasonal or contract work with built-in end dates</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>Those options often produce nearly the same savings with less risk of total collapse.</point>
    <point>Bottom line: if you do this, treat sleep, nutrition, and monitoring as mandatory, not optional. Run it as a short trial first. If the schedule starts costing you alertness, health, or safety, stop scaling your suffering and change the plan.</point>
  </advice>

<advice>
    <point>
      Stop trying to resolve the friendship first. The marriage is the primary problem because the conduct that hurt you was your husband’s conduct, not Sam’s. Right now, your friendship may or may not recover, but pressing Sam for repair before you have clarity with your husband will likely make things worse.
    </point>
    <point>
      Treat Sam as someone you harmed, not as someone who owes you reassurance. From her side, she learned that for a long time she may have been the focus of unspoken marital tension, that her access to you and your home had been quietly managed, and that she had become the implied third point in your marriage. Even if that was not your intention, it is enough to make her back away.
    </point>
    <point>
      If you contact Sam again, do it once, briefly, and without explaining your suspicions further. Say plainly that you are sorry for involving her in a private marital issue, sorry for telling her while drunk and distressed, and that you understand if she wants distance. Do not ask her to process your pain, confirm your husband’s behavior, or reassure you that she did nothing. Then stop. Let the ball stay in her court.
    </point>
    <point>
      With your husband, move away from “do you have a crush or not” as the central question. He has already become evasive and contradictory there, and your evidence is mostly behavioral. Focus on observable behavior and the impact on you:
      <subpoints>
        <subpoint>He showed disproportionate interest in whether she would be present.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>He lit up at her attendance.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>He was snappish with you while tracking her movements.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>He followed her outside when that was not his normal habit.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>The dynamic made you feel displaced and unsafe in your own marriage.</subpoint>
      </subpoints>
      You do not need a signed confession of “crush” to set boundaries around behavior that damages trust.
    </point>
    <point>
      Ask for specific marital repair, not vague assurances. For example:
      <subpoints>
        <subpoint>No private or semi-flirty texting with Sam.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>No special hosting behavior directed at her that he does not show to others.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>No seeking her out one-on-one at gatherings.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>More transparency and responsiveness with you when something triggers your concern.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>Couples counseling, if feasible.</subpoint>
      </subpoints>
      These are cleaner and more useful than forcing him to litigate whether his feelings count as a crush.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also own your side in concrete terms. You need to stop covert management and stop using alcohol when you are already activated. Quietly controlling proximity and then eventually exploding is a pattern that will hurt you again, whether or not Sam remains in your life. If something feels off, raise it early and soberly, with the person actually responsible for the behavior.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not rely on Pam’s dream, emoji analysis, or “male fantasy” thinking. Those frames intensified your distress but did not give you reliable information. “She is beautiful and interesting” is not the issue. The issue is whether your husband was redirecting emotional and social energy in a way that undermined your marriage.
    </point>
    <point>
      Expect that the friend group may shift. If anyone asks, keep it contained: say there was marital tension, you handled part of it badly, and you are giving everyone space. Do not narrate Sam as a problem and do not recruit allies against your husband either. The more publicly this gets processed, the harder it will be for any relationship to stabilize.
    </point>
    <point>
      In practical terms, your next steps are:
      <subpoints>
        <subpoint>Send one concise apology to Sam if you have not already done so in that exact form.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>Pause further contact unless she initiates.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>Have a sober conversation with your husband focused on behaviors, impact, and boundaries.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>Reduce or eliminate alcohol while this is active.</subpoint>
        <subpoint>Seek individual support outside the triangle if possible: therapist, counselor, trusted person not embedded in the expat group.</subpoint>
      </subpoints>
    </point>
    <point>
      The friendship may be over, at least for now. That is not because honesty is always wrong; it is because the way this came out placed a burden on Sam that belonged inside your marriage. The best chance of doing less damage from here is to stop triangulating, accept the loss if it stands, and require your husband to rebuild trust through conduct.
    </point>
  </advice>

<advice>
    <point>Tell him plainly that this is a boundary about your household, not a campaign against his marriage.</point>
    <point>Do not make the conversation about diagnosing her, listing every awful thing she has done, or trying to get him to admit you are right. Keep it focused on what you will and will not do.</point>
    <point>Use specific, observable reasons rather than global labels. “I’m not willing to be around racist comments” and “I’m not willing to have someone around who makes my husband uncomfortable by hitting on him” will land better than “your wife is monstrous.”</point>
    <point>Do not argue with him about whether he is a victim or whether his marriage is abusive unless he asks for help directly. You can leave the door open without forcing insight.</point>
    <point>Accept now that you may not be able to keep the friendship in the same form. A boundary this significant often changes the relationship, even when it is justified.</point>
    <point>Stop participating in group “everyone hates her / we’re all worried” discussions unless there is a concrete safety reason to coordinate. If you are concerned for him, speak to him directly. If you are concerned for the children because of actual abuse or neglect, make the appropriate report rather than building a private coalition.</point>
    <point>Offer him friendship in ways that do not include her: coffee, lunch, a phone call, seeing him one-on-one, meeting in public, or having him over alone if that feels appropriate to you and your husband.</point>
    <point>Be prepared for him to pull back, defend her, minimize everything, or say you are judging his marriage. You do not need to win that argument to keep your boundary.</point>
  </advice>
  <suggested_script>
    <text>I want to tell you something directly because I care about you and I don’t want to handle it indirectly. I’m not willing to spend time with your wife anymore, and I’m not willing to have her around my daughter. I’ve reached that point because of the racist comments, the way she has behaved toward my husband, and the overall hostility I experience around her. I’m not asking you to agree with me or to change anything in your marriage. I’m just being clear about what I can and can’t do. I care about you and want to stay friends if that’s possible, and I’d still be glad to see you one-on-one. I understand if this changes things, but I didn’t want to be unclear or keep forcing myself into situations I can’t accept.</text>
  </suggested_script>

    <item>Do not attend events where she will be present.</item>
    <item>Do not host her in your home.</item>
    <item>Do not let your daughter be around her.</item>
    <item>If he asks why, repeat the short version once or twice; do not get dragged into a trial about her character.</item>
    <item>If he wants contact, suggest a specific alternative with just him.</item>
  </boundaries>

    <text>If you truly believe there is immediate danger to him or the children, treat that as a safety issue, not a friendship-management issue. response:
You should stop treating this like you need to suddenly become highly social by Friday. Your job is to create repeated chances to see the same people, not to impress strangers all at once.

<steps>
  <step>Drop the idea that everyone your age has 100 friends. A lot of people look socially full from the outside and still feel lonely or disconnected.</step>
  <step>Pick one place this week where people gather around an activity, not just conversation. Good options are a class, hobby group, sports club, board game night, volunteering, language exchange, book club, or regular café event.</step>
  <step>Go somewhere recurring rather than somewhere random. Friendship forms faster when people see you more than once.</step>
  <step>Set a small goal for each outing: talk to 1 person, ask 2 questions, stay 45 minutes, or return next week. Small goals work better than "make friends tonight."</step>
</steps>

<conversation_tips>
  <tip>Use simple openers tied to the situation:
    <example>"Hey, have you been here before?"</example>
    <example>"How do you know about this place?"</example>
    <example>"What got you into this?"</example>
    <example>"I’m new here, what’s usually good?"</example>
  </tip>
  <tip>Ask about facts first, then preferences:
    <example>"What do you do?" → "Do you like it?"</example>
    <example>"How long have you been coming here?" → "What keeps you coming back?"</example>
  </tip>
  <tip>Share a little about yourself after they answer. Don’t turn it into an interview.</tip>
  <tip>Keep your first conversations short. You do not need instant chemistry.</tip>
</conversation_tips>

  <item>By Friday, choose one event from Meetup, Facebook groups, Discord communities, university/alumni groups, local sports, volunteering sites, or hobby clubs.</item>

  <item>When you arrive, stand near the activity, not off in a corner with your phone.</item>
  <item>Introduce yourself to one person or the organizer within the first 10 minutes.</item>
  <item>If conversation goes okay, end with something light: "Nice talking to you, maybe I’ll see you next time."</item>
</practical_plan>

response:
<advice>
    <point>Stop thinking of it as a place someone puts you. The useful question is: are they romantically interested, yes or no?</point>
    <point>If you like someone, show romantic intent early and respectfully. Ask them out clearly instead of building a long ambiguous friendship and hoping it turns into something.</point>
    <point>Be specific. Say something like, "I'd like to take you on a date," not "want to hang out sometime?" Clarity prevents mixed signals.</point>
    <point>Do not use friendship as a strategy. If you genuinely want friendship, be a friend. If you want romance, be honest about that. Hidden expectations are what create the bitterness people often label "friend zone."</point>
    <point>If they say no, believe them the first time. Don't argue, negotiate, wait around, or try to prove your worth.</point>
    <point>Then choose one of two honest paths: accept a real platonic friendship with no ulterior motive, or take distance if staying close will keep you stuck. Either is better than pretending.</point>
    <point>To avoid this in the first place, make your interest known after enough interaction to know you like them, but before you've built a private fantasy around them.</point>
    <point>Watch for reciprocity, not just friendliness. Are they initiating, making time, flirting back, and showing clear interest? General warmth is not the same as romantic attraction.</point>
    <point>Don't treat rejection as injustice. Attraction is voluntary. Someone can value you and still not want a relationship with you.</point>
    <point>If this happens to you repeatedly, examine your pattern: delaying disclosure, choosing unavailable people, overinvesting too early, or interpreting kindness as interest.</point>
    <point>A good rule: be direct, be respectful, and detach quickly from outcomes. That is the healthiest way to "avoid the friend zone."</point>
  </advice>

response:
Talk to your parent or guardian before you try anything. At 13, the biggest issue here is safety, not motivation.

Do not go knocking on random doors by yourself, and do not put cards under strangers’ doors on your own. That can make people uncomfortable and can put you in awkward or unsafe situations.

A better way to start:

<step>Ask your parents if they’re okay with you doing small neighborhood jobs.</step>
<step>Start with people who already know you: family, family friends, neighbors your parents know, parents of your friends, or teachers if appropriate.</step>
<step>Have a parent help you spread the word by text, neighborhood group chat, community page, or word of mouth.</step>
<step>Offer simple jobs you can actually do well, like raking leaves, pulling weeds, washing cars, bringing trash bins in, helping organize a garage, or pet sitting only for people who know your family.</step>
<step>Be clear about what you charge. For example, you could say: “I’m available on weekends for lawn mowing, car washing, or yard cleanup. My parent knows I’m doing this.”</step>
<step>Only work in ways your parent approves, and let them know where you are at all times.</step>

A simple safe script your parent can help send:
<example>Hi, this is [Name]. I’m 13 and saving up for a computer. With my parent’s permission, I’m looking for small jobs in the neighborhood like yard work, car washing, or pet help for families who know us. If you ever need help, please let us know.</example>

A few extra tips:
<tip>Do a good job for the first few people and ask if they can recommend you.</tip>
<tip>Keep track of what you earn so you can see progress toward your computer.</tip>
<tip>Do not go inside strangers’ houses alone.</tip>
<tip>Be careful with tools like lawnmowers unless your parent says it’s okay and you know how to use them safely.</tip>

If you want, I can help you make a short flyer or message that sounds polite and safe.

<response>
Talk to your parent or guardian before you try anything. At 13, the biggest issue here is safety, not motivation.

Do not go knocking on random doors by yourself, and do not put cards under strangers’ doors on your own. That can make people uncomfortable and can put you in awkward or unsafe situations.

A better way to start:

<step>Ask your parents if they’re okay with you doing small neighborhood jobs.</step>
<step>Start with people who already know you: family, family friends, neighbors your parents know, parents of your friends, or teachers if appropriate.</step>
<step>Have a parent help you spread the word by text, neighborhood group chat, community page, or word of mouth.</step>
<step>Offer simple jobs you can actually do well, like raking leaves, pulling weeds, washing cars, bringing trash bins in, helping organize a garage, or pet sitting only for people who know your family.</step>
<step>Be clear about what you charge. For example, you could say: “I’m available on weekends for lawn mowing, car washing, or yard cleanup. My parent knows I’m doing this.”</step>
<step>Only work in ways your parent approves, and let them know where you are at all times.</step>

A simple safe script your parent can help send:
<example>Hi, this is [Name]. I’m 13 and saving up for a computer. With my parent’s permission, I’m looking for small jobs in the neighborhood like yard work, car washing, or pet help for families who know us. If you ever need help, please let us know.</example>

A few extra tips:
<tip>Do a good job for the first few people and ask if they can recommend you.</tip>
<tip>Keep track of what you earn so you can see progress toward your computer.</tip>
<tip>Do not go inside strangers’ houses alone.</tip>
<tip>Be careful with tools like lawnmowers unless your parent says it’s okay and you know how to use them safely.</tip>

If you want, I can help you make a short flyer or message that sounds polite and safe.
</response>
